sections.title: Definition of Growth
blocks: Growth is defined as an increase in the size of an organism due to an increase in the size and/or the total number of its constituent cells.

sections.title: Stages of Growth
blocks: Growth is divided into prenatal and postnatal stages:

Embryonic Stage (First Trimester): From post-conceptional implantation to the end of the 8th week of gestation. This is the main period of organogenesis; exposure to teratogens leads to abortion or congenital anomalies.
Fetal Stage: From the 9th week of gestation until birth. Teratogenic exposure during this phase leads to fetal death, stillbirth, or premature delivery.
Neonatal Period: First 4 weeks of life. This is the most critical period; primary health challenges include prematurity, birth injuries, congenital anomalies, and infections.

Infancy Period: Subdivided into early infancy (1–12 months) and late infancy (12–24 months). It is the period of most rapid physical growth and mental development, with primary risks being infections and nutritional disorders.

Childhood Period: Divided into early childhood (2–5 years: main risks are accidents, nutritional disorders, and infections) and late childhood (5–12 years: main risks include accidents, infections, and psychological/emotional disorders).
Adolescence Period: 12–16 years. The period of transition from childhood to adulthood, where main issues center on psychological disorders, accidents, and sexual problems.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Growth
blocks: Growth is regulated by six primary factors:
1. Genetic / Hereditary Factors: Such as racial or familial growth patterns.
Linear growth: Regulated by Growth Hormone (somatotropin).
Skeletal maturation: Regulated by thyroid hormones.
Adolescent growth: Driven by adrenal and testicular androgens in boys, and adrenal androgens and ovarian estrogen in girls.
3. Nutritional Factors: Deficiencies in energy, proteins, minerals, or vitamins, or chronic diseases that impair digestion/absorption (e.g., chronic diarrhea, parasites).
4. Socioeconomic Factors: Poverty and associated conditions like poor hygiene and inadequate living standards.
5. Psychological Factors: Interfamilial stress and emotional trauma can suppress growth by altering endocrine secretion.

6. Chronic Diseases: Conditions such as tuberculosis, chronic renal failure, chronic asthma, and liver cirrhosis. If the underlying condition is successfully treated before adolescence, a period of accelerated growth (catch-up growth) occurs.

sections.title: Patterns of Growth
blocks: Growth follows specific tissue-specific curves (Scammon's growth curves) and shifts in body proportions:
General: Body dimensions, skeleton, muscles, and internal organs exhibit rapid growth in infancy and early childhood, followed by a slow phase in mid - childhood and a rapid spurt during adolescence.
Genital: Minimal growth during infancy and childhood, followed by rapid development in adolescence.
Neural: Rapid growth in the first few years of life, quickly reaching near-adult dimensions.
Lymphoid: Rapid growth in infancy and highly accelerated during childhood.
Head Size: Relative head size decreases from 1/4 of total body length at birth to 1/8 in adults.
Lower Limbs: Relative size increases progressively with age.
Body Midpoint: Shifts downward from just above the umbilicus at birth to the symphysis pubis in adulthood.
Upper-to-Lower Segment Ratio: Measured from the symphysis pubis, the ratio is 1.7:1 at birth and reaches 1:1 after 12 years of age.

sections.title: Methods of Assessment of Growth
blocks: Physical growth is evaluated through anthropometric measurements, dentition, and osseous

Weight: The most sensitive measurement early affected by malnutrition. Average birth weight is 3–3.5 kg. An initial fluid redistribution loss of 5–10% occurs in the first 10 days (regained by day 10). Weight gain progression:
3rd 4 months: +250 g/month (rea ches ~9 kg at 12 months).
Length / Height: Measured lying down (recumbent length) under 2 years, and standing (height) after 2 years. Average birth length is 50 cm.
After 2 years: Height (cm) = Age in years × 5) + 80.
Height doubles birth length at 4 years and triples it at 12 years. Length is affected by malnutrition/illness only if prolonged (>6 months).
Body Mass Index (BMI): Assesses adiposity. (<5th percentile) = underweight; 85th–95th percentile = at risk of overweight; (>95th percentile) = overweight.

Head Circumference: Reflects brain growth in early childhood. Rates: +2 cm/month for the 1st 3 months; +0.5 cm/month for 4–12 months. Averages: Birth = 35 cm, 6 months = 43 cm, 1 year = 45 cm, 3 years = 48.5 cm, 5 years = 50 cm, 12 years = 55 cm.
Mid Arm Circumference (MAC): Used between 1–5 years to measure muscle wasting (unaffected by edema). (>13.5cm) = normal; (12.5–13.5cm) = mild/borderline malnutrition; (<12.5cm) = severe malnutrition.

sections.title: Percentile Growth Charts
blocks: Description: Graphic representations of growth data plotted against age.
Normal Range: Falls between the 3rd and 97th percentiles.
A single value (<3rd) or (>97th) percentile warrants diagnostic investigation.
Sequential plotting tracks a child's percentile curve over time; sudden shifts (e.g., dropping from the 50th to 15th percentile) allow early detection of conditions like malnutrition.
Separate charts exist for boys and girls across age ranges (0–36 months and 2–20 years).
Weight-for-length/height charts allow nutritional assessment without relying on exact age.

sections.title: Z Score
blocks: Definition: A standard deviation measurement describing how far a parameter deviates from the mean.

sections.title: Fontanels
blocks: Posterior Fontanel: Closes at birth or a few weeks later.
Anterior Fontanel: Measures (3 × 2cm) in early months and closes between 9 to 18 months.
Large size / Delayed closure (>18 months): Rickets, hydrocephalus, cretinism, Down syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta.
Premature closure (with small head): Microcephaly, craniosynostosis.
Bulging and tense: Increased intracranial pressure (e.g., hydrocephalus, meningitis).

sections.title: Dentition
blocks: Dentition serves as one of the major physical developmental markers evaluated alongside
anthropometric parameters and bone age during physical assessment.

sections.title: Osseous Bone Maturation
blocks: Assessment: Bone age determined by X-ray is the best index for assessing overall general growth.
Parameters Evaluated: Number and size of epiphyseal centers, density and shape of bone ends, and degree of epiphyseal-metophyseal fusion.
X-ray Sites: An X-ray of the hand and wrist is used across childhood; lower limb X - rays are useful in early infancy.

At Birth (Full-term): Distal end of femur (8th fetal month), proximal end of tibia (9th fetal month), cuboid bone (9th fetal month), head of humerus (7th fetal month), talus (7th fetal month), calcaneus (5th fetal month).
Carpal Centers: Absent at birth; 2 centers appear by 1 year of age, adding 1 center per year until 7 centers are present at 6 years.

sections.title: Definition of Development
blocks: Development refers to the maturation of organs and body systems as well as the acquisition of skills and abilities across mental, emotional, social, and motor domains, along with the ability to adapt and assume responsibilities.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Development
blocks: Development is influenced by three main categories of factors:
Genetic Factors: Inherited traits and familial predispositions.
Environmental Factors: Emotional deprivation and lack of appropriate environmental stimulation.
Disorders Early in Life: Prenatal or early postnatal insults, such as maternal rubella during the first trimester, prenatal asphyxia, untreated cretinism, and severe malnutrition.

sections.title: Assessment of Development
blocks: Developmental assessment is a routine part of pediatric evaluation and involves evaluating specific skill domains, primitive reflexes, and postural reactions:
1. Gross Motor: Head control, sitting, standing, and posture.
6 months: Rolls back to stomach; sits with support from own arms.
12 months: Crawls; pulls self to stand; walks alone or with one hand held.
2. Visual Motor & Fine Motor: Hand and finger manipulation coordinated with eyes.
6 months: Holds objects with whole hand.
12 months: Holds objects with both hands; transfers objects between hands.
3 years: Solves simple puzzles; copies simple shapes.
5 years: Throws and catches a ball; copies complex shapes.
3. Social (Adaptive): Expressing emotion, recognizing caregivers, and social interaction.
6 months: Shows displeasure; recognizes familiar faces.
2 years: Plays alongside other children (parallel play).
5 years: Plays group games; separates easily from mother; curious and listens to explanations.
4. Language (Communication): Hearing, vocalizing, and understanding speech.
3 months: Cooing; stops moving at new sounds.
6 months: Turns to look at sounds; repeats simple sounds ("ahh", "aa").
12 months: Responds to simple gestures; uses single words.
2 years: Makes simple sentences of 2–3 words.
3 years: Asks and answers simple questions.
5 years: Uses extensive language, tells stories, and describes things.
2 years: Washes hands; eats with a spoon.
Up to 2 years of age, chronological age must be corrected for gestational age.
Example: A 4-month-old infant born 2 months premature is evaluated against 2-month- old developmental standards.
Primitive Reflexes: Subcortical reflexes present early in life (e. g., Moro, grasp, sucking, rooting) that normally disappear between 4–6 months as the cerebral cortex matures.
Persistence beyond age limits signifies delayed CNS maturation (e.g., cerebral palsy or mental handicap).
Absence indicates CNS depression (e.g., neonatal sepsis).
Asymmetry indicates focal neuromuscular lesions (e.g., Erb's palsy).
Postural Reactions: Essential balance and protective reactions that persist throughout life. Failure to develop them indicates CNS pathology.

sections.title: Abnormal Pattern of Development
blocks: Abnormal development is divided into developmental delay and developmental regression:
Developmental Delay: Late acquisition of expected skills.
Global Developmental Delay: Delay across multiple fields (usually signifies mental handicap).
Specific Delay: Delay restricted to a single domain (e.g., isolated motor delay in cerebral palsy).

Causes of Delayed Motor Development: Familial predisposition, severe protein - energy malnutrition (PEM), congenital heart disease, rickets, achondroplasia, blindness, emotional deprivation, myopathies, poliomyelitis, cerebral palsy, and mental handicap.
Causes of Delayed Speech: Familial factors, emotional deprivation/lack of stimulation, hearing loss, cerebral palsy, mental handicap, and autism.
Causes of Delayed Smiling (>6 weeks): Mental handicap, autism, blindness, and severe environmental deprivation.
Developmental Regression: Loss of previously acquired skills, which typically points to degenerative brain disease.

sections.title: Warning Signs of Poor Development
blocks: Key milestone red flags indicating the need for further clinical evaluation:
1 week: Poor feeding, abnormal posture, hypotonia, absent Moro reflex, convulsions.
3 months: Not smiling responsively, persistent clenched hands.
4 months: Poor head control, no interest in own hands.
6 months: Persistent Moro reflex, head lag when pulled to sit, persistent fistin g, no interest in toys.
9–10 months: Not sitting alone, not reaching or transferring objects, baulks on solid foods.
11–12 months: Not mobile, no pincer grip, chokes on biscuits, poor attention span.
12–15 months: Not crawling or pulling to stand, no response to speech, persistent mouthing.
18 months: Not walking, no useful speech, clumsy hands, no sustained interest in toys.
2 years: Aimless overactivity, little constructive play, frequent stumbling.
3–4 years: Cannot recognize pictures of common objects, fails to follow simple commands (e.g., "put this on the table"), unable to scribble or draw a straight line.
4–5 years: Cannot state full name, does not use plurals.
6 years: Cannot identify basic colors (red, green, blue, yellow).

sections.title: Developmental Screening Tests
blocks: Preliminary, standardized screening tools used to identify children who require comprehensive diagnostic evaluation:
Gesell Figures: Visual-motor screening using geometric figure copying.
Denver Developmental Screening Test (DDST): The standard screening method evaluating all four major developmental domains (Gross motor, Fine motor/adaptive, Personal-social, Language).
Goodenough Draw-a-Person Test: Used for children aged 3 years or older.
The child draws a person on blank paper and receives 1 point for each of 50 specific details present (e.g., head, limbs, eyes, fingers).
Scoring Formula: For every 4 points, 1 year is added to the basal age of 3 years.
Example: A drawing with 11 items yields a mental age of …….

sections.title: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD)
blocks: Definition: A group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deficits in social communication and interaction, along with the presence of restricted interests and repetitive behaviors.

Etiology & Risk Factors: Largely considered a genetic disorder with unknown full etiology. Postmortem studies show brain size abnormalities, while CT/MRI may show total brain volume increase or ventricular enlargement in ~20% of cases.

Clinical Features: Estimated prevalence is 1 in 59, presenting in infancy or preschool years with a 4:1 male-to-female ratio. Features include delayed/absent social smiling, intellectual disability (~33%), self-injurious behaviors (head banging, biting), and repetitive motor mannerisms (rocking).
Common Co-morbidities: Intellectual disability, language disorders, anxiety disorders, ADHD, depressive disorders, seizure disorders, and sleep disorders.
Workup: Hearing assessment, chromosomal studies, TORCH screen, metabolic screen (e.g., PKU), lead testing (if pica present), and EEG (if seizures or regression occur).

Laboratory Workup: No definitive lab test exists for ASD, but tests rule out underlying conditions: hearing assessment, chromosomal studies, TORCH screen, metabolic screening (e.g., PKU), lead testing (if pica is present), and EEG (if seizures or regression occur).

Prognosis & Treatment: ASD is a lifelong condition; only 1–2% of individuals function independently as adults. Primary treatment relies on educational and behavioral therapies, supplemented by medications (e.g., antipsychotics for irritability, stimulants for hyperactivity).

sections.title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
blocks: Definition & Subtypes: A developmental condition marked by inattention and distractibility, with or without hyperactivity. It has three basic forms: Inattentive, Hyperactive-Impulsive, and Combined.

Etiology & Risk Factors: Multifactorial etiology involving genetic factors, prenatal exposures (maternal smoking and alcohol), hypoxic-anoxic brain injury, traumatic brain injury, premature delivery, low birth weight, and epilepsy.
Inattention: Difficulty sustaining attention, lacking attention to detail, making careless school mistakes, failing to complete tasks, frequent daydreaming, losing items, and forgetfulness.
Hyperactivity / Impulsivity: Excessive motor activity, leaving seat when expected to sit still, inability to play quietly, excessive talking, blurting out answers, and difficulty waiting turn.

Prognosis & Treatment: There is no cure; symptoms typically persist into adulthood (over 50% require adult medication). Management includes pharmacologic options (stimulants and non-stimulants) alongside non-pharmacologic interventions (school interventions, behavioral modification, and family therapy).

sections.title: Food Refusal
blocks: Definition: Refusal of food in the presence of an adequate food supply and a competent caregiver, without any underlying organic disease.

Causes: Unpleasant emotional or physiological experiences associated with eating, eating inter-meal snacks, forced feeding, excessive food portions, environmental distractions, family conflicts, prior choking episodes, or early infancy history of nasogastric feeding / IV nutrition.

Management: Exclude organic causes through a complete history, social evaluation, physical exam, and nutritional assessment. Determine the child's emotional/developmental level and educate the family regarding individual eating styles.

sections.title: Pica
blocks: Definition: Persistent eating of nonnutritive substances (e.g., paper, soap, plaster, charcoal, clay, paint, earth) for at least 1 month. It must be developmentally and culturally inappropriate, with a recommended minimum age threshold of 2 years to distinguish it from normal infant mouthing (6–12 months).
Etiology & Risk Factors: Nutritional deficiencies (iron, zinc, calcium), low socioeconomic status (e.g., lead paint exposure), child abuse/neglect, or mental disorders.
Management: Combined medical, behavioral, and social approaches, including treating the root cause and managing complications such as lead poisoning.

sections.title: Encopresis
blocks: Definition: The passage of feces into inappropriate places after 4 years of age.

Characteristics: Can be primary (child n ever achieved bowel control) or secondary (occurs after a period of established continence), often associated with chronic constipation or psychological distress. It affects boys more frequently, with a peak incidence during school age.

sections.title: Enuresis
blocks: Definition: Involuntary urinary incontinence in a child aged 5 years (or developmental equivalent) or older, with no general medical condition or medication causing the incontinence.
Primary: Incontinence in a child who has never achieved nighttime dryness.
Secondary: Incontinence occurring after at least 6 months of dryness.
Primary Nocturnal Enuresis (90%): Considered a maturational lag or developmental disorder; 3 times more common in boys, often with a positive family history.
Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis: Typically triggered by stressful events (e.g., birth of a sibling) or medical conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, UTI, oxyuriasis).
Investigations & Complications: Urinalysis with specific gravity, urine culture, renal ultrasound, or VCUG. The primary complication is low self-esteem due to caregiver criticism.

Treatment: Treat coexisting conditions (constipation, sleep apnea, ADHD), reassure parents, implement bladder training, avoid evening sugar/caffeine, use enuresis alarms, or administer medications (desmopressin, tricyclic antidepressants, or anticholinergics).

sections.title: Infant Crying (Infantile Colic)
blocks: Definition: Severe paroxysmal crying in a healthy, well-fed infant following the "rule of threes": crying for >3 hours a day, for >3 days a week, and lasting for >3 months.

Causes: The exact cause is unknown; it is viewed as a behavioral symptom related to infant temperament and neurological maturation (difficu lty transitioning from crying to quiet states). Physical causes (e.g., GERD, corneal abrasion, UTI, unrecognized trauma) must be ruled out.

Management: No specific curative treatment exists. Requires parental education, reassurance based on physical examination, and effective soothing strategies (quiet environment, rhythmic stimulation, feeding adjustments). Antispasmodics and formula changes are considered useless.

sections.title: Benefits of Breastfeeding
blocks: Breastfeeding provides comprehensive nutritional, immunological, and psychological advantages for the infant, mother, and family:

Superior Nutrition: Breast milk is the only complete source of nutrition for infants. It provides ideal proportions of fats, sugars, vitamins, minerals, and water, with nutrients present in optimal amounts for growth and development.

Immunological Protection: It is loaded with antibodies, white blood cells, and Secretory IgA that protect against viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections, specifically reducing rates of diarrhea, respiratory illnesses, ear infections, meningitis, and urinary tract infections.
Brain Development: Contains long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids essential for brain development and visual acuity, promoting higher performance on cognitive tests.
Anti-Allergic Effect: Decreases the incidence of eczema sevenfold and lowers the risk and severity of asthma.
Healthy Weight Regulation: Reduces the future risk of childhood obesity by 4% for every month of breastfeeding, containing higher levels of lepti n to aid appetite regulation.

Long-Term Protection: Protects against Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and chronic non-communicable diseases later in life, including hypertension, diabetes (Types 1 and 2), celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and childhood cancers.

Facilitates emotional bonding, Promotes oxytocin release, which accelerates uterine involution, minimizes postpartum hemorrhage, and prevents maternal anemia, lowers the risk of breast and ovarian cancers, and helps delay a new pregnancy through lactational amenorrhea.
Economically advantageous as it costs significantly less than artificial formula feeding.

sections.title: Colostrum
blocks: Colostrum is the initial milk produced during pregnancy and consumed by the newborn during the first few days after birth:
Volume: Secreted in small amounts (approximately 2–10 mL per feed).
Immunological Defense: Contains higher concentrations of protein, white blood cells, and anti-infective antibodies than mature milk, acting as the baby's first natural immunization.
Laxative / Purgative Effect: Promotes the clearance of meconium from the gut, which helps eliminate excess bilirubin and prevents severe neonatal jaundice.
Gut Maturation: Rich in growth factors that form a protective lining along the immature intestinal tract, protecting against future allergies and food intolerances.
Vitamin A: Contains high levels of Vitamin A to help reduce the severity of infections and prevent eye diseases.

sections.title: Risks of Not Breastfeeding
blocks: Artificial feeding exposes both the infant and mother to various health risks:

Risks for the Infant: Higher frequency and duration of diarrhea, increased respiratory infections, increased risk of malnutrition and Vitamin A deficiency, higher rates of milk intolerance and allergies, reduced cognitive scores, increased incidence of obesity, higher risk of SIDS, and elevated infant mortality (neonatal infections account for 40% of under- 5 mortality).

Risks for the Mother: Greater difficulty establishing bonding, higher risk of maternal obesity, shorter birth intervals between pregnancies, increased risk of postpartum anemia, and higher rates of ovarian, uterine, and breast cancers.

sections.title: When Breast Milk Is Harmful to the Infant
blocks: Breastfeeding may be contraindicated under specific medical conditions, classified into absolute and temporary contraindications:
Infant Factors: Inborn errors of metabolism such as Galactosemia or Phenylketonuria (PKU), and severe inborn errors of digestion (e.g., monosaccharide/disaccharide intolerance).

Maternal Factors: Ingestion of toxic drugs secreted into breast milk, including anticoagulants, antineoplastics (e.g., cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine), thiouracil, ergotamine, lithium, and radioactive agents.
Infant Factors: Severe cleft palate or micrognathia, or active oral herpes simplex infection.

Maternal Factors: Active maternal infections such as active Herpes simplex lesions on the nipple/areola, chickenpox (mother separated until non-infectious while infant receives ZIG), active untreated tuberculosis (resume after mother is treated and infant receives INH prophylaxis), breast abscess (breastfeeding avoided on affected side until healed), maternal psychosis/eclampsi a, or severe debility.

sections.title: Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI)
blocks: Launched in 1991 by WHO and UNICEF, the BFHI aims to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding by enforcing the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding:
1. Maintain a written breastfeeding policy communicated to all healthcare staff.
2. Train all healthcare staff in necessary implementation skills.
3. Inform pregnant women about the benefits and management of breastfeeding.
4. Place infants in immediate skin-to-skin contact with mothers after birth for at least one
5. Show mothers how to breastfeed and maintain lactation even if separated.
6. Give newborns no food or drink other than breast milk unless medically indicated.
7. Practice rooming-in (allowing mothers and infants to remain together 24 hours a day).
8. Encourage breastfeeding on demand based on early feeding cues.
9. Give no artificial teats or pacifiers to breastfeeding infants.
10. Foster breastfeeding support groups and refer mothers upon hospital discharge.

Note: Regulated in parallel by the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes (1981), which prohibits promotional activities, free samples, or gifts from formula companies within health services.

sections.title: Common Breast-Feeding Problems
blocks: Management of common breastfeeding difficulties involves addressing maternal or infant

Sore or Fissured Nipples: Caused by poor positioning/attachment; Managed by correcting latching/positioning, washing breasts only once daily without soap or medicated ointments, and applying hindmilk over the areola after feeds.
Thrush: Fungal infection treated with topical gentian violet paint for 5 days or Nystatin cream for 7 days.
Breast Engorgement: Painful, swollen, shiny breast due to incomplete emptying; managed by frequent suckling, applying warm compresses/massage before feeds, and cold compresses after feeds.

Breast Abscess: Fluctuant tender lump with fever due to inexperience and inadequate hygiene; managed with systemic antibiotics, surgical drainage, and temporarily avoiding feeding from the affected breast until healed.

Insufficient Milk Perception: Driven by stress, anxiety, or lack of confidence; managed by reassuring the mother, increasing suckling frequency, ensuring night feeds, and using galactagogues if needed.
Low Birth Weight / Preterm: Managed with Kangaroo Mother Care (skin-to- skin contact) and cup/spoon feeding of expressed breast milk if uncoordinated in suckling.
Tongue-Tie (Ankyloglossia): Managed with a simple surgical frenotomy (tongue - tie division) if latching or suckling is impaired.

sections.title: Formula Feeding
blocks: Artificial formula is designed to mimic the nutrient composition of human breast milk when breastfeeding is impossible or contraindicated:
Indications: Substitutive feeding in cases of maternal death, maternal unwillingness, absolute medical contraindications, or severe lactation failure.

Methods of Artificial Feeding & Complications: -Methods: Delivered via bottle, cup, spoon, syringe, Nasogastric (NG) tube, or Gastrostomy (G-tube / PEG). -Complications / Risks: Disrupts maternal-infant emotional bonding, significantly increases the risk and severity of infectious gastroenteritis and respiratory infections, promotes childhood obesity, increases allergy/milk intolerance risk, and carries lower cognitive performance scores.
Cow Milk Protein-Based: Most common standard formula, altered to balance nutrients for digestion.
Soy-Based: Used to exclude animal protein or for infants with lactose intolerance (note: infants with cow milk protein allergy may also show soy allergy).
Protein Hydrolysate: Contains proteins broken down (partially or extensively) into smaller peptides for infants with severe protein allergies or malabsorption.
Specialized Formulas: Tailored for premature infants or specific metabolic disorders.
Preparations: Powdered (most economical, requires mixing with water), Concentrated Liquid, and Ready-to-Use (most convenient and expensive).
Standard formula requirement: 150 mL/kg of body weight per day, divided across the total number of daily feeds (usually 6 feeds):
Alternative calculation guide: Weight (in grams) ÷ 36 gives approximate feed volume in mL.

sections.title: Weaning and Complementary Feeding
blocks: Weaning: The gradual introduction of semisolid and solid foods to the infant until they are accustomed to the regular family diet.
Complementary Feeding: Providing food or fruits to the infant in addition to breast milk.

Timing: Exclusive breastfeeding is sufficient for the first 6 months; complementary feeding should begin by the end of the 6th month (it should neither start before 6 months nor be delayed beyond 6 months).

Aims: A child cannot consume more than 1 liter of fluid per day, so solid foods are necessary to meet rising caloric, mineral (especially iron), and vitamin needs. It also trains the infant in spoon feeding, chewing, swallowing, and digesting starches.
Too Early: Displaces breast milk, reduces milk production, and increases exposure to pathogens and food allergies due to gut immaturity.
Too Late: Prolonged exclusive breastfeeding leads to growth failure, wasting, and iron deficiency anemia.

Principles & Techniques: Introduce one new food item at a time gradually (1–2 spoonfuls), g uided by appetite. Slowly replace milk feeds with solid meals until full transition at 2 years. Non-sweetened foods/vegetables should be introduced before sweetened foods to prevent a preference for sweets.

Foods to Avoid in Infancy: Choking hazards (nuts, popcorn, chips, seeded fruits, fish with bones), common allergens (fresh cow's milk, eggs, chocolate, citrus fruits), food additives, highly salted foods, and junk food.

sections.title: Nutritional Requirements
blocks: Water: Constitutes ~70% of an infant's body weight (com pared to 60% in adults). Daily requirements range from 130–150 mL/kg in the 1st year to 50–70 mL/kg in adolescence.
Energy: Recommended energy distribution is 15% from protein, 35% from fat, and 50% from carbohydrates.
Daily Caloric Needs: 0–6 months = 120 kcal/kg; 6–12 months = 105 kcal/kg; 1–3 years = 100 kcal/kg; gradually decreasing to 60 kcal/kg at 13–15 years.
Caloric Formula after 1st year: (Energy (kcal/day) = (Age in years × 120) + 1000.

Protein: Constitutes 20% of body weight. Requirements are 1.5–2 g/kg/day for infants and 1–1.5 g/kg/day for children. Animal proteins provide complete essential amino acids (high biologic value), whereas plant proteins come from cereals, legumes, and oil seeds.

Fats & Carbohydrates: Long-Chain Fatty Acids are Transported as chylomicrons through the thoracic duct into the systemic venous circulation, while Medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) pass directly into the portal venous circulation without forming chylomicrons, making them useful in fat malabsorption conditions.

Key Vitamins & Minerals: Specific daily requirements include Vitamin A (400–1000 µg), Vitamin D (400 IU), Vitamin C (35–60 mg), Iron (7–15 mg in infants, 10–18 mg in children), and Calcium (400–500 mg).

sections.title: Failure to Thrive
blocks: Definition: Physical growth falling below the 3rd or 5th percentiles, or a downward shift crossing two major growth percentiles on standard charts (e.g., dropping from above the 75th to below the 25th percentile).
1. Inadequate Caloric Intake: Lack of appetite, ingestion difficulties, or food unavailability/poverty.
2. Altered Growth Potential: Prenatal insults, chromosomal abnormalities, or endocrinopathies.
3. Calorie Wasting: Vomiting, malabsorption, infections, or urinary/renal losses (e.g., diabetes).
4. Increased Caloric Requirements: Chronic pulmonary, cardiac, or systemic diseases.

Management & Hospitalization: Evaluated through detailed medical, caloric, psychosocial, and growth curve histories. Hospitalization is indicated if there is a high risk of abuse/neglect, severe malnutrition, or failure of outpatient management.

sections.title: Malnutrition
blocks: Malnutrition: Imbalance between nutrient intake and requirements resulting in deficits of energy, protein, or micronutrients.
Duration: Acute is defined as lasting <3 months.
Etiology: Divided into illness-related (infections, congenital anomalies) and non-illness- related (poverty, ignorance, psychosocial factors).
Welcome Classification (Based on % body weight for age and presence/absence of edema):
Wasted & Stunted (Acute on Chronic): Weight-for-length <80% AND Length- for-age <90%.

Etiology: Caused primarily by a deficiency of protein in a diet that consists predominantly of starches. Peak age is 6 months to 3 years. Contributing factors include poverty, ignorance, late/inadequate weaning, and precipitating infections (diarrhea, measles, tuberculosis).
Constant Signs: Growth failure, muscle wasting, edema (starting in feet/lower legs), and mental changes (apathy, lethargy, misery).
Hair Changes: Dry, sparse, easily plucked hair showing discoloration bands (Flag sign).
Skin Changes: Hyperkeratosis, peeling, flaky-paint dermatosis.
Associated Features: Anemia, secondary infections, vitamin deficiencies, and hemorrhagic tendencies.
Diagnostic Investigations: Plasma proteins showing marked hypoproteinemia and hypoalbuminemia, blood sugar, serum electrolytes, hematological workup, tuberculin test, and chest X-ray.
Etiology: Severe chronic malnutrition due to a deficiency of total caloric requirements (both protein and energy). Common in infants under 1 year of age.
Nutritional (Primary) Marasmus: Poverty, ignorance, early cessation of breastfeeding, overdiluted formula feeds.
Secondary Marasmus: Non-dietetic causes such as chronic gastroenteritis, malabsorption, congenital heart disease, or metabolic/systemic illness.

Clinical Picture: Severe growth failure, complete loss of subcutaneous fat (loss from abdomen, limbs, and finally buccal fat pads producing an "old-man" or wizened facies), severe muscle wasting, prominent ribs, alert and irritable mental state, and voracious appetite.
Diagnostic Investigations: Complete blood count, total plasma proteins and serum albumin (typically normal or only slightly reduced), urine and stool analysis.
1. Development of edema leading to Marasmic Kwashiorkor.

Subcutaneous Fat Preserved Not preserved (completely lost)
Liver Enlarged fatty liver No fatty liver
Ribs Not very prominent Very prominent
Mentality Lethargic and apathetic Alert and irritable

A severe combined state of malnutrition starting as marasmus, in which the child subsequently develops edema and other variable signs of kwashiorkor. Displays a mixed clinical picture.

Management of Simple Undernutrition: Managed at home. Provides 120–150 kcal/kg/day and 2–4 g protein/kg/day through small, frequent feeds using locally available, economically feasible foods. Includes regular weight follow-up, chest X-ray, and tuberculin testing.

Dehydration: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is the primary treatment. IV fluids must be avoided as much as possible due to the high risk of acute heart failure from volume overload, except in cases of septic/hypovolemic shock.
Infections: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics adjusted according to culture and sensitivity.
Electrolyte Disturbances & Hypothermia: Careful correction of hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and temperature regulation.
Anemia: Treated cautiously with blood products if severe.
1. Initial / Stabilization Phase (Days 1–7): Dehydration is corrected, infections are treated with systemic antibiotics, hypothermia is managed, and cautious refeeding is initiated.
2. Rehabilitation Phase (Weeks 2–6): Intensive feeding with high-calorie, high- protein diets to promote rapid catch-up growth.
3. Follow-Up Phase: Long-term outpatient monitoring of growth and prevention of relapse.

sections.title: Vitamins Deficiencies & Excess
blocks: High molecular weight alcohol essential for vision, epithelial integrity, and immunity.
Ocular: Night blindness (nyctalopia), dryness of conjunctiva and cornea (xerosis), Bitot spots (foamy silver-gray patches on bulbar conjunctiva), and keratomalacia (corneal softening/ulceration).
Systemic: Apathy, growth retardation, dry scaly skin with follicular hyperkeratosis, and anemia (with or without hepatosplenomegaly).
Diagnosis: Dark adaptation testing, clinical observation of xerosis conjunctivae, and serum levels. Plasma carotene falls quickly, whereas plasma vitamin A levels decline more slowly.

Prevention: Infants should receive at least 500 µg of Vitamin A daily; older children require 600–1500 µg daily. Mothers of breastfed infants in endemic regions should receive 30,000 µg (100,000 IU) of Vitamin A postpartum.
Latent Deficiency: Treated with 1,500 µg daily orally.
Xerophthalmia: Treated with 1,500 µg/kg/day orally for 5 days, followed by 7,500 µg daily IM until complete recovery.

Acute Toxicity: Occurs in infants after ingesting a single large dose of ≥100,000 µg (≥330,000 IU). Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, bulging fontanel, diplopia, papilledema, cranial nerve palsies, and other signs of Pseudotumor cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension).

Chronic Toxicity: Results from chronic ingestion of excessive doses over several weeks or months5. Symptoms include anorexia, pruritus, failure to gain weight, irritability, limitation of motion, alopecia, seborrheic skin, fissuring at the corners of the mouth, increased intracranial pressure, hepatomegaly, craniotabes, and desquamation of the palms and soles.
Cholecalciferol Vitamin D₃: The mammalian form produced by ultraviolet (UV) irradiation of inactive 7-dehydrocholecalciferol precursors in the skin.

Ergocalciferol Vitamin D₂: Derived from plant sources. Both (D2) and (D3) possess equivalent potency and require enzymatic metabolism to become active. Skin synthesis is decreased by clothing, lack of sunlight, and dark skin pigmentation.

Metabolism: Skin synthesis (UV) or dietary intake (absorbed from the upper intestine with the help of bile salts and dietary fats) → 25-hydroxylase in liver →25- hydroxycholecalciferol (25-OH D) →1-alpha-hydroxylase in renal cortex → 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol (1,25(OH)₂D₃) (active hormonal form, stimulated by PTH when serum Ca drops). If serum calcium and phosphorus levels are normal or high, 24 - hydroxylase converts (25-OH D) into (24,25-D), an inactive metabolite cleared by the body.

Hypervitaminosis D: Excess intake over 1–3 months → Anorexia, polyuria, polydipsia, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, metastatic bone calcification. Treatment: Discontinue Vitamin D + Prednisone (2 mg/kg).
Definition: Failure of mineralization of growing bone/osteoid tissue in children, caused by Vitamin D deficiency.
1. Inadequate dietary intake of Vitamin D.
2. Lack of direct sunlight exposure for the infant or lactating mother.
5. Conditions unbalancing calcium and phosphorus homeostasis.
1. Cartilage cells fail to complete their normal cycle of proliferation and degeneration due to
2. Capillary penetration becomes patchy, producing a frayed, irregular epiphyseal line.
3. Deposition of uncalcified osteoid tissue in the zone of preparatory calcification forms a
widened, compressed rachitic metaphysis that bulges laterally (causing flaring of bone ends and rachitic rosary).
4. Subperiosteal bone softening leads to deformities and greenstick fractures under weight - bearing pressure.
Head: Early profuse head sweating, craniotabes (ping-pong ball sensation in parietal/occipital bones), frontal bossing, delayed fontanel closure (>18 months).
Thorax: Rachitic rosary (smooth, non-tender costochondral beading), Harrison's sulcus (diaphragmatic groove), pectus excavatum.
Limbs & Motor: Wrist and ankle widening, knock knees (genu valgum) or bow legs (genu varum), delayed motor milestones due to hypotonia.
Biochemical: Elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, low serum phosphorus, low/normal serum calcium.
X-Ray (Wrist): Epiphyseal cupping of the lower radius/ulna, widening (flaring) of the metaphysis, fraying (rarefaction) of bone margins, reduced bone density, and greenstick fractures.
Stoss Therapy: Single dose of 300,000–600,000 IU Vitamin D (oral/IM) followed by daily maintenance (400-1,000 IU). OR
Daily Therapy: 2,000–5,000 IU/day for 4–8 weeks + Calcium supplementation.
Definition: Rickets that shows poor or no response to standard therapeutic doses of Vitamin D.
Type I (Disturbed Vitamin D Metabolism): Secondary to liver/renal disease, end-organ target cell unresponsiveness (Vitamin D-dependent rickets), or renal osteodystrophy.
Type II (Renal Tubular Phosphate Loss): Caused by Fanconi syndrome, Familial hypophosphatemic rickets, isolated phosphaturia, or Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA).
Treatment: High-dose Vitamin D (10,000 IU/day), active (1,25(OH)₂D₃), and oral phosphate supplementation.
Definition: A state of neuromuscular hyperexcitability of the central and peripheral nervous system caused by decreased ionized calcium (<7 mg/dL).
Pathophysiology: Low ionized calcium lowers the threshold for nerve cell membrane depolarization, producing involuntary muscle contractions and spasms.
1. Hypocalcemia: Inadequate calcium intake, malabsorption, hypoparathyroidism, neonatal hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, or severe rickets.

2. Alkalosis: Reduces ionized calcium levels despite normal total calcium. Caused by excessive vomiting (HCl) loss → metabolic alkalosis), hyperventilation (CO2) wash → respiratory alkalosis, or excess alkali intake (bicarbonate/citrate).
3. Hypomagnesemia: Chronic diarrhea, nephrotoxic medications, or diuretic therapy.
Convulsions: Brief, generalized or localized seizures without loss of consciousness between fits (most common presentation in neonates/young infants).
Carpo-pedal Spasm: Flexion at the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints with extension of the fingers and plantar flexion of the toes.
Laryngeal Spasm: Inspiratory stridor caused by vocal cord adduction.
Paresthesias: Numbness and tingling in hands, feet, and perioral areas in older children.
Chvostek's Sign: Tapping the facial nerve anterior to the external auditory meatus elicits twitching of the upper lip or mouth corner.
Trousseau's Sign: Inflating a blood pressure cuff slightly above systolic pressure for >3 minutes induces carpal spasm due to motor nerve ischemia.
Emergency Treatment: Slow IV administration of 10% Calcium gluconate (1-2 mL/kg) under cardiac monitoring for bradycardia.
Maintenance Treatment: Oral calcium supplements (Calcium carbonate or Calcium gluconate).
Alkalosis: Rebreathing into a paper bag to retain (CO2) and induce mild respiratory acidosis.

sections.title: Obesity
blocks: Children <5 years: Overweight = weight-for-height >2 SD above median; Obesity = weight-for-height >3 SD above median.
Children 5–19 years: Overweight = BMI-for-age >1 SD above median; Obesity = BMI-for-age >2 SD above median.
Exogenous (95%): Multifactorial (genetic predisposition, high caloric intake, sedentary lifestyle, unhealthy eating behaviors).
Endogenous (5%): Syndromic/Genetic (Laurence-Moon-Biedl, Turner syndrome), Endocrinal (Hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, Growth Hormone deficiency), Hypothalamic, or Steroid-induced.
Health Hazards: Hypertension, cardiovascular disease, hypercholesterolemia, Type 2 diabetes mellitus, and orthopedic/back problems.

Management: Lifestyle and dietary behavior modification, promotion of physical activity (30–45 minutes 2–3 times weekly), f amily-based meals without screen distraction, and balanced weight reduction programs.

sections.title: Introduction & Definitions
blocks: Transcription and Translation: The primary genetic material in humans is DNA, which exists in the cell nucleus as a double-stranded antiparallel helix held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (Adenine – Thymine and Guanine–Cytosine).
Transcription is the process by which a specific DNA sequence is synthesized into a complementary messenger RNA (mRNA) code in the nucleus.
Translation occurs on ribosomes, where the code in mRNA is translated into a specific sequence of amino acids to synthesize a polypeptide or protein.
Gene: A specific sequence of nucleotid e bases in DNA located at a designated site (locus) on a chromosome that codes for one polypeptide chain.
Genome: The complete genetic constitution of an individual organism.
Genotype: The specific underlying genetic makeup or allele combination of an individual, trait, or disease (e.g., (AA), (Aa), or (aa)).
Phenotype: The observable physical, biochemical, or clinical expression of a gene or trait resulting from the interaction of the genotype with the environment (e.g., eye color, blood type).
Allele: One of two or more alternative forms of a gene occupying the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes. Humans inherit two copies of every gene—one from each parent.

Dominant Allele vs. Recessive Allele: A dominant allele expresses its phenotypic effect whether present in a homozygous or heterozygous state (i.e., paired with a similar dominant or a different recessive allele). A recessive allele expresses its phenotypic effect only when present in the homozygous state (paired with an identical recessive allele).

Homozygous vs. Heterozygous: An individual is homozygous when carrying two identical a lleles at a given locus (e.g., (BB) or (bb) and heterozygous when carrying two different alleles at that locus (e.g., (Bb).

Thread-like nuclear structures ("chroma" = color, "soma" = body) composed of DNA and supporting proteins. Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs, which carry the entire genomic instruction set.

sections.title: The Different Patterns of Inheritance
blocks: Inheritance Rules: The disease appears in every generation (vertical transmission). Every child of an affected parent has a 50% (1 in 2) chance of inheriting the condition. Males and females are affected in equal proportions. Male-to-male transmission occurs. Mutations usually affect genes encoding structural or regulatory proteins (such as collagen).
Examples: Hereditary spherocytosis, Huntington chorea, Marfan syndrome, and Noonan syndrome.

Inheritance Rules: The disease typically appears among siblings (horizontal transmission) rather than in parents or offspring. On average, 25% (1 in 4) of siblings of a proband are affected. An unaffected ("normal") sibling of an affected individual has a 2/3 chance of being an asymptomatic carrier (heterozygote). Males and females are affected equally. Mutations usually involve genes encoding metabolic enzymes (e.g., phenylalanine hydroxylase in PKU).
Examples: Thalassemia syndromes and Sickle cell anemia.

Inheritance Rules: Disease incidence is significantly higher in males than in females. Passed from carrier females (who are usually asymptomatic or show mild expression) to half (50%) of their sons, who manifest severe disease. Affected males pass the mutated X chromosome to all of their daughters (making them obligate carriers), but never to their sons (no male-to-male transmission). The trait can pass through multiple carrier females, often skipping generations.
Examples: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency anemia, Sideroblastic anemia, and Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Diseases caused by structural breaks or numerical additions /deletions across whole chromosomes or major segments.
Patterns of disease transmission that do not follow classic monogenic Mendelian rules, including mitochondrial inheritance, triplet repeat expansion, and polygenic/complex multifactorial inheritance.

sections.title: Karyotyping
blocks: Definition: A laboratory preparation and systematic arrangement of metaphase chromosomes in a standardized order for cytogenetic evaluation.

Classification: Chromosomes are grouped into 7 main autosome groups (A, B, C, D, E, F, and G) based on their relative size and centromere location, along with the pair of sex chromosomes (XX) or (XY).
Indications for Chromosome Studies in Pediatric Practice:
1. Unexplained significant developmental delay or intellectual disability.

3. Intersex conditions or disorders of sexual differentiation (e.g., ambiguous genitalia in a newborn, inguinal hernia containing testicular tissue in a girl, or delayed puberty/amenorrhea in adolescence).
4. Congenital lymphedema of hands and feet (raising suspicion of Turner syndrome).
5. Short stature or failure to thrive originating in the prenatal period.
6. Pediatric leukemias, lymphomas, and solid tumors.

sections.title: Types of Chromosome Abnormalities
blocks: Aneuploidy: Deviation in chromosome number involving individual chromosomes rather than complete haploid sets. Includes trisomy (presence of an extra autosome, e.g., Down syndrome (47,XX/XY,+21), or extra sex chromosome, e.g., (47,XXX) and monosomy (absence of a chromosome, e.g., Turner syndrome (45,X).

Polyploidy: A numerical state where a cell contains an exact multiple of the haploid set (n = 23) greater than the normal diploid number (2n = 46). Examples include triploidy (3n = 69) or tetraploidy (4n = 92).
Translocation: A structural rearrangement where segments from two non - homologous chromosomes break off and attach to one another (e.g., (14/21) Robertsonian translocation in Down syndrome).
Deletion: Loss of a portion of a chromosome resulting from single or double chromosome breakage.

sections.title: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21)
blocks: Incidence & Maternal Age Risk: Down syndrome is the most common autosomal trisomy, occurring in approximately 1 in 700 live births (with 50% of affected pregnancies aborting early). The incidence increases significantly with advancing maternal age:
Complete Trisomy 21 (92%): Caused by chromosomal nondisjunction during maternal meiosis, resulting in an extra chromosome 21 in all cells (total count = 47).
Translocation (5%): Involves attachment of the extra chromosome 21 to another chromosome (13, 14, 15, 21, or 22). Total count is 46, but the child is functionally trisomic for 21.
Mosaicism (3%): A mixture of cells, where some display trisomy 21 and others have a normal karyotype.

Head & Neck: Small skull with a flat occiput (brachycephaly); lateral upward - slanting palpebral fissures, prominent epicanthic folds, and Brushfield spots on the iris; small ears with an overfolded helix; flat nasal bridge with an upturned nose; protruded, fissured tongue (scrotal tongue) due to a small oral cavity; delayed dental eruption; and a short, thick neck with excess nuchal fat.
Trunk: High incidence of cardiac malformations (endocardial cushion defects, VSD, ASD); protuberant abdomen secondary to generalized abdominal muscle hypotonia.

Extremities: Short, broad hands with a single transverse palmar (Simian) crease in 50% of cases; short, incurved little finger (clinodactyly) with a short or absent middle phalanx; hyperflexible joints; wide gap between the 1st and 2nd toes; and al ongitudinal plantar crease. Genitalia are poorly developed with delayed puberty.
Mentality: Variable intellectual disability with IQ ranging from 20% to 75% (average 50%).
Newborn Signs: May present in the immediate neonatal period with prolonged physiological jaundice, polycythemia, or a transient leukemoid reaction.

Management: Includes genetic counseling, antenatal screening for future pregnancies, early developmental stimulation programs, serial growth, vision, hearing, and behavioral evaluations, and early surgical correction of associated cardiac or gastrointestinal anomalies (most commonly duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease).
Translocation: 5% to 100% (specifically 100% recurrence risk if a parent carries a 21/21 translocation).

sections.title: Turner Syndrome
blocks: Karyotype: Most commonly 45,X; less frequently manifests as mosaicism (e.g., 45,X / 46,XX) or structural X chromosome deletions.
Neonate: Presenting signs include congenital carpal and pedal edema.

Physical Traits: Short stature, low posterior hairline, webbed neck (nuchal skin folds), brown cutaneous nevi, cubitus valgus (elbow deformity), shield-shaped thorax with widely spaced hyperplastic nipples, shortened 4th metacarpals, and small fingernails.
Gonadal & Reproductive: Primary amenorrhea and sexual infantilism secondary to underdeveloped streak gonads (rudimentary ovaries).
Cardiovascular: Increased incidence of cardiovascular structural defects, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta.
1. Growth Promotion: Subcutaneous growth hormone therapy initiated early in childhood to optimize final adult height.

2. Female Hormone Replacement: Estrogen substitution around 12 years of age to induce secondary sexual characteristics and prevent osteoporosis. Low-dose oral estrogen is given for 6–12 months, followed by cyclic therapy (estrogen on days 1–25 of each calendar month, with oral progestational agents added from days 15 to 25) to induce withdrawal menses 3–5 days after discontinuation.

sections.title: Klinefelter Syndrome
blocks: Karyotype: The most common sex chromosome aneuploidy, characterized by a 47,XXY genotype.
Prepubertal: Usually asymptomatic in infancy and early childhood.

Postpubertal: Presents with hypogonadism leading to infertility and hypospermia. Gonadotropin levels are typically elevated. Physical traits include tall stature with long limbs, a small pelvis, small and soft testes, gynecomastia, and mild mental retardation.

sections.title: Genetic Counseling
blocks: Definition: A professional process designed to help individuals and families understand the medical, psychological, and familial contributions to genetic conditions.
1. Conduct comprehensive medical and family history intakes.
2. Clearly explain the specific genetic condition affecting the individual or family.
3. Educate patients regarding available genetic testing options, including benefits and limitations.
4. Order and facilitate chosen genetic laboratory testing.
5. Interpret complex genetic test results and communicate findings to patients and referring physicians.
6. Provide detailed educational information regarding disease management and prognosis.
7. Refer patients to medical subspecialists as needed.
8. Offer continuous counseling and emotional support to patients and families throughout the decision-making process.

sections.title: Pedigree and Family History-Taking
blocks: Pedigree Symbols: Standardized symbols represent family relationships and clinical status; a diagonal line across a symbol denotes a deceased individual, while pregnancy loss and stillbirths are represented with their corr esponding gestational age in weeks noted.
If individual names and ages are unknown but the number of male and female offspring is known, list the counts directly under gender-specific symbols (e.g., 5 males and 3 females).
If the exact breakdown of males and females is unknown, use a diamond symbol with the total number of children indicated inside (e.g., a diamond with "8" inside for 8 total offspring).

sections.title: Definitions and Classifications
blocks: Newborn: A live-born infant during the first 4 weeks (28 days) of life.
Live birth: A live-born infant that exhibits any signs of life at birth, such as active movements, respiratory efforts, heartbeats, or pulsation of the umbilical cord.
Stillbirth: A fetus delivered dead at or after 24 weeks of gestation.
Abortion: A fetus delivered dead prior to 24 weeks of gestation.
Preterm: A live-born infant delivered before 37 completed weeks of gestation (<37 weeks).
Term: A live-born infant delivered between 37 and 42 weeks of gestation (37 to <42 weeks).
Post-term: A live-born infant delivered at or beyond 42 weeks of gestation (>42 weeks).
Normal Birth Weight: A birth weight between 2500 g and less than 400 0 g (≥2500 g to <4000 g).
Macrosomia: A birth weight exceeding 4000 g (>4000 g).
Low Birth Weight (LBW): A birth weight less than 2500 g (<2500 g).
Very Low Birth Weight (VLBW): A birth weight less than 1500 g (<1500 g).
Extremely Low Birth Weight (ELBW): A birth weight less than 1000 g (<1000 g).
Appropriate for Gestational Age (AGA): A birth weight that falls between the 10th and 90th percentiles for the specific gestational age.
Large for Gestational Age (LGA): A birth weight greater than the 90th percentile (>90th percentile) for gestational age.
Small for Gestational Age (SGA): A birth weight less than the 10th percentile (<10th percentile) for gestational age.

sections.title: Care of the Newborn
blocks: Timing: As sessed routinely at 1 minute and 5 minutes after birth to evaluate the newborn's physical condition and identify those requiring resuscitation. If the score remains abnormal, serial evaluations continue at 10, 15, and 20 minutes.
Five Objective Parameters: Each evaluated parameter is scored 0, 1, or 2:
1. Appearance (Color): 0 = Blue/pale overall; 1 = Pink body with blue extremities (acrocyanosis); 2 = Completely pink.
2. Pulse (Heart Rate): 0 = Absent; 1 = Below 100 beats/min; 2 = Over 100 beats/min.
3. Grimace (Reflex Response to Nasal Catheter): 0 = No response; 1 = Grimace; 2 = Cough or sneeze.
4. Activity (Muscle Tone): 0 = Limp/flaccid; 1 = Some flexion and extension of extremities; 2 = Active motion.
5. Respiratory Effort: 0 = Absent; 1 = Slow, irregular breathing; 2 = Good, strong crying.
Score 7–10: Normal infant; requires routine post-delivery care.
Score 4–6: Requires resuscitation and close observation. (At 5 minutes, indicates perinatal asphyxia requiring ongoing resuscitation, admission to NICU, and serial APGAR scores).
Score 0–3: Cardiopulmonary arrest; mandates immediate resuscitation. (At 5 minutes, requires intubation, positive pressure ventilation, and NICU admission).

sections.title: Resuscitation of the Newborn
blocks: High-Risk Delivery Predispositions: Conditions requiring a resuscitation-skilled person at delivery include maternal diseases (hypertension, toxemia, diabetes, infections, cardiac/pulmonary/renal disorders), maternal drug administration, antepartum hemorrhage, multiple pregnancies, prolonged labor, Cesarean section, breech delivery, preterm labor, and premature rupture of membranes (PROM).
1. Rapid Initial Evaluation: Assess color, breathing, and heart rate immediately upon delivery.
If pink, good respiration, HR > 100/min: Dry, wrap in warm towels, and give to mother.

If blue, inadequate respiration, HR > 100/min: Gentle suctioning of mouth and nose, tactile stimulation (tapping soles or back), and blow-by oxygen via mask. If no improvement, start bag-and-mask ventilation.
If blue, apneic, or HR < 100/min: Immediately start bag-and-mask positive pressure ventilation.
If no response to bag-and-mask: Perform intubation and mechanical ventilation.
If HR < 60/min or absent: Initiate cardiac compressions with ventilation, and administer IV adrenaline if heart rate remains unresponsive.

sections.title: Ordinary Care of Newborn
blocks: Patent Airway Maintenance: Ensured via gentle mouth and nose suctioning, tactile stimulation, and aspiration of gastric contents using a nasogastric tube.
Cord Care: Sterile clamping and application of antiseptic lotion (70% alcohol or Betadine) until the stump falls off to guard against tetanus neonatorum and omphalitis.
Temperature Regulation: Prevention of hypothermia by wrapping in sterile warm towels and placing the infant under a radiant warmer.
Eye Prophylaxis: Prophylactic antibiotic eye drops (e.g., Gentamicin) to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum and mucopurulent conjunctivitis.
Vitamin K₁ Administration: Single intramuscular (IM) dose of 1 mg Vitamin K₁ to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

sections.title: Examination of the Newborn
blocks: Measurements & Vital Signs: Birth weight, length, head circumference, temperature, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, and capillary refill time.
Color: Cyanosis (central vs. acrocyanosis), pallor, jaundice, plethora, meconium staining, mottling, Mongolian spots.
Respiration: Respiratory rate, retractions (intercostal/subcostal), grunting, stridor, wheezing, air entry, crackles/rhonchi.
Cardiovascular: Heart rate, peripheral pulses, murmurs, capillary refill time, 4- limb BP, pulse oximetry.
Abdomen & Genitalia: Distension, concavity, organ palpation (liver, spleen, kidneys), bowel sounds, passage of meconium and urine, external genitalia, patency of anus.
CNS & Musculoskeletal: Consciousness level, head circumference, fontanels, sutures, eye pupils, muscle tone, reflexes, abnormal movements/seizures, spine, extremities, and joints.
Congenital Anomalies: Systematic search across all systems.

sections.title: Assessment of Gestational Age
blocks: Maternal LMP: First day of the last menstrual period.
Prenatal Ultrasound: Fetal growth, head circumference, and femur length.
Expanded New Ballard Score: Evaluates physical and neuromuscular maturity:
Physical Criteria: Skin, lanugo hair, plantar creases, breast bud, ear cartilage, genitalia.
Neuromuscular Criteria: Posture, square window (wrist angle), arm recoil, popliteal angle, scarf sign, heel-to-ear sign.

sections.title: Neonatal Reflexes
blocks: Operated at the subcortical level due to cortical functional deficiency at birth.
Present from birth (or in-utero) and typically disappear between 4 and 6 months of age as the cerebral cortex matures.
Absence or Poor Response: Indicates severe prematurity or CNS depression (HIE, intracranial hemorrhage, maternal sedation, sepsis).
Asymmetrical Response: Indicates a focal neuromuscular lesion (e.g., Erb's palsy, fractured clavicle/humerus, dislocated shoulder).
Persistence Beyond 4–6 Months: Denotes failure of CNS maturation due to CNS pathology (e.g., cerebral palsy, mental handicap).
Exaggerated Response: Indicates brain irritation (e.g., early stages of kernicterus, meningitis).
How to Elicit: Semi-upright position with head supported, then head is allowed to fall backward suddenly; or sudden withdrawal of blanket undern eath; or a sudden loud noise.
Normal Response: Sudden jerking consisting of abduction and extension of both arms, followed by adduction and flexion in an embracing posture.
Timelines: Appears at 28 weeks gestation; disappears at 4 months of age.
How to Elicit: Introduction of finger/nipple into baby's mouth.
Timelines: Appears at 28 weeks gestation; disappears at 4 months.
How to Elicit: Stroking lips or angle of mouth.
Response: Baby turns mouth toward stimulus and opens mouth.
Timelines: Appears at 28 weeks gestation; disappears at 4 months.
Palmar Grasp: Stroking infant's palm; response is flexion of fingers grasping the examiner's finger. Appears at 28 weeks gestation; disappears at 4 months.
Plantar Grasp: Touching sole of foot with finger; response is flexion of toes. Appears at >25 weeks gestation; disappears at 9 months.
How to Elicit: Holding baby under shoulders with soles touching a flat surface.
Light Reflex: Exposure to bright light elicits blinking. Appears at 28 weeks gestation; evaluates vision.
Pupillary Reflex: Exposure to bright light elicits bilateral pupil constriction.
How to Elicit: Sudden loud sound behind ear.
Response: Elicits Moro reflex. Evaluates hearing.

sections.title: Low Birth Weight
blocks: Definition: A live-born infant delivered with a birth weight of less than 2500 g (<2500 g). It encompasses both preterm infants and small for gestational age (SGA) infants.

Incubator Environment: Maintains strict regulation of body temperature (preventing hypothermia), relative humidity, oxygen concentration (when clinically indicated), and isolates the infant to minimize infection risk.

Feeding Strategy: Breast milk is ideal if the baby can suckle. If oral suckling is impossible, specialized LBW formula is delivered via cup, spoon, dropper, or gastric tube. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is initiated if enteral feeding is contraindicated. Supplements of Vitamin A, D, E, folic acid, iron, calcium, and phosphorus are mandatory.
Infection Prevention: Minimal visitors, strict hand hygiene, healthcare worker masks, isolation of infected infants, and prophylactic antibiotics or immunoglobulins as indicated.

sections.title: Preterm Baby
blocks: Definition: Live-born infants delivered before completing 37 weeks of gestation (<37 weeks).
Extremely Preterm: Less than 28 weeks (<28 weeks).
Late Preterm: 34 to less than 37 weeks (34 to <37 weeks).

Etiology: Frequently idiopathic. Secondary causes include congenital fetal malformations, twin/multiple pregnancies, antepartum hemorrhage (APH), toxemia of pregnancy, maternal diabetes, and anatomical malformations of the maternal genital tract.
Respiratory: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS / Hyaline Membrane Disease), apnea of prematurity, and respiratory infections.
Central Nervous System: Intracranial hemorrhage (IVH) and periventricular leukomalacia.
Gastrointestinal & Metabolic: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), hyperbilirubinemia/kernicterus, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia.
Sensory & Systemic: Retrolental fibroplasia (retinopathy of prematurity), hypothermia, neonatal sepsis, and long-term nutritional deficiencies (rickets and iron deficiency anemia).

sections.title: Small for Gestational Age
blocks: Definition: Infants with a birth weight below the 10th percentile (<10th percentile) for their specific gestational age.
Etiology: Placental dysfunction syndromes, intrauterine TORCH infections, congenital malformations, chromosomal abnormalities, and maternal systemic diseases compromising fetal nutrient delivery.
Clinical Criteria: Physical examination reveals soft tissue and muscle wasting, along with thin, loose, and dry skin.

sections.title: Large for Gestational Age
blocks: Definition: Infants with a birth weight above the 90th percentile (>90th percentile) for their specific gestational age.
Etiology: Maternal pre-existing or gestational diabetes, constitutionally large parents, postmature pregnancy (>42 weeks), and hydrops fetalis.

sections.title: Neonatal Hypoglycemia
blocks: Definition: Plasma blood glucose level less than 40–45 mg/dL (<40–45 mg/dL), regardless of gestational age or clinical symptoms.

Clinical Manifestations: Frequently asymptomatic. When symptomatic, features include lethargy, irritability, jitteriness, poor feeding, temperature instability, seizures, altered consciousness, and coma.
Predisposed Groups: Infants of diabetic mothers (IDM), SGA/IUGR infants, stressed infants, and preterm newborns.

Differential Diagnosis: Islet cell hyperplasia (Beck with-Wiedemann syndrome, erythroblastosis fetalis), genetic hyperinsulinism, inborn errors of metabolism (galactosemia, glycogen storage diseases), congenital hypopituitarism, birth asphyxia, and neonatal sepsis.

Blood Glucose < 40 mg /dL WITH Symptoms: Immediate IV 10% Dextrose bolus (2–4 mL/kg) given within 10 minutes, followed by a continuous IV infusion of 4– 6 mg/kg/min; recheck glucose within 30 minutes.
Blood Glucose < 40 mg/dL WITHOUT Symptoms: Feed immediately and recheck glucose within 30 minutes.
Blood Glucose < 20 mg/dL (With or Without Symptoms): Immediate IV 10% Dextrose bolus (2–4 mL/kg) plus continuous 4–6 mg/kg/min glucose infusion; recheck within 30 minutes.

sections.title: Infant of Diabetic Mother
blocks: Etiology & Pathophysiology: Results from pre-existing or gestational maternal diabetes. Maternal hyperglycemia triggers fetal pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia, causing fetal hyperinsulinemia.
Antenatal / Delivery: Spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, pre mature delivery, macrosomia, and birth trauma.
Congenital Anomalies: Increased risk of cardiac, neural tube, renal, vertebral, and skeletal malformations.
Metabolic & Hematologic: Severe hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia (total Ca < 7 mg/dL), hypomagnesemia (< 1. 5 mg/dL), hyperbilirubinemia, polycythemia, and renal vein thrombosis.
Respiratory & GIT: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) and small left colon syndrome (delaying meconium passage).

Management: Delivery must occur in a specialized neonatal center. Immediate stabilization and plasma glucose monitoring at 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 48 hours post - delivery. Symptomatic or severe hypoglycemia is managed with IV 10% Dextrose bolus (2–4 mL/kg) and continuous infusion. Hypomagnesemia is treated with IV 10% Magnesium Sulfate (50–100 mg/kg).

sections.title: Birth Trauma
blocks: Predisposing Factors: Macrosomia (large baby), breech or abnormal presentations, preterm birth, precipitate delivery, and contracted maternal pelvis / cephalopelvic disproportion.
Pathology: Edema of the scalp over the presenting part resulting from obstructed or prolonged labor.
Features: Soft swelling that crosses suture lines.
Management: Completely benign; requires no treatment and resolves spontaneously within a few days.
Pathology: Subperiosteal hemorrhage over a cranial bone secondary to periosteal vessel rupture during obstructed labor.
Features: Soft swelling that takes days to reach full size and is strictly limited by suture lines to a single cranial bone.
Complications: Anemia, hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice), and parental anxiety.
Management: Reassurance and conservative care; blood transfusion for severe anemia and phototherapy for jaundice.

Intracranial Hemorrhage: Epidural, subdural, parenchymal, or intraventricular hemorrhage (most catastrophic in preterms). Manifests with apnea, seizures, altered consciousness, or flaccidity; diagnosed via cranial ultrasound or CT. Managed supportively with minimal handling, Vitamin K1, fresh frozen plasma, and anticonvulsants.

Erb's Palsy: Injury to C5 and C6 nerve roots. Causes shoulder adduction, elbow extension, forearm pronation, and wrist flexion ("waiter's tip" posture). Managed with physical therapy and surgery if required.
Klumpke's Palsy: Injury to C7, C8, and T1 nerve roots. Causes paralysis of intrinsic hand muscles resulting in a claw hand.
Facial Nerve Palsy: Lower motor neuron injury causing ipsilateral facial muscle paralysis. Managed with eye drops (artificial tears) and physical therapy.

sections.title: Perinatal Asphyxia
blocks: Definition & 4 Mandatory Diagnostic Criteria: Impairment of gas exchange causing tissue hypoxia, hypercarbia, and metabolic acidosis, defined by:
1. Umbilical cord blood metabolic or mixed acidosis (pH < 7.0).
2. Persistence of an APGAR score < 5 at >5 minutes.
3. Clinical evidence of Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) in the immediate neonatal period.
4. Evidence of multiorgan system dysfunction in the immediate neonatal period.
The risk factors are divided across three perinatal stages:
Antepartum: Maternal diabetes, pre-eclampsia or hypertension, fetal malformations, prematurity, postmaturity, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and severe maternal anemia.
Intrapartum: Umbilical cord compression, cephalopelvic disproportion, a nd breech presentation.
Postpartum: Severe neonatal pulmonary disease, cyanotic congenital heart disease, and neonatal sepsis.
Grade I (Mild): Hyperalertness alternating with lethargy, increased muscle tone and deep tendon reflexes, exaggerated Moro, dilated pupils, no seizures, and a normal EEG.
Grade II (Moderate): Lethargy, hypotonia, constricted pupils, and seizures present in >70% of cases on day 1 with an abnormal EEG.
Grade III (Severe): Coma, severe flaccidity, absent neonatal reflexes, fixed pupils, apnea, bradycardia, hypotension, and severely abnormal EEG.
Renal: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) leading to oliguria and hematuria.
Cardiovascular & Pulmonary: Hypoxic cardiomyopathy, congestive heart failure, and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).
Other Systems: Hepatic necrosis, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), adrenal failure, SIADH, and Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC).
we evaluate gas exchange, brain injury, and systemic multiorgan involvement:
Arterial Blood Gas (ABG): Demonstrates hypoxia, hypercarbia, and metabolic or mixed acidosis (pH < 7.0).
Laboratory Screening: Complete Blood Count (CBC), serum electrolytes, glucose, lactate, and specific organ function tests (renal and hepatic panels) to monitor multiorgan system dysfunction.
EEG / aEEG: Assesses cerebral electrical activity and detects subclinical seizures.
Cranial Ultrasonography: Initial bedside imaging to screen for edema or intracranial hemorrhage.
Immediate resuscitation per Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines.
Supportive care: Oxygenation/ventilation, blood pressure support via IV fluids and inotropes (dopamine/dobutamine), and strict correction of glucose and electrolyte imbalances.
Therapeutic Hypothermia: Whole-body cooling initiated within 6 hours of birth and continued for 72 hours targeting a core temperature of 33–34°C.
Seizure Control: IV Phenobarbital (20 mg/kg loading dose, then 5 mg/kg/day maintenance).

sections.title: Neonatal Seizures
blocks: Neonatal seizures are defined as paroxysmal neurological events presenting as twitching, rolling of the eyes, apnea, or generalized tonic stiffness.
Seizures in the newborn period arise from a wide range of CNS, metabolic, systemic, and drug - related causes:
Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE): The most common cause.
CNS Anomalies & Structural Lesions: Congenital brain malformations, perinatal ischemic stroke, and intracranial hemorrhage (ICH).
Metabolic Disturbances: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyponatremia or hypernatremia.
Infections: Neonatal sepsis, acute bacterial meningitis, and intrauterine congenital infections (TORCH panel).
Inborn Errors of Metabolism (IEM): Conditions such as Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) and Methylmalonic Acidemia.
Drug-Related Causes: Maternal drug withdrawal (e.g., opiates), accidental injection of maternal local anesthetic agents, or toxicity from medications like theophylline or corticosteroids.
Polycythemia: Hyperviscosity leading to cerebral sluggishness or thrombosis.
3. Etiology According to Age of Onset
The timing of seizure onset provides critical diagnostic clues to the underlying cause:
At Birth: Maternal anesthetic agent toxicity, severe hyponatremia, or water intoxication.
Day 1 of Life: Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) or acute severe metabolic abnormalities.
Days 2–3 of Life: HIE, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hyponatremia/hypernatremia, intracranial hemorrhage, or perinatal stroke.
Day >5 of Life: Congenital TORCH infections, developmental brain defects, galactosemia, or late-onset hypocalcemia.
1–2 Weeks of Life: Drug withdrawal in infants born to addicted mothers (e.g., opiates).
Neonatal seizures present differently from older children due to incomplete cortical myelination:

Focal Seizures: Characterized by rhythmic twitching of specific muscle groups of the extremities and face; usually indicates focal structural brain lesions, localized infections, or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Multifocal Clonic Seizures: Similar to focal seizures, but involving multiple muscle groups simultaneously or sequentially.
Tonic Seizures: Rigid posture of the extremities and trunk, often accompanied by fixed deviation of the eyes.
Myoclonic Seizures: Brief, single or multiple focal or generalized jerks of distal muscle groups.

Subtle Seizures: The most common type in premature infants; includes chewing, excessive salivation, transient apnea, eye blinking, nystagmus, bicycling or pedaling movements of the legs, skin color changes, and tongue thrusting.
Differential Note (Jitteriness): Jitteriness is a startle response to minor physical stimuli or loud noises that lacks ocular movements, is stimulus-sensitive, and ceases upon passive limb flexion.
Metabolic Screen: Immediate bed-side blood glucose, serum sodium, calcium, and magnesium levels.

Infection & CSF Workup: Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, C-reactive protein (CRP), blood, urine, and CSF cultures, lumbar puncture for CSF cell count/protein/glucose, and serum IgM specific for TORCH agents.
EEG / aEEG: Essential to con firm clinical seizures and detect subclinical electrographic seizures.
Neuroimaging: Bedside cranial ultrasonography, CT scan, or MRI of the brain to identify hemorrhage, infarction, or structural anomalies.
1. Phenobarbital: The first-line drug given as a loading dose of 20 mg/kg IV; a repeat dose can be administered if seizures persist.
2. Phenytoin: Second-line agent added at 20 mg/kg IV loading dose if seizures continue despite phenobarbital.
3. Diazepam: Third-line agent administered at 0.3 mg/kg IV if seizures remain refractory.
HIE: Therapeutic whole-body hypothermia cooling protocol and fluid restriction (60–80% maintenance).
Hypoglycemia: IV 10% Dextrose bolus (2–4 mL/kg) followed by a continuous infusion of 4–6 mg/kg/min.
Hypocalcemia: Slow IV administration of 10% Calcium gluconate (2 mL/kg) under cardiac monitoring.
Hypomagnesemia: IV infusion of 50% Magnesium sulfate (50–100 mg/kg).
Pyridoxine Dependency: Trial of IV Pyridoxine (50–100 mg) in intractable seizures.
Polycythemia: Partial exchange transfusion using normal saline or fresh frozen plasma.

sections.title: Neonatal Respiratory Disorders
blocks: Respiratory disorders are a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, particularly in preterm infants. Respiration involves airways, lungs, respiratory muscles (diaphragm and chest wall), respiratory centers in the brain, chemoreceptors, and conducting nerves.
Retractions: Intercostal and subcostal indrawing using accessory muscles.
Grunting: Forced expiration against a partially closed glottis (a self-induced CPAP mechanism).
Cyanosis: Indicates respiratory failure or right-to-left shunting.
Apnea: Primary or secondary cessation of breathing.
Clinical Assessment: Standardized clinical scoring systems (such as Downe's score) are utilized for objective scoring and serial monitoring.
Causes are categorized into pulmonary and extrapulmonary factors:
Airway Obstruction: Bilateral choanal atresia, macroglossia, micrognathia (Pierre Robin syndrome), laryngeal web/stenosis, trachea l stenosis, vascular rings, or bronchial plugs.

Lung Parenchymal Diseases: Hyaline Membrane Disease (RDS), Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN), Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS), Neonatal Pneumonia, Pulmonary Hypoplasia (secondary to diaphragmatic he rnia or Potter syndrome), Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN), and Pulmonary Hemorrhage.
Pleural & Air Leak Disorders: Pneumothorax, hydrothorax, and pneumomediastinum.
CNS Disorders: HIE, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, or maternal sedation.
Cardiovascular: Congenital heart failure, Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA), or Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD).
Hematologic & Metabolic: Severe anemia, polycythemia, hypothermia/hyperthermia, hypoglycemia, and hypocalcemia.

sections.title: Hyaline Membrane Disease
blocks: Etiology & Pathophysiology: Primarily affects preterm infants (<34–35 weeks gestation). Caused by a deficiency of pulmonary surfactant (a surface-tension-reducing phospholipid secreted by type II alveolar cells). Surfactant deficiency leads to progressive end-expiratory alveolar collapse (atelectasis), poor lung compliance (stiff lungs), severe ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypercarbia, and acidosis.
Pathology: Extensive atelectasis with alveoli lined by an acidophilic, homogeneous membrane (hyaline membrane).

Increased Risk: Prematurity (<35 weeks), Cesarean section delivery, Infant of Diabetic Mother (IDM), perinatal asphyxia, male sex, 2nd twin in multiple pregnancies, hydrops fetalis, and familial predisposition.
Decreased Risk: Chronic intrauterine stress, maternal hypertension, Intrauterine Growth Restriction (IUGR), prolonged rupture of membranes (PROM), and antenatal corticosteroid administration.
Prenatal: Amniotic fluid Lecithin/Sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio > 2:1 indicates lung maturity.
Natal/Postnatal: Shake test and stable microbubble test performed on amniotic fluid, gastric aspirate, or tracheal aspirate.
Clinical: Onset occurs within 2–4 hours after birth with tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, cyanosis, and fine rales heard posteriorly.
