Chest X-Ray: Displays fine reticulogranularity ("ground glass" appearance), air bronchograms, and "white lung" with decreased lung volumes.
Antenatal Prevention: Two doses of Betamethasone (12 mg IM, 24 hours apart) given to mothers with anticipated preterm labor.
Supportive Care: Incubator thermoregulation, IV fluid/nutritional support, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, acid-base correction, and dopamine for hypotension.
Oxygen & Ventilatory Support: Humidified O2 via nasal cannula, head box, CPAP, or mechanical ventilation targeting PaO₂ 55–70 mmHg (SpO2 89–94%) and PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg.
Specific Treatment: Exogenous Surfactant replacement administered directly through an endotracheal tube (as prophylactic or rescue therapy).
Acute: Air leak syndromes (pneumothorax), nosocomial infections (Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas), Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH), and Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).
Chronic: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD), Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP), and Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL).

sections.title: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn
blocks: Pathophysiology: A benign, self-limited condition in term or late preterm infants caused by delayed absorption of fetal lung fluid, resulting in transient pulmonary edema.
Risk Factors: Elective Cesarean section, macrosomia, prolonged labor, male sex, maternal excessive sedation, and low 1-minute Apgar score (<7).

Clinical Picture: Tachypnea, intercostal/subcostal retractions, nasal flaring, and grunting appearing shortly after birth. Air entry is normal, cyanosis is usually absent, and the condition resolves spontaneously within 48–72 hours.
Chest X-Ray: Shows prominent perihilar streaking, hyperaeration, and fluid in the interlobar fissures or pleural space.

sections.title: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome
blocks: Pathophysiology: Inhalation of meconium-stained amniotic fluid in utero or with the first breath. Thick meconium causes physical airway obstruction and ball-valve atelectasis/emphysema; thin meconium causes severe chemical pneumonitis and surfactant inactivation.
Risk Factors: Post-term pregnancy, maternal hypertension/preeclampsia, IUGR/SGA, maternal cardiac/respiratory disease, abnormal fetal heart rate patterns, and biophysical profile score <6.

Diagnosis: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid, meconium-stained infant (skin, nails, cord), direct visualization/suction of meconium below vocal cords upon intubation, and chest X- ray showing patchy atelectasis and coarse heterogeneous opacities.

sections.title: Neonatal Pneumonia
blocks: 1. Congenital Pneumonia: Ingestion or aspiration of infected amniotic fluid; manifests prior to delivery, at delivery, or after a brief latent period (associated with PROM, chorioamnionitis, maternal UTI).
2. Postnatal-Acquired Pneumonia: Infection transmitted from caregivers or contacts via direct contact or droplets.
3. Aspiration Pneumonia: Secondary to choking or vomiting (associated with cleft lip/palate, tracheoesophageal fistula [TOF], or GERD).

Clinical Manifestations & Diagnostics: Respiratory distress, bronchial breathing, and fine rales. Chest X-ray demonstrates homogeneous or patchy consolidation/opacities; blood/CSF cultures and CRP confirm infection.

sections.title: Apnea
blocks: Definition: Cessation of breathing for ≥20 seconds, or any pause accompanied by cyanosis and bradycardia (heart rate <100 beats/min).

Pathological Apnea: Onset during the 1st day or after 2 weeks of life in preterms, or at any time in term infants. Secondary to underlying CNS, cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, GIT, or septic disorders.

Apnea of Prematurity (Idiopa thic/Primary): Onset on days 2–7 of life due to developmental immaturity of the brainstem respiratory center, characterized by an attenuated response to (CO2) and a paradoxical respiratory depression to hypoxia.
Caffeine Citrate: Loading dose of 20 mg/kg, followed 24 hours later by 5 mg/kg/day maintenance.
Theophylline: Loading dose of 6 mg/kg IV, followed by 2 mg/kg every 8 hours maintenance.
Doxapram: Continuous IV infusion at 1 mg/kg/hr.
Nasal CPAP: Administered at 4–6 cm H2O for obstructive or mixed apnea.

sections.title: Neonatal Cyanosis
blocks: Central Cyanosis: Bluish discoloration visible in the tongue, lips, and oral mucosa; indicates arterial desaturation and improves with oxygen administration.
Peripheral Cyanosis (Acrocyanosis): Discoloration restricted to the hands, feet, and ears due to peripheral arteriolar constriction/sluggish blood flow; improves with warming.

Etiology: Respiratory diseases, Cyanotic Congenital Heart Diseases (TGA, TAPVR, Tricuspid Atresia, Truncus Arteriosus, TOF), CNS depression, Polycythemia, Methemoglobinemia, Hypoglycemia, Hypothermia, and Neonatal Sepsis.
Hyperoxia Test: Measures arterial PaO2 after 100% O2 administration to differentiate cardiac right-to-left shunts PaO2 remains <100 mmHg) from primary pulmonary pathology (PaO2 rises >150–200 mmHg).
Echocardiography, Chest X-ray, ABG, CBC, and cranial ultrasonography.

Treatment: Oxygenation/ventilation, Prostin (PGE1) infusion for duct-dependent cyanotic heart lesions, IV glucose, broad-spectrum antibiotics, partial exchange transfusion for polycythemia, and Methylene Blue or Vitamin C for methemoglobinemia.
Here is a detailed, source-grounded breakdown of Topic 9 (Neonatal Infections) and Topic 10 (Neonatal Hematologic Disorders) from Chapter 5 of the Al-Azhar Handbook of Pediatrics and Child Health:

sections.title: Neonatal Infections
blocks: Intrauterine infections are transmitted across the placenta to the fetus and are collectively known as the TORCH infections:
Early spontaneous abortion or late stillbirth, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR/SGA), prematurity, and congenital malformations.
Microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, developmental delay, and hearing loss.

Congenital Rubella Syndrome: Cataracts, hearing loss, congenital heart disease (Patent Ductus Arteriosus [PDA], Pulmonary Stenosis [PS]), microcephaly, microphthalmia, retinopathy, glaucoma, meningoencephalitis, Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), thrombocytopenic purpura, and Diabetes Mellitus.
Congenital Parvovirus B19: RBC aplasia, severe anemia, congestive heart failure, generalized edema, and non-immune Hydrops Fetalis.
Serum TORCH titers measuring specific IgM and IgG antibodies.
Demonstration of a 4-fold rise in IgG titer over a 2–4 week interval.
Viral or pathogen identification in clinical specimens (urine, saliva, CSF).
Supportive Care and hyperimmune specific immunoglobulins or IVIG.
Toxoplasmosis: Spiramycin, or Pyrimethamine plus Sulfadiazine.
Intrapartum (Intranatal) Infections: Acquired during labor and passage through the birth canal:
Viral: HSV, HIV, Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV).
Bacterial: Group B Streptococcus (GBS), E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydia.
Postpartum (Postnatal) Infections: Acquired after delivery from the community, hospital environment, or caregivers:
Bacterial: Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (CoNS), Staph aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Neonatal sepsis is a clinical syndrome characterized by systemic signs of infection accompanied by bacteremia and circulating bacterial toxins.
Chorioamnionitis: Indicated by intrapartum fever (>38°C), foul vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, maternal leukocytosis, and elevated CRP.
Premature delivery and maternal urinary tract infection (UTI).
Preterm birth and low birth weight (LBW).
Invasive procedures (IV catheters, endotracheal tubes, chest tubes).
Congenital defects (meningocele, tracheoesophageal fistula [TOF], obstructive uropathy, cleft lip/palate) and male sex.
Contaminated nursery equipment/personnel and failure to adhere to strict infection control protocols (nosocomial infections).
B. Pathogens by Pattern of Onset
Early-Onset Sepsis (First 3 Days of Life): Acquired intrapartum from the mother. Dominant pathogens include Group B Streptococcus, Gram-negative enterococci, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes.

Late-Onset Sepsis (After 3 Days of Life): Acquired postnatally from the hospital or community. Dominant pathogens include Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, Staph aureus, E. coli, Klebsiella, and Pseudomonas.
Symptoms are often subtle and non-specific (described as "just not doing well"):
General: Lethargy, reduced activity, poor crying, we ak suckling, hypothermia or fever, and shock.
Respiratory: Apnea, tachypnea, intercostal/subcostal retractions, grunting, and cyanosis.
Cardiovascular: Tachycardia or bradycardia, hypotension, poor capillary refill, and heart failure.
Gastrointestinal: Poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distension, and paralytic ileus.
Hematologic & Hepatic: Pallor, jaundice, petechiae, purpura, active bleeding, and hepatosplenomegaly.
CNS: Irritability, seizures, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, diminished Moro and sucking reflexes, bulging fontanel, neck rigidity, and a high-pitched cry.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Demonstrates leukocytosis (>20,000/µL), leukopenia (<5,000/µL), neutropenia (<1,500/µL), or neutrophilia (>8,000/µL).
Arterial Blood Gas (ABG): Shows metabolic acidosis.
Diagnostic Cultures: Blood, CSF, urine, and local lesion/catheter site cultures.
Imaging: Chest X-ray to confirm pneumonia.
Empiric Antibiotic Therapy: Initiated immediately after obtaining culture samples:
Late-Onset Sepsis: Vancomycin + Gentamicin and/or a 3rd-generation Cephalosporin.
Duration: 10–14 days for proven sepsis; 14–21 days if meningitis is present.
Immunotherapy: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG), Granulocyte-Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF), or exchange transfusion in severe cases.

Supportive Management: Thermoregulation in an incubator, fluid/electrolyte balance, correction of hypoxia/acidosis, FFP and platelet transfusions for Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC), and phototherapy or exchange transfusion for hyperbilirubinemia.

sections.title: Neonatal Anemia
blocks: Definition: A Hematocrit (Hct) <40%–45% (<0.40–0.45) in a newborn.
Fetomaternal Blood Group Incompatibility: Rh, ABO, and minor blood group incompatibilities (Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn).
Infections & Drugs: Bacterial, viral (TO RCH), parasitic infections, or drug - induced (penicillin, cephalosporins, sulfonamides).
Obstetric Causes: Placenta previa, abruptio placentae, umbilical cord incision/rupture during C-section.
Transfusion Syndromes: Feto-maternal transfusion or twin-to-twin transfusion (donor twin).
External / Internal Bleeding: Umbilical/circumcision bleeding, cephalhematoma, subgaleal hematoma, adrenal hemorrhage, intracranial hemorrhage, pulmonary hemorrhage, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Diamond-Blackfan syndrome, Fanconi anemia, osteopetrosis, congenital leukemia, intrauterine Parvovirus B19 or rubella infections, or physiological anemia of prematurity.
Acute Blood Loss: Features of hypovolemic shock —severe pallor, cold extremities, weak thready pulse, hypotension, poor perfusion, and metabolic acidosis.
Chronic Blood Loss: Pallor, irritability, failure to thrive; severe cases show tachypnea, tachycardia, and a tender enlarged liver (congestive heart failure).
Hemolysis: Triad of pallor, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly.
CBC: Low Hb, low Hct, and low RBC count.
Reticulocyte Count: Increased in hemolysis and acute blood loss; decreased in bone marrow aplasia.
Blood Grouping & Coombs' Test: Performed on both infant and mother to confirm immune hemolysis.
Peripheral Blood Film & Special Tests: Evaluates RBC morphology (spherocytes, osmotic fragility test), G6PD enzyme assay, CRP, and TORCH screen.
Packed RBC Transfusion: Administered at 15–20 mL/kg over 2 hours if severe anemia (Hct <30%) is present or if the infant has underlying cardiac/pulmonary disease.
Partial Exchange Transfusion: Used in s everely anemic infants to prevent volume overload:
Oral iron (2–4 mg/kg/day) for breastfed infants.
Vitamin E (15–25 IU/day) for preterm infants.
Recombinant human erythropoietin (250–400 IU/kg IV/SC every other day for 2– 4 weeks) for anemia of prematurity.

sections.title: Polycythemia
blocks: Passive Polycythemia: Delayed cord clamping, materno-fetal transfusion, or twin-to- twin transfusion (recipient twin).

Active Polycythemia (Increased Erythropoiesis from Intrauterine Hypoxia): Placental insufficiency (IUGR/SGA), maternal hypertension/preeclampsia, maternal chronic hypoxemia, Infant of Diabetic Mother (IDM), chromosomal trisomies (21, 18, 13), and cyanotic congenital heart disease (e.g., TGA).
General/CNS: Plethora, cyanosis, jaundice, lethargy, jitteriness, seizures, hypotonia, and cerebral venous thrombosis.
Cardiopulmonary: Cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and increased pulmonary vascular markings on X-ray.
Renal & GIT: Decreased GFR, decreased sodium excretion, renal vein thrombosis, poor feeding, and Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC).
Hematologic & Metabolic: Jaundice, petechiae, thrombocytopenia, DIC, hypoglycemia, and hypocalcemia.
Partial Exchange Transfusion: Indicated for all symptomatic polycythemic infants using Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP), normal saline, or 5% albumin to lower the Hematocrit to 50%–60%:

sections.title: Hemorrhagic Disease of the Newborn
blocks: Definition: A neonatal bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency of Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, and X). It occurs because the newborn's gut is sterile at birth and bacterial synthesis of Vitamin K is delayed, particularly in breastfed infants.

Classic Type: Manifests between Days 2 and 5 of life with gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis, melena, rectal bleeding), cutaneous bruising, bleeding from the nose, mouth, venipuncture sites, umbilical stump, or circumcision.

Early-Onset Type: Manifests within the first 24 hours of life. Associated with maternal ingestion of medications that interfere with Vitamin K during pregnancy (phenytoin, phenobarbital, salicylates, warfarin, rifampin, or INH).

Late-Onset Type: Manifests between 1 week and 6 months of life. Seen in infants with fat malabsorption, cholestasis, biliary atresia, or cystic fibrosis; intracranial hemorrhage is a frequent and dangerous complication.
Platelet Count, Bleeding Time (BT), and Fibrinogen: Normal.
Prothrombin Time (PT) and Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT): Markedly prolonged.
CBC: Normal, unless significant hemorrhage causes normocytic normochromic anemia.
Prophylaxis: Universal administration of a single intramuscular dose of 1 mg Vitamin K1 to all newborns at birth.
Slow IV infusion of 1–5 mg Vitamin K1 (stops bleeding within a few hours).
Fresh Frozen Plasma (10 mL/kg) for severe, active bleeding.
Transfusion of packed RBCs or whole blood to correct severe anemia.
Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia (NH): A biochemical term indicating an elevated Total Serum Bilirubin (TSB) >1 mg/dL.
Neonatal Jaundice (NJ): A clinical term referring to the yellowish discoloration of the sclera and skin.
While adults appear jaundiced when TSB exceeds 2–2.5 mg/dL, newborns manifest clinical jaundice only when TSB exceeds 5–7 mg/dL.

Marked indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia carries a risk of neurotoxicity and permanent brain damage (bilirubin encephalopathy / kernicterus), whereas direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia indicates underlying hepatic or metabolic disease.
Bilirubin processing involves four sequential physiological steps:
75% arises from the breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent RBCs within the reticuloendothelial system and ineffective erythropoiesis in the bone marrow (1 g of Hb generates 34 mg of bilirubin).
25% arises from non-erythroid heme sources in the liver (myoglobin, cytochromes, catalase, peroxidase).
Properties: Biliverdin is water-soluble, non-neurotoxic, and excretable; bilirubin is fat-soluble, crosses the blood-brain barrier, is neurotoxic, and non-excretable.
Unconjugated bilirubin travels in the bloodstream tightly bound to serum albumin (1 g of albumin binds up to 8.5 mg of bilirubin).
Bound bilirubin cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and is non-toxic.

Free (u nbound) bilirubin is neurotoxic and increases when TSB exceeds albumin-binding capacity or when displaced by drugs (e.g., sulfonamides, ampicillin, ceftriaxone, indomethacin, free fatty acids). Albumin infusion (0.5–1 g/kg) increases total binding capacity.
Uptake: Fat-soluble bilirubin dissociates from albumin in hepatic sinusoids, crosses the hepatocyte membrane, and binds to cytoplasmic ligandin (Y protein) to prevent efflux.

Conjugation: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin (UCB) is converted in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum to water-soluble, non-neurotoxic conjugated (direct) bilirubin (CB) by the enzyme uridine diphosphate glucuronyl transferase (UDP-GT).
Secretion: CB (monoglucuronide and diglucuronide) is actively transported across bile canaliculi into bile against a concentration gradient via an ATP-dependent transporter.
Note: Phenobarbital increases ligandin concentration, UDP-GT activity, and CB secretion.
CB passes through the biliary tree into the gastrointestinal tract.
The majority of CB is reduced by intestinal bacteria into urobilinogen and excreted in stool.
A small fraction of urobilinogen is reabsorbed and excreted in urine.
A small fraction of CB is converted back to UCB by the intestinal mucosal enzyme β-glucuronidase, reabsorbed into portal circulation, and returned to the liver (enterohepatic circulation).

sections.title: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia & Neonatal Jaundice
blocks: Fetomaternal blood group incompatibility (Rh, ABO, minor groups).
Intrauterine or neonatal infections (TORCH, bacterial sepsis).
Gastrointestinal obstruction (pyloric stenosis, intestinal atresia, Hirschsprung's disease).
Meconium ileus or meconium plug syndrome (Cystic fibrosis).
C. Extravascular Blood Accumulation: Cephalhematoma, cutaneous bruises, enclosed hemorrhages.
D. Polycythemia: Delayed cord clamping, materno-fetal or twin-to-twin transfusion.
Gilbert's disease (deficiency of ligandin / Y protein).
Crigler-Najjar syndrome Type I (complete absence of UDP-GT) and Type II (partial deficiency of UDP-GT).
Dubin-Johnson and Rotor's syndromes (defect in canalicular ATP-dependent transporter).
Intrahepatic biliary atresia / paucity of bile ducts.
Congenital TORCH infections, sepsis, RDS, perinatal asphyxia, Infant of Diabetic Mother (IDM), severe erythroblastosis fetalis (inspissated bile syndrome).

Detailed History: Family history of anemia/jaundice/gallstones; previous siblings requiring phototherapy/exchange transfusion; maternal illness during pregnancy (TORCH); maternal drug intake (sulfonamides); delivery events (trauma, oxytocin, delayed cord clamping, asphyxia); feeding history (caloric intake, vomiting).

Physical Examination: Assessment of gestational age (prematurity, SGA); search for pallor, petechiae, purpura, extravascular hematomas, cephalhematoma, hepatosplenomegaly, and signs of hypothyroidism.
1. Total and Direct Serum Bilirubin (TSB) or Transcutaneous Bilirubin (TcB).
2. Complete Blood Count (CBC) with reticulocyte count, Hct, and peripheral blood film for RBC morphology.
3. Maternal and infant blood grouping (ABO and Rh) and Coombs' test (direct and indirect).
4. Infection screening: CRP, blood/urine/CSF cultures, and serum TORCH titers.
5. Liver function panel (elevated direct bilirubin in cholestasis).
6. Special hemolytic screens: G6PD assay and osmotic fragility test.

sections.title: Physiological Jaundice
blocks: 1. Higher RBC mass per kg and shortened RBC lifespan (90 days vs. 120 days in adults) leading to increased bilirubin load.
2. Increased enterohepatic recirculation due to high levels of intestinal β- glucuronidase, low enteral intake, and absence of normal gut bacterial flora.
3. Impaired hepatic uptake and conjugation due to low levels of ligandin (Y protein) and low activity of UDP-GT.
Full-Term Infants: Appears on Days 2–3, peaks on Days 4–5 (peak level <12 mg/dL), and disappears by Days 6–8.
Preterm Infants: Appears on Days 3–4, peaks on Days 6–8 (peak level <15 mg/dL), and disappears by Days 10–12.
Rate of Bilirubin Rise: <0.2 mg/dL/hr or <5 mg/dL/24 hr.
Clinical Exam: Completely normal physical exam without lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia, or organomegaly.

sections.title: Pathological Jaundice
blocks: Jaundice is classified as pathological if it meets any of the following criteria:
1. Appearance of clinical jaundice within the first 24 hours of life.
2. Persistence of clinical jaundice beyond 14 days of life.
3. TSB exceeding >12 mg/dL in term or >15 mg/dL in preterm infants.
4. Rate of TSB rise exceeding >0.2 mg/dL/hr or >5 mg/dL/24 hr.
5. Direct (conjugated) bilirubin level ≥2 mg/dL or ≥ 20% of total TSB.
6. Presence of underlying clinical illness (lethargy, poor feeding, apnea, tachypnea, temperature instability, vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly, bleeding).
Pathophysiology & Timeline: Starts around Days 6–14 of life; serum bilirubin continues to rise instead of declining, reaching peak levels of 15–20 mg/dL before gradually declining over 3–10 weeks.
Diagnostic & Therapeutic Test: Temporary discontinuation of breastfeeding for 48 hours causes a prompt drop in serum bilirubin, confirming the diagnosis.
Differentiation: Must be distinguished from Early Breast-Feeding Jaundice (onset Days 2–4), which is caused by low fluid/caloric intake and increased enterohepatic recirculation.
Mechanism: Occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus (inherited from an Rh-positive father).
Sensitization: Fetomaternal hemorrhage during delivery, abortion, or invasive procedures introduces fetal D-antigen into maternal circulation.
First Pregnancy: Maternal immune response forms IgM anti-D antibodies, which cannot cross the placenta; the firstborn infant is unaffected.
Subsequent Pregnancies: Re-exposure to Rh-positive fetal cells triggers rapid production of IgG anti-D antibodies, which cross the placenta and cause fetal red cell destruction.
Severe: Hydrops Fetalis (severe fetal anemia, high-output heart failure, generalized edema, and ascites); managed in utero with intrauterine transfusion via fetoscopy.
Mild-to-Moderate: Early-onset severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and anemia appearing within 24 hours of birth.
Mechanism: Occurs when a Group O mother carries a fetus with Group A, B, or AB blood.
Features: Group O mothers possess naturally occurring IgG anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their serum.
1. Can affect the first pregnancy without prior maternal sensitization.
2. Causes milder hemolysis because A and B antigens are widely expressed on non - erythroid tissues, diluting antibody density on RBCs.
Increase enteral feedings (both volume and caloric density) to promote bowel motility and decrease enterohepatic recirculation.
Discontinue drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin.
Correct aggravating co-morbidities: hypoxia, acidosis, hypothermia, and infection.

Mechanism: Delivers light energy in the blue-green spectrum (430–490 nm) to photo-isomerize fat-soluble unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble structural isomers (lumirubin) excreted in bile and urine without conjugation.
Technical Standards: Irradiance >30\W/cm2/nm; light source positioned 30–40 cm from the infant; continuous exposure with shield protection over eyes and testicles; position changes every 2 hours.

Side Effects: Dehydration (increased insensible water loss), watery diarrhea, skin erythema/rash, temperature instability, retinal damage, and Bronze Baby Syndrome (dark grey-brown skin discoloration occurring if direct bilirubin is elevated).
Volume: Double-volume exchange calculated as 2 × 85 mL/kg.
Efficacy: Removes 50% –60% of circulating bilirubin, clears maternal anti-RBC antibodies, and corrects severe anemia.
Rh Incompatibility: Ideally, fresh packed O Rh-negative RBCs cross - matched against mother and baby, re-suspended in AB Rh-positive fresh frozen plasma; or fresh O Rh-negative whole blood.
ABO Incompatibility: Fresh O Rh-negative or O Rh-positive whole blood matching the infant's Rh type.
Other Causes (Infections/G6PD): Fresh whole blood matching the baby's own blood group.

Complications: Vascular thrombosis/embolism, cardiac arrhythmias, volume overload/arrest, electrolyte disturbances (hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia), thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, necrotizing enterocolitis, infections (HIV, Hepatitis B/C, sepsis), and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD).
Phenobarbital: Oral 4-5 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses; in duces hepatic ligandin (Y protein) and UDP-GT enzyme synthesis.
Inhibiting Enterohepatic Recirculation: Increased enteral feeds, oral agar, or oral activated charcoal to bind intestinal bilirubin.

Inhibiting Immune Hemolysis: High-dose Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) (0.5-1 g/kg) occupies Fc receptors on reticuloendothelial macrophages, blocking antibody-coated RBC uptake and hemolysis in Rh/ABO disease.

sections.title: Immunodeficiency Disorders
blocks: Deficiencies in host defense systems create an immunologic imbalance leading to increased
susceptibility to infections, autoimmune disorders, or malignancies. The host defense system is organized into three primary components:

Anatomic-Mucociliary Barrier: The skin and mucous membranes form the physical interface between the body and the external environment. Structural or anatomic defects must always be considered in children presenting with recurrent localized infections.
Innate Immunity: Rapid, non-specific first-line defense required for both immediate protection and activation of adaptive immunity:
Polymorphonuclear Neutrophils (PMNs): Ingest pyogenic bacteria and fungi.
Macrophages (derived from monocytes): Kill facultative intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium, Toxoplasma, and Legionella.
Natural Killer (NK) Lymphocytes: Mediate cytotoxic destruction of virally infected cells and malignant cells.
Complement Proteins: Activated in a sequential cascade to lyse pathogens or promote opsonization and phagocytosis.
Acute-Phase Proteins (e.g., C-Reactive Protein): Recognize damaged tissue and pathogens, activate complement, and trigger inflammatory cytokines.
Chemokines & Cytokines: Recruit inflammatory cells and regulate the overall immune response.
Adaptive Immunity: Antigen-specific responses mediated by T lymphocytes (cell - mediated immunity) and B lymphocytes (humoral immunity).
Phagocytic Disorders: Chediak-Higashi syndrome, Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD), Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).
B-Cell (Humoral) Disorders: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's), Common Variable Immunodeficiency (CVID).
T-Cell (Cellular) Disorders: X-linked Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
Complement Disorders: Congenital deficiencies of components C1 through C8, Hereditary Angioedema (HANE).
Categorized by Etiology: Congenital/embryogenesis defects (e.g., DiGeorge syndrome) and idiopathic causes.
Result from underlying systemic conditions or external therapies:
Viral Infections: Measles, Roseola, Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV.
Protein-Losing States: Nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy.

Other Causes: Prematurity, immunosuppressive medications (corticosteroids, radiation, antimetabolites), malignancies (leukemias, lymphomas), acquired asplenia, chronic blood transfusions, acquired neutropenia, bone marrow transplantation / Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD), Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), and sarcoidosis.

sections.title: Common Clinical Features of Immunodeficiency
blocks: The clinical signs of immunodeficiency are stratified by frequency of occurrence:
Persistent infections showing incomplete or no response to antimicrobial therapy.
Paucity (absence or marked underdeveloped size) of lymph nodes and tonsils.
Persistent sinusitis or mastoiditis (commonly caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. aureus, or Pseudomonas spp.).
Failure to thrive or growth retardation in infants/children; weight loss in adults.
Infections caused by unusual or opportunistic organisms.
Diverse skin lesions: rash, seborrhea, pyoderma, necrotic abscesses, alopecia, eczema, or telangiectasia.
Hearing loss secondary to chronic otitis media.
Evidence of autoimmunity (autoimmune thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia) and hematologic abnormalities (aplastic anemia, neutropenia).
Severe viral illness (e.g., severe varicella, herpes simplex).
Deep tissue infections (cellulitis, osteomyelitis, organ abscesses).
Chronic gastrointestinal inflammation, lymphoid hyperplasia, or sprue-like syndrome.
Autoimmune endocrinopathies/rheumatologic diseases (thyroiditis, pernicious anemia, alopecia).
Pyoderma gangrenosum, adverse reactions to live vaccines, delayed umbilical cord detachment, and chronic stomatitis/peritonitis.

sections.title: Initial Immunologic Testing of the Child with Recurrent Infections
blocks: When evaluating a child with recurrent infections, targeted screening tests assess specific immune compartments:
Complete Blood Count (CBC) with Differential & ESR: Evaluates total leukocytes and systemic inflammation.
Absolute Lymphocyte Count: Normal results generally rule against severe T-cell defects.
Absolute Neutrophil Count: Rules out congenital or acquired neutropenia and LAD (where counts are markedly elevated even between infections).
Platelet Count: Normal results exclude Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (which features micro-thrombocytopenia).
Howell-Jolly Bodies: Absence rules against functional or anatomic asplenia.
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): Normal results indicate chronic deep bacterial or fungal infections are unlikely.
Serum IgA measurement (if abnormal, measure IgG and IgM).
Specific antibody titers following immunization (Tetanus, Diphtheria, H. influenzae, Pneumococcus).
Candida albicans intradermal skin test (evaluates delayed-type hypersensitivity; 0.1 mL of 1:1,000 dilution for age ≥ 6 years; 1:100 dilution for age < 6 years).
Respiratory burst assay (e.g., evaluation for Chronic Granulomatous Disease).
Serum CH50 assay (measures total classical complement pathway activity).

sections.title: General Management of Patients with Immunodeficiency
blocks: 1. Blood Product Safety: Avoid blood transfusions unless products are irradiated and CMV-negative to prevent fatal Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD) and opportunistic CMV transmission.
2. Vaccine Precautions: Strictly avoid live virus vaccines in patients with severe T-cell defects or severe agammaglobulinemia, as well as in their household contacts.
3. Pulmonary Care: Monitor serial pulmonary function tests, and utilize chest physiotherapy and postural drainage in patients with recurrent pneumonia to prevent bronchiectasis.
4. Infection Prophylaxis & Management: Use prophylactic antibiotics, as minor localized infections can rapidly disseminate. Promptly evaluate diarrheal stool for Giardia and Clostridium difficile.
5. Exposure Reduction: Avoid unnecessary exposure to individuals with active contagious infections.
6. Immunoglobulin Replacement: Administer Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) at a dose of 400–500 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks for severe antibody deficiency states.

sections.title: Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS)
blocks: Definition & Etiology: AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 (HIV- 1), a retrovirus that produces a profound primary deficiency in T-cell immunity and secondary B-cell dysfunction in children.
Perinatal (Vertical) Transmission: Accounts for ~85% of pediatric cases (transmission risk is 20–25% without intervention, with a large proportion occurring during delivery).
Breastfeeding: Transmits HIV from an infected mother to her infant.
Blood & Organ Products: Contaminated blood transfusions or tissue transplants.
Adolescent Transmission: Acquired via sexual contact and intravenous drug abuse.
Progressive depletion of CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes.
Impaired T-cell and mononuclear macrophage function.
Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia with impaired synthesis of specific functional antibodies.
Category E: Perinatally exposed infant (infection unconfirmed).
Category A (Mildly Symptomatic): Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, parotitis, recurrent upper respiratory infections, and otitis media.
Category B (Moderately Symptomatic): Chronic oral candidiasis, persistent diarrhea, failure to thrive, anemia, thrombocytopenia, Lymphocytic Interstitial Pneumonitis (LIP), and cardiomyopathy.

Category C (Severely Symptomatic / AIDS-Defining): Recurrent serious bacterial infections, opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia [PCP], Mycobacterium avium-complex, Candida esophagitis, disseminated cryptococcosis, toxoplasmosis, cryptosporidiosis, disseminated TB), wasting syndrome, progressive encephalopathy (developmental delay, paresis, dystonia, brain atrophy/calcifications), and malignancies (lymphoma).

Infants <18 Months (Perinatal Exposure): Transplacental maternal IgG antibodies persist up to 18 months, making standard ELISA/Western blot unreliable. Diagnosis requires HIV p24 antigen detection, HIV DNA/RNA PCR, or viral culture of blood lymphocytes.
Children >18 Months: Confirmed via ELISA and Western blot serology.

Antiretroviral Therapy (ART): Combination therapy using nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (Zidovudine/AZT, Didanosine/ddI, Zalcitabine/ddC, Stavudine/d4T, Lamivudine/3TC) and Protease Inhibitors.
Recommended for all perinatally exposed infants from 6 weeks to 12 months of age.
For infected children aged 1–6 years if CD4 < 500/uL; for >6 years if CD4 < 200/uL.
Drug of Choice: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) administered 3 days per week (or Dapsone if TMP-SMX is not tolerated).
Prevention: Antiretroviral treatment (ZDV) of HIV-infected mothers during pregnancy and labor, decreasing births to infected women, and avoiding breastfeeding where safe formula options exist.
Age of Onset: T-cell defects present early in the neonatal period, whereas B-cell defects typically manifest after 6 months of age as maternal transplacental IgG wanes.
Transfusion Safety: Blood transfusions in patients with T-cell defects must be irradiated to prevent fatal Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD).
Severe dental caries is a frequent presenting sign in B-cell defects.
Skin or internal organ abscesses point toward phagocytic defects.
Eczematous skin rash occurs in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and Hyper-IgE syndrome.
Petechial skin rash with thrombocytopenia is specifically characteristic of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

sections.title: Bronchial Asthma
blocks: Asthma is a heterogeneous disease usually characterized by chronic airway inflammation.
It is defined by a history of respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough.
Trigger Exposure: Antigens activate a cellular response involving T-lymphocytes, B - cells, neutrophils, mast cells, and eosinophils.
Mediator Release: Inflammatory cells release mediators including cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, GM-CSF, IL-13), leukotrienes (LTs), platelet-activating factor (PAF), and histamine.
Airway Changes: Mediators induce mucosal edema, mucus hyper-secretion, and smooth muscle contraction.
Airway Obstruction: Results in the characteristic clinical presentation of coughing, breathlessness, wheezing, and chest tightness.
Respiratory Infections: Viral respiratory tract infections are common triggers.
Allergens: Indoor inhalants, animal dander, house dust mites, pollens, and grass.
Irritants: Tobacco smoke and cold air.
Other Factors: Direct animal contact, weather changes, exercise, and emotional stress.
Gastroesophageal Reflux (GERD): Increases airway reactivity mediated through a vagal reflex.
1. Recurrent Wheezing in Early Childhood: Primarily triggered by common viral infections of the respiratory tract.
2. Chronic Asthma Associated with Allergy: Persists into later childhood and often adulthood.
Clinical index used to define the risk of asthma in young children presenting with recurrent wheezing:
Major Criteria: Parent with asthma, clinical diagnosis of eczema, or inhalant allergen sensitization.
Minor Criteria: Allergic rhinitis, wheezing apart from colds, blood eosinophils >4%, or food allergen sensitization.
6. Clinical Picture of Acute Asthma Exacerbation
Symptoms: Shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough, wheezy chest, and non-focal chest pain.
Inspection: Increased respiratory rate, chest indrawing (accessory muscle use), and cyanosis in severe attacks.
Auscultation: Diminished air entry, harsh vesicular breathing with prolonged expiration, expiratory wheezing (sibilant or sonorous), and crepitations/rales due to excessive secretions.
Pulmonary Index Score: Based on respiratory rate, wheezing, inspiration:expiration ratio, and accessory muscle use:
Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR): Measured using a Peak Flow Meter.
Oxygen Saturation & Arterial Blood Gases (ABG): Evaluated using Wood's score for respiratory lung function.
Transient N on-Atopic Wheezing: Common in early preschool years; recurrent cough/wheeze triggered by viral URTI that usually resolves without increased risk for future asthma.
Persistent Atopy-Associated Asthma: Begins in early preschool years, strongly associated with clinical or biological atopy, carrying the highest risk for persistence into adulthood.
Severity: Classified as Intermittent vs. Persistent (Mild, Moderate, or Severe).
Control Level: Well controlled, Not well controlled, or Very poorly controlled.
Management Patterns: Easy-to-control, Difficult-to-control, Exacerbators, or Refractory.
Clinical Evaluation: Suggestive medical history and characteristic clinical exam findings.
Radiology: Chest X-ray to exclude alternative thoracic pathologies.
Functional & Laboratory Tests: Pulmonary function testing, total and specific serum IgE, skin prick testing, provocation/challenge testing, and elimination diets.

Diagnostic Indicators: High suspicion if wheezing/cough occurs with exercise, laughter, or crying without an infection; presence of personal/familial atopy; or rapid clinical response to inhaled short-acting bronchodilators or controller therapy.
Upper Respiratory Tract: Allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinitis, sinusitis, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, nasal foreign body.

Middle Respiratory Tract: Laryngotracheobronchomalacia, laryngotracheobronchitis, laryngeal web/cyst/stenosis, chronic bronchitis, vocal cord paralysis, tracheoesophageal fistula, vascular rings/slings, foreign body aspiration.

Lower Respiratory Tract: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), viral bronchiolitis, GERD, tuberculosis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, chronic aspiration, primary ciliary dyskinesia).
Non-Pharmacologic Pillars: Patient and parent education, environmental control/trigger avoidance, self-monitoring, and scheduled follow-up visits.
Rescuers: Rapid-acting inhaled beta2 agonists (SABA; e.g., Salbutamol).
Controllers: Inhaled glucocorticosteroids (ICS), long-acting beta2 agonists (LABA; add-on for >5 years), leukotriene modifiers (Montelukast), and Theophylline (with plasma level monitoring).
Supplemental Oxygen: Delivered by face mask (1 L/min) targeting SpO 2 94– 98%).
Short-Acting beta2-Agonist (SABA): (2–6) puffs of Salbutamol via sp acer or 2.5 mg via nebulizer every 20 minutes for the first hour.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Oral Prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg, max 20 mg for children <2 years).
Ipratropium Bromide: Added (1–2) puffs or 250 mcg nebulized every 20 minutes for 1 hour) in moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
Nebulized Magnesium Sulfate: Isotonic 150 mg (3 doses in first hour) for children ≥2 years with severe exacerbations.

sections.title: Status Asthmaticus
blocks: Status asthmaticus is a clinical diagnosis defined by increasingly severe asthma that is not responsive to drugs that are usually effective.
2. Factors Associated with Increased Risk of Severe Exacerbation

History Indicators: Steroid-dependent asthma, prior ICU admission/mechanical ventilation, sudden-onset distress, poor therapy compliance, poor recognition of attack severity, or prior respiratory arrest, severe hypoxia, or seizures.

Physical Exam Indicators: Pulsus paradoxus >20 mmHg, hypotension, severe tachycardia, tachypnea, cyanosis, severe dyspnea, lethargy/agitation, suprasternal/intercostal retractions, or a "quiet chest" with severe respiratory distress.
Therapeutic Indicators: Over-reliance on inhalers, delayed systemic steroid administration, sedation, or delayed hospital/ICU admission.
3. ICU Management Protocol for Status Asthmaticus
1. Oxygenation: Administer O2 (2–3 L/min) maintaining SpO2 > 92% and PaO2 > 70 mmHg.
2. Baseline Diagnostic Tests: Immediate ABG, CBC, serum electrolytes, and chest X-ray.
3. Continuous Monitoring: Cardiac and respiratory monitoring (if HR >160/min), temporarily pause beta2-agonists to evaluate for heart failure.
4. Hydration & Electrolytes: IV fluid rehydration at 60% maintenance dose with potassium supplementation (to correct β₂-agonist-induced hypokalemia).
5. Inhaled Bronchodilators: Inhaled β₂-agonist every 20 minutes (or continuous) plus Ipratropium bromide (250–500 mcg) every 20 minutes for the first hour only).
6. IV Aminophylline: Administer 5 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes every 6 hours (or continuous 0.75–1.25 mg/kg/hr), maintaining serum levels between 12–15 mcg/mL.
7. Parenteral beta2-agonists: If unresponsive, start IV Terbutaline 10 mcg IV bolus then 0.6 mcg/kg/min continuous infusion up to 6 mcg/kg/min or IM Epinephrine.
8. IV Corticosteroids: IV Methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) 1–2 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours for 48 hours, followed by 1–2 mg/kg/day.
9. Acid-Base Correction: IV Sodium Bicarbonate infusion in the presence of metabolic acidosis.
10. IV Magnesium Sulfate: 40–50 mg/kg IV (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes for children >2 years of age.
11. Mechanical Ventilation: Initiate volume-cycled mechanical ventilation if serial ABGs show lack of response.
Avoid exposure to environmental tobacco smoke during pregnancy and the first year of life.
Advise breastfeeding for general health benefits.
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic use during the first year of life. Organ specific allergic disorders and food allergy

sections.title: Allergy: Definitions & Core Concepts
blocks: Allergic / Atopic Patient: An individual displaying an altered state of reactivity to common environmental and food antigens that do not cause reactions in unaffected individuals.

Allergic Diseases Spectrum: These represent the most common chronic conditions affecting children and young adults; most are partially controllable but not curable. Different allergic conditions frequently coexist in the same child.
Hypersensitivity: Objectively reproducible symptoms or signs initiated following exposure to a defined stimulus (e.g., food, drug, pollen) at a dose that is usually tolerated by most people.
Allergy: A hypersensitivity reaction initiated by specific immunological mechanisms, which can be IgE-mediated (e.g., peanut allergy) or non-IgE-mediated (e.g., celiac disease).

Atopy: A personal and/or familial tendency to produce IgE antibodies in response to ordinary exposures to potential environmental allergens (usually proteins). Strongly associated with asthma, allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, eczema, and food allergy.
Immune Tolerance: The absence of an active immune response against a particular antigen (e.g., the normal absence of an allergic immune response to peanuts or house dust mites).

Sensitization: Demonstrating a positive test to an allergen via a skin prick test or specific IgE assay. Sensitization alone does not equate to active clinical allergy unless a clinical reaction occurs upon exposure; however, a higher number of positive tests increases the likelihood of clinical allergy.
The Allergic (Atopic) March: The natural disease progression where infants initially presenting with food allergy and eczema subsequently develop allergic rhinitis and/or asthma later in childhood.
Anaphylaxis, Allergic rhinitis, Allergic conjunctivitis, Asthma, Atopy, Drug allergy, Eczema (Atopic dermatitis), Food allergy, Insect sting hypersensitivity, and Urticaria.

sections.title: Anaphylaxis
blocks: An acute, life-threatening systemic IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction characterized by urticaria, acute airway obstruction, and circulatory collapse. It has a rapid onset and may cause death.
Foods: Peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, seeds, fruits, and grains.
Drugs: Penicillin, cephalosporins, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opiates, muscle relaxants, thiamine, vitamin B2, and insulin.
Hymenoptera Venom: Honeybee, yellow jacket, wasp, hornet, and fire ant stings.
Allergen Immunotherapy: Desensitization injections or extracts.
Exercise: Food-specific exercise-induced or postprandial (non-food-specific) exercise - induced.
Vaccinations: Tetanus, measles, mumps, and influenza vaccines.
Miscellaneous & Idiopathic: Radiocontrast media, intravenous immunoglobulins, cold temperature, chemotherapeutic agents, blood products, inhalants, or idiopathic causes.
Onset occurs within minutes to hours after antigen exposure due to mediator release from mast cells and basophils:
Respiratory: Edema of the larynx and epiglottis (causing hoarseness and stridor), bronchospasm, hypoxia, nasal congestion, sneezing, and rhinorrhea.
Circulatory: Vasodilation, intravascular volume loss, hypotension, circulatory collapse, cardiac arrhythmias, palpitations, and syncope.
Gastrointestinal: Vomiting, diarrhea, dysphagia, and abdominal cramps.
1. Rapid assessment of airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs), dermatologic examination, and mental status.
2. Intramuscular Epinephrine: Administer 0.01 mg/kg (1:1,000 solution) IM; repeat every 20 minutes as needed.
3. Oxygenation & Airway: Administer 100% oxygen; secure and maintain a patent airway.
4. IV Resuscitation: Establish large-bore IV access and infuse isotonic IV fluids (20 mL/kg), repeating as necessary.
5. Continuous vital sign, cardiac, and pulse oximetry monitoring.
6. Rapid focused history regarding triggering events, known allergies, current medications, and underlying asthma.
1. H₁ Antagonist: Diphenhydramine (1–2 mg/kg PO, IM, or IV).
2. Corticosteroids: Prednisone (1 mg/kg PO) or Methylprednisolone (1–2 mg/kg IV).
3. Inhaled Bronchodilators: Nebulized Albuterol/Salbutamol (1.25–2.5 mg) every 20 minutes or continuously.
Prevention: Strict avoidance of known triggering antigens, prescription of emergency epinephrine self-administration auto-injector kits, and wearing medical identification bracelets.

sections.title: Hereditary Angioedema
blocks: A dominantly inherited disorder caused by either a defective function or an absolute deficiency of the C1 esterase inhibitor enzyme.
Features recurrent cutaneous swelling without accompanying urticaria.
Airway Involvement: Swelling of upper airways leading to life-threatening respiratory compromise.
Gastrointestinal Involvement: Intestinal wall edema presenting with severe colicky abdominal pain.
Acute Attack Treatment: Recombinant C1 inhibitor concentrate or kinin receptor antagonists.
Long-Term Prophylaxis: Low-dose anabolic steroids or tranexamic acid.

sections.title: Allergic Rhinitis
blocks: A disorder of the nasal mucosa characterized by nasal blockage, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and nasal pruritus.
Seasonal Allergic Rhinitis (Hay Fever): Triggered by outdoor pollens and grasses; presents with rhinorrhea, nasal blockage, sneezing, and pale nasal mucosa on physical exam.
Chronic / Perennial Rhinitis: Primarily caused by indoor year-round allergens such as house dust mites, animal dander, mold, and cockroaches.
Vasomotor Rhinitis: Non-allergic rhinitis resulting from local autonomic nervous system imbalance.
Episodic Rhinitis: Occurs intermittently upon casual exposure to specific external allergens.
Non-Anatomical: Non-allergic non-infectious (vasomotor) rhinitis, infectious rhinosinusitis, non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome (NARES), physical rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa.
Anatomical: Adenoidal hypertrophy, CSF rhinorrhea, choanal atresia, congenital anomalies, nasal foreign body, nasal polyps, septal deviation, tumors, turbinate hypertrophy.
2. Pharmacotherapy: Antihistamines, nasal decongestants, topical/systemic corticosteroids, and atropine-like anticholinergic nasal sprays.

sections.title: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema)
blocks: A common, intens ely pruritic, maculo-papular erythematous chronic skin disorder that usually begins in infancy and follows a chronic, fluctuating course with seasonal variations.
Infants & Young Children: Involves predominantly the face (sparing the nose), trunk, and extensor surfaces of the arms. Lesions are typically erythematous, papulo-vesicular, and exudative.
Older Children: Distribution shifts to flexural skin surfaces (elbow and knee flexures). Lesions are predominantly dry, hyperkeratotic, and lichenified.
Oral non-sedating antihistamines to control itching.
Frequent application of skin lubricants and moisturizers.
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial skin infections.
Topical corticosteroids applied to active inflammatory lesions.

sections.title: Food Allergy
blocks: An immune system reaction occurring shortly after consuming a specific food; even tiny amounts of the offending protein can trigger clinical signs ranging from digestive symptoms to hives or swollen airways.
Over 80% of affected children present during the first year of life, and many have co - existing atopic eczema.
Over 90% of pediatric food allergies are caused by eight primary food groups:
Clinical Picture: Symptoms appear rapidly, usually within 30 minutes (up to 1–2 hours) after food ingestion:
Gastrointestinal: Acute vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps.
Skin: Erythema, acute urticaria, and angioedema.
Diagnosis: Skin prick testing, serum specific IgE antibody assay, and diagnostic oral food challenge.

Treatment: Strict dietary elimination of the causative protein, dietetic counseling, and a written emergency action plan with rescue medications (non-sedating antihistamines +/ - epinephrine auto-injector). Reactions often persist into late childhood and adulthood.
Clinical Picture: Symptoms have a delayed onset, appearing 2 to 72 hours after food consumption:

Gastrointestinal: Delayed vomiting, excessive crying ("colic"), altered bowel transit (loose/frequent stools or severe constipation), abdominal cramps, food refusal/aversion, and blood or mucus in stools.
Systemic & Skin: Growth failure (failure to thrive) and persistent or worsening eczema.
Treatment: Trial diagnostic elimination of the suspected food protein followed by re - introduction, prolonged dietary elimination of proven causative proteins, and specialized dietetic support.

sections.title: Drug Hypersensitivity
blocks: The true rate of confirmed drug hypersensitivity in children is low.
Children with documented genuine drug allergy must avoid not only the specific primary drug but also cross-reactive pharmaceutical agents.
Severe, life-threatening idiosyncratic drug reactions can occasionally occur.

sections.title: Insect Sting Hypersensitivity
blocks: Most commonly caused by stings from bees and wasps.
Large Local Reactions: Painful, extensive swelling surrounding the sting site.
Systemic Reactions: True sting allergy presents with severe systemic involvement (anaphylactic shock and/or respiratory compromise) in 10% to 25% of cases.
Intramuscular Adrenaline (Epinephrine) for systemic anaphylactic manifestations.

sections.title: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)
blocks: Chronic arthritis of one or more joints occurring for at least 6 weeks in a child younger than 16 years of age.
Arthritis is defined clinically as joint swelling or the presence of two or more of the following: heat, pain on motion, or limitation of motion.
Oligoarticular JIA: Involves 4 joints or fewer. It occurs more frequently in girls, with a peak incidence in children between 2 and 4 years of age.
Polyarticular JIA: Involves more than 4 joints. It is more common in girls and displays two peak ages of onset: 1 to 4 years and 6 to 12 years.
Systemic-Onset JIA: Characterized by spiking fever and systemic inflammation.
Immunogenetic Susceptibility: Underpinned by underlying genetic predisposition.
Environmental Triggers: Viral infections, such as Parvovirus B-19, Rubella, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Immune Dysregulation: Enhanced T-cell reactivity to bacterial proteins.
Initial Presentation: Morning stiffness, easy fatigability, joint pain later in the day, pain on movement, and joint swelling.
Oligoarticular Subtype: Predominantly affects joints of the lower limbs, especially the knee and ankle; the hip joint is notably not involved.
Polyarticular Subtype: Involves both large and small joints (20% to 40% of cases). Rheumatoid nodules may develop on the extensor surfaces of the elbows and Achilles tendon.
Fever: Intermittent spiking fever with daily temperature spikes for a minimum of 2 weeks.
Rash: An evanescent, salmon-colored, circular macular rash (2–5 mm) occurring on the trunk and proximal extremities during fever spikes.
Koebner Phenomenon: Cutaneous hypersensitivity demonstrating rash formation secondary to superficial skin trauma.
Organ & Tissue Involvement: Arthritis, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis (pericardial effusion), and uveitis.
Permanent joint damage and persistent arthritis leading to significant disability.
Psychosocial impact, including anxiety and frequent school absenteeism.
Inflammatory Markers: Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and increased C-Reactive Protein (CRP).
Hematology: Leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and anemia of chronic disease.
Serology: Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) titer is increased in 40% to 85% of cases. Rheumatoid Factor (RF) is positive in 8% of polyarticular cases.

Imaging: X-rays of the hands and cervical spine show soft tissue swelling, osteoporosis, periostitis, cartilage erosions, and bony destruction/fusion. MRI of affected joints provides detailed evaluation.
Ophthalmologic Screening: Slit-lamp eye examination is mandatory to detect asymptomatic iridocyclitis and scleritis.
Methotrexate: The safest and most effective DMARD, dosed at 10–15 mg/m²/week orally or IM.
Other DMARDs include Sulfasalazine, Hydroxychloroquine, D-penicillamine, Gold salts, and IVIG.

Third-Line Therapy (Glucocorticoids): Oral Prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg/day) used as bridge therapy in severe systemic cases. Local topical or intra-articular steroid drops/injections are used for iridocyclitis.
Fourth-Line Therapy: Cytotoxic immunosuppressive agents such as Azathioprine and Cyclophosphamide.

sections.title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
blocks: Definition: A chronic, multisystem, autoimmune disease characterized by periods of increased disease activity caused by inflammation of blood vessels and connective tissue.

Pathogenesis: Loss of T-lymphocyte regulatory control leads to hyperactivity of B - lymphocytes and massive production of circulating autoantibodies. These autoantibodies form immune complexes that become trapped in microvasculature, triggering tissue inflammation and ischemia.
1. Malar Rash: Fixed, flat or raised erythema over the malar eminences, tending to spare the nasolabial folds.
2. Discoid Rash: Erythematous raised patches with adherent keratotic scaling; older lesions may show atrophic scarring.
3. Photosensitivity: Skin rash resulting from an unusual reaction to sunlight.
4. Oral Ulcers: Painless oral or nasopharyngeal ulcerations observed by a physician.
5. Arthritis: Non-erosive arthritis involving 2 or more peripheral joints, characterized by tenderness, swelling, or effusion.
6. Serositis: Pleurisy (pleuritic chest pain or friction rub) or pericarditis.
7. Renal Disorders: Persistent proteinuria > 0.5 g/day or > 3+ or cellular casts (red cell, hemoglobin, granular, tubular, or mixed).
8. Neurological Disorders: Seizures or psychosis occurring in the absence of offending drugs or metabolic derangements (e.g., uremia, ketoacidosis, electrolyte imbalance).
9. Hematological Disorders: Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia (with reticulocytosis), leukopenia <4,000/μL, lymphopenia <1,500/μL, or thrombocytopenia <100,000/μL.
10. Antinuclear Antibodies: Abnormal titer of ANA at any point in time in the absence of drugs associated with drug-induced lupus.
11. Hypocomplementemia: Low or undetectable serum C3 and C4 complement levels.
Peak age of onset is approximately 12 years.
Driven by genetic factors and triggered by environmental events: sun exposure, drug reactions, pubertal hormonal shifts, and infections.
General: Fatigue, fever, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Skin: Malar rash and discoid lesions.
Musculoskeletal: Arthralgia, non-erosive arthritis, myalgia, and myositis.
Renal: Glomerulonephritis, hypertension, nephrotic syndrome, and progress to renal failure.
Cardiovascular: Pericarditis (with risk of cardiac tamponade) and valvular thickening.
Neurologic: Seizures, psychosis, ischemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, and aseptic meningitis.
Pulmonary: Pleuritic pain, pulmonary hemorrhage, and pneumonitis.
Gastrointestinal: Pancreatitis, mesenteric arteritis, serositis, chronic lupoid hepatitis, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly.
Reproductive: Repeated spontaneous fetal loss, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and congenital heart block.
Chemistry & Inflammatory Markers: Hypoalbuminemia, elevated serum creatinine, and elevated ESR with characteristically normal CRP levels.
ANA: Positive in 99% of SLE patients.
Anti-dsDNA: Highly specific for SLE; present in >75% of active cases.
Anti-Smith (Anti-Sm): Highly specific for SLE; present in up to 50% of patients.
Complement Monitoring: Low C3 and C4 levels reflect disease flares.
Mainstay Therapy: Hydroxychloroquine is a core maintenance drug.
NSAIDs: Used as first-line agents for mild articular/serosal symptoms alongside hydroxychloroquine.
Corticosteroids: Pulse IV Methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day for 3 days), followed by oral Prednisolone (1–2 mg/kg/day) tapered over months as complement levels rise.

sections.title: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura
blocks: Definition: An autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation and narrowing of blood vessels (arteries, veins, and capillaries).
Large-Vessel: Takayasu arteritis, Giant cell arteritis.
Medium-Vessel: Polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, Rheumatoid vasculitis.
Definition: A small-vessel vasculitis of unknown etiology characterized by tissue leukocytic infiltration, vascular inflammation, hemorrhage, and ischemia.

Etiology: Caused by an abnormal immune response following environmental triggers. Approximately two-thirds of cases develop days after an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). Some cases are linked to post-vaccinations (typhoid, cholera, yellow fever, measles, or hepatitis B).
Skin (Hallmark): Palpable purpura —raised, palpable hemorrhagic skin lesions occurring in the absence of thrombocytopenia.
Constitutional: Low-grade fever and fatigue in over 50% of children.
Joints: Arthritis or arthralgia occurs in 75% of children, most commonly affecting the ankles and knees.
Gastrointestinal: GI vasculitis presenting with bowel angina, diffuse abdominal pain, or bowel ischemia.
Renal & Other Systems: Renal vasculitis (hematuria, proteinuria, acute nephritis), pancreatitis, and orchitis.
1. Pediatric Age Group: Onset of symptoms at ≤ years of age.
2. Palpable Purpura: Raised hemorrhagic skin lesions without low platelets.
3. Bowel Angina: Diffuse abdominal pain or clinical bowel ischemia.
4. Diagnostic Skin Biopsy: Histologic changes showing granulocytic infiltration within arteriole and venule walls.
NSAIDs: Short-term course for acute arthritis.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Oral Prednisone (1 mg/kg/day for 1–2 weeks, followed by tapering) indicated for severe gastrointestinal bleeding or acute nephritis.

sections.title: Kawasaki Disease
blocks: An acute febrile medium-sized vessel vasculitis syndrome of early childhood that notably targets the coronary arteries.
Requires fever lasting longer than 5 days plus at least 4 of the 5 following main clinical features:
1. Changes in Peripheral Extremities: Initial erythema or edema of palms and soles, followed by membranous desquamation of finger and toe tips, and transverse nail grooves (Beau's lines).
2. Polymorphous Rash: Non-vesicular rash, usually generalized or concentrated in the groin and lower extremities.
3. Oropharyngeal Changes: Erythema, fissuring, and crusting of the lips; "strawberry tongue"; and diffuse mucosal injection of the oropharynx.
4. Conjunctival Changes: Bilateral, non-purulent, painless bulbar conjunctivitis.
5. Cervical Lymphadenopathy: Unilateral cervical lymph node enlargement with a diameter >1.5 cm.

sections.title: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF)
blocks: A genetic autoinflammatory disorder causing recurrent fevers and painful inflammation of the abdomen, chest, and joints. It predominantly affects individuals of Mediterranean ancestry (Jewish, Arab, Armenian, Turkish, North African, Greek, or Italian).
Attack Paroxysms: Symptoms occur in paroxysmal attacks lasting 48 to 96 hours.
Periodic Fever: Temperature rises rapidly to 38–40°C in predictable cycles lasting 3–5 days every month or several times per year.
Serositis & Pain: Severe abdominal pain (peritonitis) with fever, pleuriti s, and pericarditis.
Other Features: Scrotal swelling and pain (mimicking testicular torsion), arthritis, arthralgia, and myalgia.
Secondary AA Amyloidosis: Deposition of amyloid protein causing persistent proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, and terminal renal failure.
Renal Vein Thrombosis: Develops in one-third of patients who progress to amyloidosis.
Prognosis Note: Long-term compliance with colchicine therapy prevents amyloidosis and extends survival.

sections.title: Limping Child
blocks: An abnormal gait usually caused by pain, muscle weakness, or physical deformity.
2. Non-Accidental Injury & Neoplastic Diseases: Such as Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).
3. Hematological Diseases: Such as Sickle Cell Disease.
4. Infective Diseases: Such as pyomyositis or discitis.
6. Neuromuscular Diseases: Such as cerebral palsy or muscular dystrophy.
7. Trauma & Anatomic Abnormalities: Such as limb length discrepancy.
8. Rheumatological Diseases: Such as Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.

sections.title: Fever
blocks: Definition: Defined as a rectal temperature ≥38°C; a temperature >40°C is termed hyperpyrexia. Normal body temperature fluctuates within a defined range 36.6–37.9°C rectally, reaching its peak in the early evening and its lowest point in the morning.
Febrile Patients at Increased Risk of Serious Bacterial Infections:
Immunocompetent Patients: Neonates, patients with hyperpyrexia (>40°C), and children presenting with fever accompanied by petechiae.
Immunocompromised Patients: Children with sickle cell disease, asplenia, primary immunodeficiency, malignancy, congenital heart disease, or central venous lines.
Patterns of Fever: Intermittent, sustained, remittent, relapsing, biphas ic, periodic, and factitious fever.
Acetaminophen: 10–15 mg/kg/dose orally, repeated every 4 hours as needed.
Ibuprofen: 5–10 mg/kg/dose orally, repeated every 8 hours (indicated in children ≥ 6 months of age).
Aspirin: Not recommended in pediatric fever due to the risk of developing Reye syndrome.

sections.title: Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)
blocks: Definition: Documented fever >38.3°C (101°F) lasting for at least 8 days, in which no clear diagnosis is established after initial outpatient or inpat ient evaluation (comprising a thorough history, physical exam, and initial screening laboratory tests).

FUO vs. Fever Without Focus (FWF): FWF refers to an acute fever where the source has not yet been identified upon initial evaluation; it is distinguished from FUO by duration (FWF can evolve into FUO if no cause is found after 7--8 days).
Causes: Infectious, rheumatologic (autoimmune/connective tissue), autoinflammatory, oncologic, neurologic, genetic, and factitious/iatrogenic processes.
Evaluation: Requires systematic history and physical examination, screening laboratory tests, and targeted secondary laboratory or imaging studies guided by initial findings.

sections.title: Acute Exanthematous Diseases
blocks: Infectious Causes: Rubella (German measles), Roseola infantum, Erythema infectiosum, Infectious mononucleosis (EBV), Scarlet fever, Enteroviral infections, and Typhoid fever.
Noninfectious Causes: Sweat rash, drug rash, and childhood rheumatic diseases.

Infectious Causes: Varicella (Chickenpox), Herpes simplex virus (HSV), Variola virus (smallpox), Monkeypox, Coxsackie virus (Hand-foot and mouth disease), and Impetigo / Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).
Noninfectious Causes: Papular urticaria, insect bites, and drug rashes.

sections.title: Measles (Rubeola)
blocks: Essentials of Diagnosis: History of exposure 8 --12 days prior; a 3 --5 day prodromal phase (fever, conjunctivitis with photophobia, coryza, and prominent cough); Koplik's spots; and a confluent maculopapular rash.
Transmission & Host: Humans are the only natural host; transmitted via contact with respiratory secretions or droplets.
Period of Infectivity: Extends from 4 days prior to until 5 days after the appearance of the rash.
Prodromal Phase: Mild fever followed by conjunctivitis, photophobia, coryza, harsh cough, and Koplik's spots (small white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the premolars).

Exanthem Phase: Onset of the red maculopapular rash starts at the hairline/forehead, behind the ears, and upper neck, spreading downward over the trunk and limbs while prodromal symptoms begin to subside. Prominent cervical and occipital lymphadenopathy is common in severe cases.

Diagnosis & Differential Diagnosis: Diagnosed clinically. Differentiated from Rubella, Roseola, Infectious Mononucleosis, Toxoplasmosis, Scarlet fever, Meningococcemia, Kawasaki disease, and drug rashes.
Complications: Otitis media and pneumonia (mos t common); rare, severe encephalitis; and diarrhea with dehydration or dysentery.

Treatment: Supportive care, oral Vitamin A as a single dose (200,000 IU for children ≥1 year; 100,000 IU for 6 --12 months; 50,000 IU for infants <6 months, and broad - spectrum antibiotics for secondary bacterial infections.
Prevention & Post-Exposure Prophylaxis: Isolation from day 7 post-exposure to 5 days post-rash; active immunization with Measles vaccine.
Exposure within 48 hours: Administer Measles vaccine to confer lasting immunity.
Exposure within 2 --5 days: Administer intramuscular Immunoglobulin (0.25 mL/kg for prevention, or 0.5 mL/kg for attenuation).

sections.title: Rubella (German Measles)
blocks: Etiology & Transmission: Caused by the Rubella virus (an RNA virus); transmitted via respiratory droplets, direct contact, or transplacentally.
Incubation & Contagiousness: Incubation period is 2 --3 weeks. Contagious 7 days before until 7--8 days after rash disappearance; infants with congenital rubella shed virus for ≥10–12 months.

Clinical Manifestations: Prodromal stage is very short and mild. Tender suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy is evident at least 24 hours before the rash appears. The rash starts on the face and spreads rapidly: on day 2 it becomes pinpoint and scarlatiniform with mild itching, and by day 3 it disappears without scarring or significant desquamation.
Complications & Treatment: Complications include arthritis/arthralgia a nd encephalitis. Managed supportively with antipyretics.

First-trimester maternal infection disrupts organogenesis, causing intrauterine growth retardation (SGA/FTT), sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, mental retardation, congenital heart disease (Patent Ductus Arteriosus, Pulmonary Stenosis), cataracts, glaucoma, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone lesions.

Pregnancy Management: Termination is recommended if clinical rubella, a 4-fold IgG titer rise, or IgM positivity is confirmed in the 1st trimester. Passive Immunoglobulin IM is reserved for non-immune pregnant women who refuse termination.
Prophylaxis: Active immunization with MMR vaccine (contraindicated in pregnancy; women must avoid pregnancy for 3 months post-vaccination).

sections.title: Roseola Infantum
blocks: Etiology & Transmission: Caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6 & HHV-7); transmitted via droplet infection.
Incubation & Demographics: Incubation period is 1 --2 weeks (average 10 days). Peaks in infants aged 6--15 months (occurs predominantly in spring).
Sudden onset of high fever lasting 3 --4 days without localizing physical signs (frequently triggers febrile convulsions).
On the 4th day, the temperature drops precip itously to normal alongside the sudden appearance of a rose-colored maculopapular rash.
The rash begins on the trunk and rapidly spreads to the arms and neck, sparing the face ("a rainbow following the storm"), and fades within 24 hours.
Diagnosis & Treatment: Diagnosed clinically; managed with antipyretics and supportive measures (no specific antivirals required).

sections.title: Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)
blocks: Stage 1: Erythematous facial flushing producing a classic "slapped-cheek" appearance.
Stage 2: Macular reticular (lace-like) rash spreading rapidly to the trunk and proximal extremities.
Stage 3: Resolves spontaneously without desquamation, but tends to wax and wane over 1--3 weeks.

Other Clinical Manifestations: Arthropathy, fetal hydrops (from intrauterine infection), myocarditis, transient aplastic crisis in patients with underlying chronic hemolytic anemia, and chronic pancytopenia in immunocompromised hosts.
Diagnosis & Treatment: Diagnosis is based on the typical clinical rash; treatment is entirely supportive.

sections.title: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
blocks: Clinical Manifestations: Manifests as acute herpetic gingivostomatitis, ocular conjunctivitis/keratoconjunctivitis, genital herpes, CNS infections (encephalitis and meningoencephalitis), or disseminated systemic neonatal infection.

sections.title: Varicella (Chickenpox)
blocks: Etiology & Transmission: Caused by Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV); transmitted via direct contact, respiratory droplets, or airborne routes.
Infectivity & Incubation: Period of infectivity extends from 24 hours before rash onset until all lesions have fully crusted. Incubation period is 2--3 weeks.
Mild, short prodromal phase followed by a pleomorphic rash occurring in successive crops.
Lesions rapidly evolve from macules to papules to clear, fragile, oval tear-drop- shaped vesicles on an erythematous base.
Vesicle contents become cloudy within 24 hours, forming pustules and eventually crusts by days 9--14.
The rash displays a centripetal distribution (dense on the trunk, sparse on extremities), causes intense pruritus, and may involve mucous membranes with oral ulceration.
Complications: Secondary bacterial skin infection, hemorrhagic complications (thrombocytopenia, purpura, hematuria, GI bleeding), encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, and Reye syndrome.
Treatment: Antihistamines, calamine lotion, and non-aspirin antipyretics (paracetamol). High-risk patients receive oral Acyclovir (20 mg/kg/dose 4 times daily for 5 days).

sections.title: Monkeypox
blocks: Causative Agent & Transmission: Caused by the Monkeypox virus; transmitted via respiratory droplets or direct contact.
First Stage: Presents with fever, exhaustion, irritability, muscle pain, and prominent lymphadenopathy.
Second Stage: Within 1 to 3 days, the patient develops a maculovesicular rash.

Treatment & Vaccine: No specific curative treatment is available; Smallpox vaccine, antiviral agents, and Vaccinia Immune Globulin (VIG) are used for outbreak control. A dedicated Monkeypox vaccine is currently under development.

sections.title: Infectious Mononucleosis
blocks: Definition & Etiology: Infectious mononucleosis is a clinical syndrome caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Incubation Period: Typically 30 to 50 days in adolescents; it may be shorter in younger children.
Prodromal Phase: Features malaise, fatigue, headache, and abdominal pain lasting 1 to 2 weeks (extending 2 to 4 weeks in older children).
Core Symptoms: High fever, pharyngitis with significantly enlarged, exudative tonsils, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Rash: A maculopapular rash develops in about 10% of cases. If ampicillin is administered, approximately 80% of patients develop a diffuse, bright erythematous rash.
Splenic Rupture: A critical risk occurring predominantly during the 2nd week of illness.
Airway Obstruction: Severe laryngeal and tonsillar edema causing acute upper respiratory distress.
Neurological: Seizures, ataxia, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and Bell’s palsy.
Systemic/Glandular: Hepatitis, pancreatitis, parotitis, and orchitis.
Hematologic: Acute immune hemolytic anemia and Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP).
Oncogenic Potential: Late association with malignancies such as Burkitt’s lymphoma in African children.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Demonstrates leukocytosis with characteristic atypical lymphocytosis.
Monospot Test: Used for rapid screening (non-specific).
Serology: Specific EBV antibody detection yields the most definitive diagnosis.
Management is primarily supportive with adequate rest.
Acyclovir: Reserved for life-threatening EBV complications.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Indicated for severe airway obstruction, ITP, or acute hemolytic anemia.

sections.title: Mumps (Epidemic Parotitis)
blocks: Definition & Etiology: Caused by the Mumps virus (a Paramyxovirus); humans serve as the sole natural host.
Mode of Transmission: Respiratory droplet infection.

Contagiousness: Patients are contagious from 1 day before until 9 days after the onset of parotid swelling. Transplacental immunity protects infants for the first 6 months, and natural infection confers lifelong immunity.
Prodromal Period: Short 1–2 day phase marked by fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, and pain behind the ear elicited during chewing or swallowing.
Salivary Gland Enlargement: Predominantly involves the parotid gland (though submandibular and sublingual glands may be affected):
Painful, tender swelling that obliterates the anatomical angle of the mandible.
Reddening and swelling at the opening of Stensen's duct.
Swelling usually subsides within 3 to 7 days; it may start unilaterally a nd progress to bilateral involvement.
Nonspecific: Leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, and elevated serum amylase levels.
Serology: Diagnostic 4-fold rise in serum mumps IgG or positive Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA) for mumps IgM antibody.
Neurological: Meningoencephalitis, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, Guillain - Barré syndrome, and transient facial nerve palsy.

Orchitis & Epididymitis: Develops toward the end of the 1st week of illness (usually unilateral; bilateral in 3%) presenting with severe pain, swelling, and testicular tenderness. Complete infertility from bilateral testicular atrophy is rare, though partial reproductive impairment is common.
Oophoritis: Manifests as lower abdominal pain and tenderness; does not compromise future fertility.
Acute Pancreatitis: Marked by high fever, severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting, accompanied by elevated serum amylase and lipase.
Prevention: Active immunization via the MMR vaccine.

sections.title: Influenza Virus Infection
blocks: Definition: Influenza viruses produce a wide range of acute respiratory illnesses responsible for significant pediatric morbidity and mortality during seasonal epidemics.
Initial Source of Infection: Migratory wild birds, infected domestic pigs, and excretions/secretions of pet birds.

Modes of Human Transmission: Inhalation of contaminated dust or fine water droplets generated during poultry slaughtering/de-feathering, direct contact with mucous membranes/conjunctiva, hand-borne transfer from contaminated surfaces, or consumption of raw poultry products (e.g., duck blood pudding).

Clinical Symptoms: Incubation period of 2 to 4 days (up to 8 days). Presents with high fever (37.5°C–40°C), sore throat, rhinitis, cough, muscle aches, conjunctivitis, and severe neurological manifestations including acute encephalopathy, seizures, ataxia, and coma.
Transmission & Incubation: Transmitted p erson-to-person via airborne droplets produced by coughing and sneezing. Incubation ranges from 1 to 4 days (average 2 days).
Clinical Symptoms: High fever (94%), cough (92%), sore throat (66%), diarrhea (25%), and vomiting (25%).

Hospitalization: Approximately 9% of patients require hospital admission, with over 30% of hospitalized cases requiring ICU admission due to severe pneumonia progressing to Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
Age <1 year & weight <15 kg: 30 mg twice daily.
Weight >40 kg or Age >13 years: 75 mg twice daily for acute illness (or 75 mg once daily for at least 10 days as chemoprophylaxis).
Complications: Otitis media, pneumonia, acute renal failure, myocarditis, sepsis, encephalitis/myelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and Reye syndrome (if aspirin/salicylates are co-administered).

sections.title: Enteroviruses: Poliomyelitis & Encephalitis
blocks: Enteroviruses comprise Poliovirus, Coxsackieviruses, and Echoviruses.

Definition & Serotypes: An acute viral infection affecting the central nervous system, leading to aseptic meningitis and/or destruction of anterior horn cells resulting in flaccid paralysis. Caused by 3 RNA e nterovirus serotypes (Types 1, 2, and 3) without cross - immunity; Type 1 causes the most severe epidemics.
Mode of Transmission & Reservoir: Feco-oral (primary) and droplet transmission; humans are the only known reservoir.

Pathogenesis: Virus enters via the GIT, multiplies in Peyer's patches and intestinal lymph nodes. If neutralizing antibodies are inadequate, the virus invades the CNS by traveling along peripheral nerve pathways.
2. Abortive Poliomyelitis: Mild, non-specific febrile illness.
3. Non-Paralytic Poliomyelitis: Presents with meningeal irritation.
4. Paralytic Poliomyelitis (occurs in ~0.1% of infected individuals):
Spinal Paralytic: Asymmetrical lower motor n euron (LMN) flaccid paralysis affecting major muscle groups without sensory loss.
Bulbar Poliomyelitis: Involves cranial nerve nuclei.

Diagnosis: Isolation and identification of poliovirus from stool samples. CSF shows non- specific pleocytosis (initial PMN predominance shifting to lymphocytes) with normal/rising protein and normal glucose.
Non-Paralytic: TB, pyogenic, or aseptic meningitis, and meningism (pneumonia, typhoid).

Paralytic: Guillain-Barré syndrome (symmetrical LMN paralysis with sensory changes and cytoalbuminous dissociation), post-diphtheritic polyneuritis, acute transverse myelitis, and acute traumatic sciatic neuritis.
Complications: Respiratory failure, heart failure, hypertension, urinary tract infections, urinary retention/calculi, pneumonia, and thoracic deformities.
Treatment: Supportive care (no antiviral exists); strict bed rest in a neutral limb posture, avoidance of IM injections, analgesia, and mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure.

Definition & Mechanisms: Inflammatory process of the brain parenchyma resulting from either direct viral infection of the brain tissue or an immune-mediated CNS response developing days after an extraneural infection.
Etiology: Viruses are the primary cause (Arboviruses, Enteroviruses, HSV); may also stem from non-viral infections, metabolic, toxic, or neoplastic causes.

Clinical Manifestations: Preceded by a prodrome of cough, sore throat, fever, headache, and abdominal discomfort. Progresses to severe lethargy, behavioral changes, focal neurological deficits, seizures, maculopapular rash, fulminant coma, transverse myelitis, or peripheral neuropathy.
