Laboratory & Imaging Studies: CSF reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis, mild protein elevation, and normal glucose (increased RBCs suggest HSV). CT/MRI shows diffuse brain edema or focal lesions. EEG is the definitive test, showing diffuse slow-wave activity. Brain biopsy is reserved for obscure, severe cases.
Treatment: Intensive supportive care (airway protection, control of elevated ICP, and anticonvulsants). IV Acyclovir is the specific treatment of choice for HSV encephalitis.

sections.title: Scarlet Fever
blocks: Definition & Causative Agent: An upper respiratory tract infection presenting with a distinct exanthem, caused by erythrogenic exotoxin produced by Group A β--hemolytic streptococci (GABHS) in individuals lacking specific antitoxin antibodies.
Onset: Abrupt onset with high fever, chills, headache, vomiting, sore throat, and severe abdominal pain.
Throat: Beefy red pharynx with edematous anterior pillars and hyperemic, exudative tonsils.
Exanthem (Rash): Appears within 24 to 48 hours; red, pin-point, finely granular rash that blanches on pressure and feels like goose skin or coarse sandpaper.
Pastia's Sign: Transverse dark hyperemic lines in the skin creases of the antecubital fossa.
Circumoral Pallor: Flushed forehead a nd cheeks contrasting with marked pallor around the mouth.
Strawberry Tongue: Initially coated as a "white strawberry tongue", which desquamates after a few days to leave a red, swollen "red strawberry tongue" with prominent papillae.
Desquamation: Rash fades after 3 to 4 days, followed by characteristic skin desquamation.
Laboratory Findings: Leukocytosis up to 15,000/μL, elevated Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer above 350 Todd units, positive throat culture for GABHS, and positive rapid antigen detection tests.
Diagnosis: Clinical presentation is characteristic; mild or atypical cases must be differentiated from other pediatric maculopapular exanthems.
Antipyretics and analgesics for symptom control.
Procaine Penicillin (400,000 U/day IM), Oral Penicillin V (400,000 U/day for 10 days), or Benzathine Penicillin (600,000–1,200,000 U IM single dose).
For Penicillin Allergy: Erythromycin (40 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses for 10 days) or Azithromycin (10 mg/kg/day orally as a single dose for 5 days).
Prevention: Avoid overcrowding and maintain close observation of contacts; no vaccine exists due to the multiplicity of GABHS strains.

sections.title: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
blocks: Definition & Terminology: An acute bacterial respiratory tract infection. The term pertussis (meaning "intense cough") is preferred over whooping cough because many infected individuals do not develop a characteristic whoop.
Etiology: Caused by Bordetella pertussis, a Gram-negative bacillus.
Mode of Transmission: Respiratory droplet infection. Pertussis is extremely contagious, with attack rates approaching 100% in susceptible individuals exposed to aerosol droplets at close range.
Period of infectivity extends from 1 week before to 3 weeks after the onset of symptoms.
Neither natural infection nor vaccination confers complete or lifelong immunity.
Demographics: Affects any age group, but is most common during the first few years of life. Newborns lack transplacental immunity and are fully susceptible.
1. Catarrhal Stage (1–2 weeks): Non-distinctive upper respiratory symptoms including nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, low-grade fever, sneezing, lacrimation, and conjunctival injection.

2. Paroxysmal Stage (2–6 weeks): Cough gradually worsens and becomes paroxysmal—a repetitive series of severe coughs during a single expiration followed by a sudden, deep inspiratory gasp (whoop). During an attack, the chin and chest are held forward, the tongue protrudes, eyes bulge, and the face becomes cyanotic or purple. Post-tussive vomiting is common, with expectoration of thick, tenacious mucoid sputum. Repeated paroxysms interfere with sleep and feeding, predisposing to protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) and respiratory alkalosis (which reduces ionized calcium, triggering tetany). Between paroxysms, the child appears well with minimal chest signs. In infants <3 months of age, classic paroxysms and whoops are usually absent and are replaced by life - threatening apnea and cyanosis.
3. Convalescent Stage (1–2 weeks): Paroxysms decrease in frequency and severity, vomiting subsides, and appetite returns (this stage may be prolonged over several weeks).

Suspect pertussis in any patient presenting with a persistent cough >14 days accompanied by post-tussive vomiting or whoop, especially in the absence of fever, systemic symptoms, or focal chest signs.
In infants <3 months, attacks of apnea or cyanosis are key diagnostic clues (pertussis is an occasional cause of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome [SIDS]).
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Marked leukocytosis (>20,000/mm³) with a characteristic predominant lymphocytosis.
Microbiology: Isolation of B. pertussis via culture of nasopharyngeal swab/aspirate during the early catarrhal phase.

Respiratory: Secondary bacterial pneumonia (most common cause of death), otitis media, sinusitis, atelectasis (due to mucus plugging), bronchiectasis, interstitial/subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, diaphragmatic rupture, and reactivation/dissemination of primary tuberculosis.
Gastrointestinal: Severe vomiting leading to malnutrition, dehydration, alkalosis, and tetany; increased intra-abdominal pressure causes rectal prolapse and umbilical/inguinal hernias.
Neurological: Convulsions secondary to cerebral anoxia during paroxysms (common in infants), tetany, and intracranial hemorrhages.
Hemorrhagic: Mechanical bleeding secondary to coughing fits (epistaxis, subconjunctival hemorrhage, hemoptysis, intraventricular and subarachnoid hemorrhage).
Post-Exposure Prophylaxis: All close household contacts should receive Erythromycin (40 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 10–14 days) plus a DTaP booster if under 6 years of age.
Isolation: Respiratory isolation of cases for 5 days after starting effective antibiotic therapy.
Symptomatic: Supportive care, bed rest, soft diet, fluid hydration, and anti - tussives for severe spasmodic cough.
Specific Antibiotic: Erythromycin (40 mg/kg/day orally for 14 days).

Differential Diagnosis: Bordetella parapertussis, mediastinal lymphadenopathy compressing the trachea, airway foreign body aspiration, viral bronchiolitis, bronchitis, bronchial asthma, and post-nasal drip syndrome.

sections.title: Enteric (Typhoid) Fever
blocks: Definition & Etiology: A systemic bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi (serotypes A, B, and C). Salmonellae are Gram-negative, facultative anaerobic bacilli that do not ferment lactose.
Antigenic Structure: H (flagellar), O (somatic cell wall), and Vi (capsular envelope) antigens.
Epidemiology: Endemic in many developing nations; S. typhi infects humans exclusively. Chronic biliary/intestinal carriers serve as the reservoir for new cases.
Incubation Period & Invasion Site: 1 to 3 weeks. The upper small intestine is the predominant site of tissue invasion.

Pathogenesis: Ingested bacilli invade the intestinal mucosa and are phagocytosed by monocytes. Monocytes fail to kill the bacteria, transporting them via the bloodstream (bacteremia) to mesenteric lymph nodes, reticuloendothelial system organs (liver, spleen, bone marrow), gallbladder, and intestine.
Clinical Picture: Ranges from mild gastroenteritis to severe fulminant septicemia.
General Symptoms: High fever, severe headache, anorexia, lethargy, jaundice, and marked weight loss.
Systemic Signs: Hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain and tenderness, diarrhea or constipation, delirium, and confusion.
Characteristic Findings: Relative bradycardia (high fever accompanied by an unexpectedly low pulse rate) and leukopenia.
Intestinal Perforation (typically involving terminal ileal Peyer's patches), heralded by a sudden drop in body temperature and blood pressure accompanied by a rapid spike in pulse rate.
Hepatitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, toxic myocarditis, and pneumonia.
Cultures: Blood culture is positive during the 1st week; urine and stool cultures become positive after the 2nd week. Bone marrow aspirate culture has the highest yield.
Widal Serology: Titer ≥1:250 (or a 4-fold rise in paired titers) suggests active infection.
First-line / Empiric: Ceftriaxone (50–75 mg/kg/24 hr IV/IM).

Alternatives: Ampicillin (200 mg/kg/24 hr), Amoxicillin (100 mg/kg/24 hr), Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (10 mg TMP / 50 mg SMX /kg/24 hr), or Chloramphenicol (50–100 mg/kg/24 hr). Azithromycin is indicated for resistant endemic strains.
Chronic Carriers: Cholecystectomy may be required to eradicate chronic gallbladder shedding.
1. Live Attenuated Oral Vaccine: For children ≥6 years of age (4 doses; booster every 5 years).
2. Injectable Polysaccharide Vaccine: For children ≥2 years of age (single dose; booster every 2 years).
Differential Diagnosis: Acute bronchitis, bronchopneumonia, gastroenteritis, brucellosis, infective endocarditis, and infectious mononucleosis.

sections.title: Nontyphoidal Salmonellosis
blocks: Epidemiology: Most common in children <4 years of age, with the highest incidence occurring in infants <1 year. Transmitted via fecal-oral contamination. Peak occurrence is during late summer.

Clinical Manifestations: An acute, self-limited gastroenteritis lasting 3 to 7 days. Onset is abrupt with nausea, vomiting, crampy abdominal pain, loose watery stools (frequently containing mucus, leukocytes, and blood), malaise, headache, chills, and fever (38.3°C–38.9°C) with signs of septicemia.
Complications: Dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemic shock, post-infectious reactive arthritis, focal abscesses, osteomyelitis, empyema, pneumonia, and meningitis (especially in neonates).
Diagnosis: Stool culture is indicated if fever, bloody/mucoid/leukocytic stools are present. Blood, urine, CSF, and bone marrow cultures are performed in complicated or systemic cases.
Primary focus is fluid rehydration and electrolyte correction.

Antibiotics: Antimicrobials are not indicated for uncomplicated enteritis in healthy older children. They are indicated for high-risk groups (infants <3 months, immunocompromised, severe malnutrition, or systemic spread) using Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, Amoxicillin, or TMP-SMX.
Differential Diagnosis: Infectious gastroenteritis of other etiologies, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, reactive arthritis, septic shock, and active ulcerative colitis.

sections.title: Brucellosis
blocks: Definition & Etiology: A systemic zoonotic infection caused by Gram-negative, aerobic, non-spore-forming, non-motile coccobacilli of the genus Brucella.
Human Pathogens: Brucella abortus (cattle), Brucella melitensis (goats/sheep; most virulent), Brucella suis (swine; highly virulent), and Brucella canis (dogs).

Routes of Infection: Inoculation through skin cuts/abrasions or conjunctival sac, inhalation of infectious aerosols, or ingestion of contaminated unpasteurized milk, dairy products, or undercooked meat.
Classic Triad: Fever, arthritis / arthralgia, and hepatosplenomegaly.
Associated Symptoms: Abdominal pain, headache, night sweats, weakness, fatigue, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, pharyngitis, and skin rash.
CBC: Non-specific (WBC count is low or normal).
Definitive Diagnosis: Isolation of Brucella species from blood or bone marrow cultures.
Serum Agglutination Test (SAT): Titer ≥1:160 is diagnostic. Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA) confirms recent infection.
Children <9 Years: TMP-SMX (TMP 10 mg/kg/day, SMX 50 mg/kg/day) orally for 45 days PLUS Rifampin (15–20 mg/kg/day) orally for 6 weeks.
Children ≥9 Years: Doxycycline (200 mg/day) orally for 6 weeks PLUS Rifampin (600–900 mg/day) orally for 6 weeks.
Complicated Disease (Meningitis, Osteomyelitis, Endocarditis): Prolonged therapy for 4–6 months with Doxycycline + Rifampin PLUS IM Streptomycin (1 g/day) or IV/IM Gentamicin (3–5 mg/kg/day).
Prevention: Eradication of infection in livestock, pasteurization of milk and dairy products. No human vaccine is currently available.
Differential Diagnosis: Cat-scratch disease, typhoid fever, tuberculosis, atypical mycobacterial infections, rickettsial diseases, Yersinia, and coccidioidomycosis.

sections.title: Diphtheria
blocks: Etiology & Pathophysiology: Caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, a Gram - positive, non-motile bacillus. Toxigenic strains produce a potent exotoxin responsible for systemic myocarditis, neuritis, and acute tubular necrosis/nephritis. Local infection generates a characteristic fibrinous pseudomembrane.
Epidemiology: Humans are the sole known reservoir. Transmitted via close contact with respiratory droplets from cases or asymptomatic carriers.

1. Tonsillar / Pharyngeal Diphtheria (most common form): Insidious onset of malaise, low-grade fever, and sore throat. Within 1–2 days, a thin white membrane forms over the tonsils, extending to the uvula, soft palate, pharyngeal wall, larynx, and trachea. The membrane thickens, turning gray with a foul, garlic-like breath odor. Attempted removal causes marked capillary bleeding. Soft tissue swelling and prominent cervical lymphadenitis produce a classic "bull-neck" appearance. Severe toxemia is marked by tachycardia out of proportion to fever.

2. Laryngeal Diphtheria: Occurs secondary to pharyngeal extension (or as a primary infection in 10% of cases). Causes progressive hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, dyspnea, and fatal upper airway obstruction.
3. Cardiac Involvement (Diphtheritic Myocarditis): Develops in ~10% of cases between days 7 and 14 of illness. Presents with heart failure, AV block, arrhythmias, and circulatory collapse.
4. Toxic Neuropathy: Cranial nerve dysfunction (palatal and ocular paralysis) and peripheral motor neuropathy (extremity paralysis) with elevated CSF protein.
5. Other Organ Systems: Diphtheritic hepatitis, nephritis, and gastritis.
Diagnosis: Isolation of C. diphtheriae on selective culture media (e.g., Löffler or tellurite media) from swabs taken beneath the pseudomembrane.

Differential Diagnosis: Streptococcal pharyngotonsillitis, Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV), CMV, Toxoplasmosis, viral tonsillitis, primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, agranulocytosis/leukemia, and laryngeal tumors.
Specific Neutralization: Immediate IV/IM administration of Diphtheria Antitoxin (DAT) as soon as diphtheria is clinically suspected (do not delay for lab culture results).
Antibiotic Therapy: Penicillin G or oral Erythromycin for 14 days to eliminate the organism and stop toxin production.
Airway Management: Emergency endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy for laryngeal obstruction.
Active Immunization: Diphtheria toxoid (Penta / DTP / DT / Td).
Contact Management: Isolation of cases; close contacts receive oral Erythromycin or IM Benzathine Penicillin + a diphtheria toxoid booster for previously immunized individuals.

sections.title: Acute Bacterial Meningitis
blocks: Acute bacterial meningitis is one of the most common and serious central nervous system (CNS)
infections occurring in infants and children, characterized by acute inflammation of the meninges.
The primary causative pathogens vary significantly according to the age of the child and host immune status:

First 2 Months of Life: Group B Streptococcus, Gram-negative enteric bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Children Aged 2 Months to 12 Years: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis.

Alterations in Host Defenses (Anatomic Defects or Immune Deficits): Predispose to less common or opportunistic pathogens, such as Pseudomonas aeru ginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella species, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Bacterial meningitis most commonly results from hematogenous dissemination of
microorganisms from a primary distant site of infection (e.g., upper respiratory tract or nasopharynx).
The onset of acute bacterial meningitis follows two main clinical patterns:

Rapid / Dramatic Presentation (Less common, but severe): Sudden onset with rapidly progressive signs of shock, purpura, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and unresponsiveness, frequently resulting in death within 24 hours.

Gradual / Subacute Presentation (More common): Preceded by several days of fever with upper respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms, followed by no n-specific signs of CNS infection such as lethargy or irritability.
Nonspecific Findings: Fever, anorexia, poor feeding, myalgia, arthralgia, tachycardia, hypotension, and various cutaneous signs (petechiae, purpura, or an erythematous macular rash).
Signs of Meningeal Irritation: Nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness), back pain, positive Kernig's sign, and positive Brudzinski's sign.

Symptoms and Signs of Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICP): Severe headache, vomiting, bulging anterior fontanel or widening of sutures, cranial neuropathies, hypertension accompanied by bradycardia, apnea or hyperventilation, stupor, and coma.

Seizures: Focal or generalized seizures occur secondary to cerebritis, cortical infarction, or electrolyte disturbances. Seizures present at onset or within the first 4 days carry no negative prognostic significance.
A lumbar puncture (LP) for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is essential whenever bacterial meningitis is suspected:
Parameter Normal CSF Acute Bacterial Meningitis CSF
Pressure Clear; 50–80 mm H₂O Turbid; Elevated pressure (100–300 mm H₂O)
Protein 20–45 mg/dL ↑ 100–500 mg/dL Glucose 75% of serum
↓ <50% of serum glucose Microbiology Negative Gram stain & Culture positive for specific
Vancomycin (60 mg/kg/day IV divided every 6 hours) PLUS either Cefotaxime (200 mg/kg/day) IV divided every 6 hours) or Ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day) IV as a single daily dose or divided every 12 hours.
For β-Lactam Allergy: Chloramphenicol (100 mg/kg/day) IV divided every 6 hours).
Duration: Intravenous antibiotic therapy is continued for at least 7 to 14 days.

IV Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg/dose) every 6 hours for 2 days in children older than 6 weeks with acute bacterial meningitis caused by H. influenzae type b to decrease permanent auditory nerve damage (sensorineural hearing loss). Maximum benefit is achieved when administered 1–2 hours prior to initiating antibiotics.

Supportive & Symptomatic Therapy: Continuous clinical monitoring, correction of dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, prompt seizure control, and management of increased ICP and neurological complications.

Active Immunization: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) conjugate vaccine (3-dose primary series at 2, 4, and 6 months) and Quadrivalent Meningococcal vaccine for high - risk children >2 years of age.
Meningococcal exposure: Rifampin (10 mg/kg/dose) every 12 hours for 2 days.
Hib exposure: Rifampin (20 mg/kg) once daily for 4 days.
Sepsis or meningitis caused by other pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, Group A Streptococcus), Rocky Mountain spotted fever, ehrlichi osis, epidemic typhus, and infective endocarditis.
Viral meningoencephalitis (petechial rashes can occur with enteroviruses, influenza, measles, EBV, CMV, and parvovirus).

Non-infectious purpuric/petechial lesions: Protein C orS deficiency, platelet disorders (ITP), Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), connective tissue disorders, drug eruptions, and trauma/non-accidental injury.

sections.title: Tetanus Neonatorum
blocks: Caused by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacillus that produces a potent neurotoxin (tetanospasmin).
Infection is introduced through the umbilical stump during or after delivery by using
Onset: Gradual onset beginning with refusal of feeding.
Trismus & Rigidity: Within 2 days, trismus (lockjaw) develops, causing an inability to suck.
Muscle Stiffness: Generalized muscle stiffness progresses to continuous muscular rigidity and opisthotonos (extreme hyperextension of the spine).
Convulsions: Reflex muscle spasms and generalized convulsions triggered by minor stimuli, leading to secondary cyanosis.
Prolonged laryngeal spasm with total upper airway obstruction.
Muscle relaxants and sedatives: IV Diazepam (0.1–0.2 mg/kg) every 3–6 hours to provide both muscle relaxation and seizure control.
Minimal handling in a quiet, dark environment; airway maintenance.
Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) of human origin: 3,000–6,000 units IM.
If TIG is unavailable: Antitetanic Serum (ATS) 100,000 units.
Crystalline Penicillin G: 100,000 U/kg/day IV divided every 4–6 hours for 10 to 14 days to eradicate vegetative cells.
Immunization of non-immune pregnant women with Tetanus Toxoid during antenatal care.
Strict aseptic care and clean delivery procedures for the umbilical stump.
Other causes of neonatal generalized seizures (HIE, metabolic crises).
Neonatal Hypocalcemia / Tetany: Features laryngeal and carpopedal spasms, but trismus is characteristically absent.
Narcotic/drug withdrawal syndromes in infants born to addicted mothers.
Local causes of trismus (parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal abscesses or brainstem encephalitis).

sections.title: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
blocks: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic, granulomatous infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium
tuberculosis (responsible for ~98% of cases) or Mycobacterium bovis (~2%).
TheM. tuberculosis complex includes 5 closely related species: M. tuberculosis, M. bovis, M. africanum, M. microti, and M. canetti.
M. tuberculosis is an acid-fast, aerobic bacillus.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately one-third of the global
population (~2.5 billion people) is infected with M. tuberculosis.
Person-to-person spread primarily via airborne mucus droplet nuclei produced by coughing, sneezing, or speaking.
Ingestion of contaminated, unpasteurized cow's milk causes gastrointestinal/biliary TB (M. bovis).

Contact with open cavitary TB cases, overcrowding, unpasteurized milk, malnutrition, young age (<5 years), intercurrent infections (measles, pertussis, HIV), lack of BCG vaccination, immunodeficiency or immunosuppression, poverty, lack of access to healthcare, and poor treatment adherence.

1. Exposure: A child has shared air/had significant contact with an adult or adolescent with infectious TB, but lacks proof of infection. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) or Interferon - Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) is negative, chest radiograph is normal, physical exam is normal, and symptoms are absent.

2. Tuberculosis Infection (TBI): The child inhales droplet nuclei containing M. tuberculosis, which survive intracellularly within alveolar macrophages and regional lymph nodes. The hallmark of TBI is a positive TST or IGRA result, but the child has no clinical signs or symptoms, a normal physical exam, and a chest X-ray that is either normal or reveals only a calcified parenchymal granuloma.
3. Tuberculosis Disease: Clinical signs, symptoms, or radiographic manifestations caused by active multiplying M. tuberculosis become apparent.
Hypersensitivity / Allergy Reactions: Erythema nodosum, phlyctenular conjunctivitis, and a positive tuberculin skin test.
Primary (Childhood Type) vs. Post-Primary (Adult Type) TB:
Feature Primary TB (Childhood Type) Post-Primary / Reactivation
Target Population Infants and young children Older adolescents and adults
Lesion Location Subpleural focus (Ghons focus) in

lower/middle lobes Apical and posterior segments of upper lobes Lymph Node Involvement Marked regional (hilar/mediastinal) lymphadenopathy Regional lymph nodes are NOT enlarged Cavitation / Hemoptysis Cavitation and hemoptysis are rare Cavity formation and hemoptysis are common Healing & Spread Heals by calcification; hematogenous spread common Heals by fibrosis; hematogenous spread rare

Intrapulmonary Manifestations (60% of cases): Primary subpleural focus, extended primary lesion, consolidation-collapse (segmental lesion), bronchopneumonia, hilar or paratracheal lymphadenopathy, endobronchial TB (ulcer, papilloma), emphysema or atelectasis, pleural/pericardial effusion, and apical fibrocaseous TB with cavitation.

Extrapulmonary Manifestations (25–35% of cases): Lymphadenitis (cervical [scrofula], mediastinal, axillary, inguinal), Abdominal TB (tabes mesenterica, peritonitis, enteritis), CNS TB (basila r meningitis, tuberculoma), Musculoskeletal (osteomyelitis, arthritis, Pott's disease of spine), Otitis media/laryngitis, Genitourinary TB (epididymitis, salpingitis, nephritis), and Miliary TB (acute or chronic hematogenous dissemination).

Primary Pulmonary TB: Occurs from birth to 7 years; incubation period 2–4 weeks with gradual onset. Symptoms include dry cough, difficulty breathing, chest pain, low - grade fever, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss. Signs include tachypnea, wheezing, and respiratory distress.

Progressive Primary Pulmonary TB: Incubation period 3–9 months. Marked by severe cough with purulent expectoration, high fever, rapid weight loss, night sweats, diminished breath sounds, rales, and bronchial dullness.

Reactivation TB: Occurs in older children (7–18 years) with gradual onset. Symptoms include chronic cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, anorexia, weight loss, and night sweats. Physical exam reveals dullness over infiltrates and hyper-resonance over pulmonary cavities.

Pleural TB Effusion: Incubation period months to 4 years. Symptoms include dyspnea, chest pain, fever, anorexia, night sweats, and weight loss. Physical exam reveals chest wall bulging, intercostal fullness, tenderness, stony dullness on percussion, and absent breath sounds over the effusion.
Tuberculosis Score Chart (TSC): Standardized scoring based on clinical history, contact history, and physical findings.
Inflammatory Markers: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) is characteristically markedly elevated.

Radiology: Chest X-ray demonstrating primary parenchymal focus, caseation, cavitation, lobar/segmental atelectasis, miliary mottling ("snowstorm" appearance), hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, or pleural/pericardial effusion.

Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux Test): Intradermal injection of 0.1 mL containing 5 units of Purified Protein Derivative (PPD) into the volar surface of the left forearm; induration is measured 48 to 72 hours later:
Positive Test (≥10 mm induration): Indicates TB infection.
Doubtful Test (5–9 mm) induration): Secondary to previous BCG vaccination or atypical mycobacterial infection.
Negative Test (<5 mm) induration): No infection (or false-negative due to severe immunosuppression/miliary disease/malnutrition).
BCG Test: Diagnostic test where a rapid inflammatory reaction within 2–3 days indicates prior active TB infection (versus a normal delayed response).
Microbiology: Microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain) and culture (Löwenstein- Jensen media) performed on early morning gastric aspirates, sputum, pleural fluid, or CSF.
Histopathology: Biopsy of lymph nodes or tissue demonstrating typical caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells.
Molecular & Serologic Diagnostics: Polymera se Chain Reaction (PCR) and QuantiFERON-TB Gold (IGRA) assays.
Active Immunization: BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guérin) Vaccine administered intradermally in the first 3 months of life (typically at birth).
Chemoprophylaxis: Oral Isoniazid (INH) (10–15 mg/kg as a single daily dose for 3 months) for asymptomatic child contacts of open infectious cases.
Environmental control, avoiding overcrowding, and pasteurization of milk.
Prophylaxis for Contacts: Single drug Isoniazid (INH) for 3 months.
Uncomplicated Pulmonary TB: Two drugs —INH + Rifampin (RIF) for 6 months.
Pulmonary & Extrapulmonary TB: Three drugs —INH + RIF + Pyrazinamide (PZA) for 6 to 9 months.
Resistant / Severe TB: Four to six drugs —INH, R IF, PZA, Streptomycin (STM), Ethambutol (EMB), or Ethionamide (ETH) for 9 to 12 months.
Directly Observed Therapy (DOT): A designated healthcare worker directly observes the patient swallow every dose of anti-TB medication to ensure compliance and prevent drug resistance.

Corticosteroid Adjunctive Therapy: Oral Prednisone (1–2 mg/kg/day for 1–2 months) indicated for TB pleurisy, pericarditis, basilar meningitis, miliary TB, peritonitis, or endobronchial TB to reduce exudative inflammation, decrease tissue fibrosis, and prevent adhesions.

Surgical Interventions: Surgical excision of persistent necrotic TB lymphadenopathy or osteomyelitis, ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for obstructive hydrocephalus in TB meningitis, and lung lobectomy for extensive atelectasis or severe bronchiectasis.

sections.title: Parasitic Infections
blocks: Etiology: Caused by Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan that exists either as a resistant infectious cyst or as an invasive motile trophozoite.
Epidemiology: Humans serve as the natural host and reservoir. Transmission occurs through ingestion of food and water contaminated with cysts, or via direct person-to- person contact.

Pathogenesis: Ingested cysts hatch into trophozoites in the intestine, invading the mucosa to form characteristic flask-shaped ulcers. Trophozoites can metastasize via the portal circulation to the liver, or less commonly to the pleura, lungs, brain, or skin.

Intestinal Amebiasis: Frequently asymptomatic, or presents as acute cramping diarrhea containing blood and mucus (amebic dysentery), accompanied by high fever, severe abdominal pain, tenesmus, headache, and chills.
Hepatic Amebiasis: Presents as an amebic liver abscess with fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, distension, and a tender, enlarged liver.
Complications: Local intestinal perforation, severe GI hemorrhage, intussusception, toxic megacolon, and extraintestinal amebic abscesses (hepatic, pleural, pulmonary, or brain).

Diagnosis: Demonstration of E. histolytica cysts or trophozoites in stool samples, intestinal ulcer biopsy, or liver abscess aspirate; positive serum amebic antibody titers in >90% of invasive cases; abdominal ultrasound or CT to delineate liver abscesses.
Treatment: Oral Metronidazole (30–50 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 10 days) or Tinidazole (single oral dose of 50–60 mg/kg). Repeat stool examination 2 weeks post - therapy as a test of cure.
Etiology: Caused by Giardia lamblia, a flagellated protozoan. Ingested cysts hatch in the duodenum into trophozoites, which attach to the brush border and cause symptoms.
Epidemiology: Infects humans and animals; transmitted person-to-person via the fecal - oral route or ingestion of contaminated water/food.
Acute: Sudden onset of explosive, watery, foul-smelling diarrhea, flatulence, abdominal distension, nausea, anorexia, and weight loss.
Chronic: Persistent diarrhea with malabsorption, flatulence, abdominal distension, and crampy abdominal pain.
Diagnosis: Examination of serial stool specimens (at least 3); direct aspirate/examination of duodenal contents; duodenal biopsy (rarely); ELISA for Giardia antigen in stool; PCR/DNA probes.
Treatment: Oral Metronidazole (15 mg/kg/day for 7 days), Tinidazole (single oral dose of 50 mg/kg; 90% cure rate), or Furazolidone (6–8 mg/kg/day for 10 days).
Etiology: Caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, a large intestinal nematode.

Epidemiology: Humans ingest food or water contaminated with embryonated Ascaris eggs; hatched larvae penet rate the intestinal mucosa, migrate through the venous system to the lungs, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature into adult worms in the small intestine. Hand-to-mouth soil contact is the primary route.
Pulmonary Phase (Larval Migration): Cough, blood-stained sputum, dyspnea, and marked peripheral eosinophilia.
Intestinal Phase (Adult Worms): Abdominal pain, distension, and mechanical intestinal obstruction; biliary tract or pancreatic duct obstruction with s teatorrhea may occur.
Diagnosis: Demonstration of characteristic Ascaris eggs on stool microscopy.

Treatment: Mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg as a single dose; drug of choice), Flubendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg once), Pyrantel pamoate (11 mg/kg once daily for 3 days, max 1 g), or Albendazole (400 mg PO single dose).
Prevention: Improved personal hygiene, handwashing, and proper sanitation.
Etiology: Caused predominantly by Ancylostoma duodenale.

Epidemiology: Infective larvae in damp soil penetrate intact human skin (usually the soles or between toes), migrate through lungs and trachea, are swallowed, and attach to the small intestinal mucosa to suck blood and shed eggs.
Ground Itch: Pruritic maculopapular rash at the site of larval skin entry.
Gastrointestinal: Abdominal pain, anorexia, indigestion, fullness, and diarrhea.
Major Complication: Severe hypochromic microcytic iron deficiency anemia with pica; chronic heavy infection leads to hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, and high-output heart failure.
Diagnosis: Fresh stool microscopy demonstrating hookworm eggs and occult blood; marked eosinophilia; severe microcytic anemia.

Treatment: Pyrantel pamoate (11 mg/kg once daily for 3 days, max 1 g), Mebendazole (100 mg twice daily for 3 days or 500 mg once), or Albendazole (400 mg PO single dose). Anemia is treated with oral elemental iron (6 mg/kg/day) or packed RBC transfusions in severe cases.
Epidemiology: Extremely common in children across all socioeconomic classes; transmitted via ingestion/inhalation of infective eggs, which hatch in the stomach and mature in the cecum.

Clinical Manifestations: Nocturnal perianal pruritus and restlessness caused by gravid female worms migrating to the perianal folds at night to deposit eggs. Secondary vulvovaginitis and salpingitis can occur in young girls.

Diagnosis: Microscopic examination of clear adhesive tape (Scotch tape test) applied to the perianal area early in the morning before bathing; accidental observation of adult pinworms in the perianal area.

Treatment: Simultaneous treatment of all household family members is essential, with a repeat dose 2 weeks later: Pyrantel pamoate (11 mg/kg single dose, max 1 g; drug of choice), Mebendazole or Flubendazole (100 mg PO single dose), or Albendazole (400 mg PO single dose).
Etiology: Caused by blood flukes (trematodes): Schistosoma h aematobium, Schistosoma mansoni, S. japonicum, S. intercalatum, and S. mekongi.

Epidemiology: Humans are infected in fresh water when free-swimming cercariae shed from freshwater snails penetrate intact skin. Immature worms migrate through the bloodstream to mature in specific organ venous plexuses:
S. haematobium: Vesical/urinary bladder venous plexus.
S. mansoni / intestinal species: Mesenteric venous plexus.
Acute (Katayama Fever): Fever, systemic malaise, cough, and abdominal pain secondary to egg deposition.
S. haematobium: Bladder mucosal granulomas causing terminal hematuria, dysuria, frequency, and obstructive uropathy.

S. mansoni / Intestinal: Intestinal and hepatic egg deposition causing mucosal ulceration, abdominal coli c, bloody diarrhea, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, ascites, and esophageal variceal bleeding.
Urinary: Recurrent cystitis, urinary bladder wall calcification and fibrosis, hydronephrosis, pyelonephritis, renal failure, urinary fis tulae, and squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
Gastrointestinal & Hepatic: Intestinal polyposis, severe anemia, hypersplenism, portal hypertension, esophageal varices, and liver cell failure.
Systemic: Stunting/dwarfism and ectopic egg deposition (e.g., cor pulmonale / cardiopulmonary schistosomiasis).

Diagnosis: Microscopy demonstrating characteristic eggs in urine (S. haematobium with a terminal spine) or stool (S. mansoni with a lateral spine); mucosal biopsy (rectal or bladder); intradermal skin test (wheal >9 mm); ELISA and hemagglutination tests.
Treatment: Praziquantel (drug of choice: 40 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses for 1 day; or 60 mg/kg/day in 3 doses for S. japonicum / S. mekongi) or Niridazole (15 mg/kg/day for 10 days).
Prevention: Eradication of snail intermediate hosts, improved sanitation, avoidance of fresh water contact, and mass drug administration.
Etiology: Caused by 4 main human Plasmodium species: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium ovale, and Plasmodium malariae.
Epidemiology: Transmitted via the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, transplacentally, or through blood transfusions.
Incubation Period: 6 to 16 days depending on the species.
Prodrome of sudden high fever with chills, dropping abruptly to normal after 2–12 hours, and recurring every 2–3 days (paroxysmal cycle).
Accompanied by severe headache, abdominal and back pain, nausea, vomiting, and progressive splenomegaly.
Typical malarial paroxysms consist of 3 successive stages: Cold Stage (intense shivering), Hot Stage (high fever), and Sweating Stage (profuse diaphoresis).
Protective Factor: G6PD-deficient individuals exhibit natural resistance against severe P. falciparum infection.
1. Cerebral Malaria: Severe confusion, generalized seizures, and coma.
2. Blackwater Fever: Massive intravascular hemolysis producing severe hemoglobinuria and acute renal failure.
4. Acute Peripheral Circulatory Collapse: Hypotension, shock, and coma.
7. Chronic Complications: Stunting, severe chronic anemia, and increased susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections.
Diagnosis: Typical paroxysms and marked splenomegaly; thick and thin blood film microscopy (gold standard to identify species and parasite density); elevated ESR.

Differential Diagnosis: Influenza, infectious mononucleosis, viral hepatitis, infective endocarditis, bacteremia/sepsis, typhoid fever, brucellosis, visceral leishmaniasis, viral encephalitis, meningitis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and lymphoma.
Chloroquine-sensitive: Chloroquine phosphate (10 mg base/kg, then 5 mg base/kg at 6, 24, and 48 hours).

Resistant or Severe Falciparum: Pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine (single dose), Quinine sulfate (30 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses for 3 days), or IV Quinidine gluconate (10 mg/kg loading dose over 1–2 hours, then 0.02 mg/kg/min continuous infusion until oral therapy can be tolerated).

sections.title: Immunization
blocks: Immunization: The clinical process of initiating, enhancing, or augmenting a host's resistance to an infectious disease.
Vaccination: The physical administration of any vaccine or toxoid to prevent a specific infectious disease.
For infants and children who missed routine immunizations due to illness, neglect, or lack of access:
Infants <14 Months of Age: Resume and complete vaccinations according to the standard schedule without restarting previously given doses.
1. First Visit: DTP (1) + OPV (1) + Tuberculin Skin Test.
5. 1 Year Later: Booster dose of OPV + DTP (if <5 years old).
C. Vitamin A Supplementation Schedule (9 Doses)
In Egypt, oral high-dose Vitamin A supplementation is integrated into child healthcare visits to prevent deficiency, xerophthalmia, and infectious complications:
A total of 9 doses are administered starting at 9 months of age and continuing through 5 years of age (given at 9 months, 12 months, 18 months, and every 6 months thereafter up to age 5).

sections.title: Gastroenteritis
blocks: Inflammation of the digestive tract resulting in vomiting, diarrhea, or both, often accompanied by fever or abdominal cramps.

Acute Gastroenteritis: Defined by increased stool frequency ≥3 loose or watery stools in 24 hours, or an increase exceeding the child's usual baseline by 2 or more), with or without vomiting or fever. It typically lasts less than 1 week and no longer than 2 weeks.
Viral (30–50%): Rotavirus (most common), Norwalk virus, Enteric adenovirus, Influenza virus.

Bacterial: E. coli (5 types: Enteropathogenic, Enterotoxigenic, Enteroinvasive, Enterohemorrhagic O157:H7, Enteroadhesive), Shigella, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae, Staphylococcus, Campylobacter jejuni, Yersinia enterocolitica.
Parasitic: Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium.
2. Parenteral Diarrhea: Diarrhea associated with extra-intestinal systemic infections (upper respiratory tract infection, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, otitis media).
3. Dietetic Diarrhea: Underfeeding (starvation diarrhea) or overfeeding.
1. Osmotic Diarrhea: Ingestion of non-absorbable solutes that draw water into the intestinal lumen to maintain osmolality (e.g., lactose intolerance).
2. Secretory Diarrhea: Active chloride secretion by intestinal crypt cells.
3. Motility Changes: Increased or decreased intestinal transit time.
5. Decreased Surface Area: Destruction of villus tips by pathogens like Rotavirus.
6. Mucosal Invasion (Invasive Diarrhea): Direct tissue invasion by Salmonella, Shigella, or Yersinia.
Increased frequency or fluidity of bowel movements.
Preceding vomiting, fever, abdominal pain, foul-smelling stools, bloody/mucoid stools, and signs of secondary complications.
Hypokalemia: Muscle weakness, cramps, paralytic ileus (abdominal distension), flaccid paralysis of extremities, polyuria, polydipsia. ECG findings: Flattened T wave, depressed ST segment, U waves.

Hyperkalemia (seen in hypertonic dehydration): Cardiotoxicity precedes skeletal muscle signs; paresthesia, muscle weakness. ECG findings: Peaked T wave, prolonged PR interval, flattened P wave, widened QRS, ventricular fibrillation, asystole.
Metabolic Acidosis: Manifests as rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul respiration).
3. Gastrointestinal Complications: Abdominal distension secondary to paralytic ileus (hypokalemic or toxic), intussusception, perianal excoriation, and upper/lower GI bleeding.
6. Central Nervous System Complications: Seizures/Convulsions due to electrolyte imbalance, thromboembolic cerebral infarction, febrile convulsions, encephalitis, hypoglycemia, or hypocalcemia.
Profuse and frequent watery stools, repeated vomiting, eating or drinking poorly, high fever, or blood in the stool.
Stool Examination: Microscopy showing >10 pus cells/HPF indicates invasive bacterial diarrhea; stool pH and test for reducing substances confirm carbohydrate malabsorption (lactose intolerance).
Serum Electrolytes: Evaluation of sodium, potassium, and acid-base status.
1. Rehydration Therapy: Essential cornerstone of care (Plan A, B, or C).
Milk should not be routinely restricted; can be mixed with rice/cereals.
Mashed banana provides K⁺, calories, and pectin (binding agent).
Zinc Supplementation: 10 mg/day for infants <6 months; 20 mg/day for children ≥ months for a total of 14 days.
Antibiotics: Antibiotics are not required in 30–50% of cases (ORS alone is sufficient).

Indications for Antibiotics: Proven bacterial diarrhea, parasitic diarrhea (E. histolytica managed with Metronidazole 20–40 mg/kg), severe protein-energy malnutrition, diarrhea with high-grade fever, septicemia, or overt dysentery.
5. Symptomatic Care: Antipyretics for fever and antiemetics as clinically indicated.

sections.title: Dehydration
blocks: Excessive loss of body water and electrolytes resulting from diarrhea, vomitus, sweat, burns, urine, or inadequate fluid intake.
Minimal or No Dehydration: <5% loss of body weight in infants <3% in older children.
Mild to Moderate Dehydration ("Some Dehydration"): 5–10% loss of body weight in infants (3–6% in older children.
Severe Dehydration: >10% loss of body weight in infants >6% in older children.
Types of Dehydration (Based on Serum Sodium)
Isotonic Dehydration: Serum Na⁺ 130–150 mEq/L (most common).
Fluid: Administer Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) after each watery stool:
Plain water and home fluids; avoid high-sugar drinks.
Food: Continue frequent breastfeeding and age-appropriate feeding.
Educate on Danger Signs: Return immediately if diarrhea worsens over 3 days, persistent vomiting occurs, fever persists >2 days, dehydration reappears, or the child drinks poorly.
Fluid: ORS given over a 4-hour period:
Dose: 75 mL/kg (or 50-100 mL/stool) administered by cup and spoon in frequent small sips.
If vomiting occurs: Pause for 10 minutes, then resume ORS at a slower rate.
If child refuses ORS: Introduce Nasogastric Tube (NGT) feeding.
Re-evaluation: Reassess clinical status after 4 hours to choose Plan A, B, or C.
Plan C: Hospital Admission (Treat Severe Dehydration / Shock)
Indication: Severe dehydration or hypovolemic shock.
Intravenous Fluid Type: Polyelectrolyte solution or Ringer's Lactate.
Clinical Monitoring: Continuously check pulse, level of consciousness, body weight, sunken eyes, skin pinch, and urine output.
Weight Function NaCl 3.5 g/L Replaces Na⁺ loss; facilitates secondary active absorption
KCl 1.5 g/L Replaces K⁺ loss; prevents hypokalemia and paralytic
Glucose 20 g/L Provides energy; facilitates sodium absorption across the
intestinal brush border via Na⁺–glucose cotransport

sections.title: Chronic Diarrhea and Malabsorption
blocks: Acute Diarrhea: Passage of loose/watery stools >3 times/day for <14 days.
Persistent Diarrhea: Diarrhea of infectious origin continuing beyond 14 days.
Chronic Diarrhea: Diarrhea lasting > 2weeks with an insidious onset, usually of non- infectious origin.
Intractable / Protracted Diarrhea: Diarrhea 3–4 loose stools/day lasting >2 weeks in infants <1 year of age, accompanied by weight loss or failure to gain weight.
Classic diagnostic triad: Chronic diarrhea + Abdominal distension + Failure to thrive.
3. Mutations in apical membrane transport proteins congenital Na⁺/H⁺ or Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻
exchanger defects causing natal secretory diarrhea.
4. Reduction in anatomic surface area (Short bowel syndrome, Celiac disease).
5. Alterations in intestinal motility (Scleroderma, intestinal pseudo-obstruction).
Secretory: Congenital chloride diarrhea, bacterial enterotoxins, bile acid malabsorption, food allergies, dysmotility, gastrinoma, VIPoma.
Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Ulcerative Colitis, Crohn's Disease).
Infectious agents (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile, HSV, CMV, Amoebiasis).
Ischemic or radiation colitis, Colorectal neoplasia/lymphoma.
Enteric/Mucosal: Celiac disease, Whipple disease, intestinal lymphangiectasia, short bowel syndrome, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.
Maldigestion: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (Cystic Fibrosis), low lumina bile acid levels.

Etiology: An autoimmune disorder occurring in genetically susceptible individuals sensitized to gliadin (the protein fraction of gluten found in wheat, rye, and barley), causing proximal small intestinal mucosal destruction.
Clinical Features: Typical onset at 2–3 years of age:
Chronic bulky diarrhea, failure to thrive, vomiting, abdominal distension, anemia, anorexia, irritability, growth retardation, and pallor.
Small Bowel Biopsy (Gold Standard): Demonstrates villous atrophy and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.
Lifelong Gluten-Free Diet: Complete elimination of wheat, rye, and barley (substituted with rice and maize).
Definition: Diarrhea resulting from brush-border lactase enzyme deficiency in the small intestine following the ingestion of lactose-containing food (milk).
Primary: Rare autosomal recessive congenital lactase deficiency, presenting as soon as milk feeds start.
Secondary: Common acquired secondary damage to the intestinal mucosa following acute gastroenteritis, severe malnutrition, or drug toxicity.
Explosive watery diarrhea, perianal skin excoriation (secondary to acidic stools), abdominal distension, failure to thrive, flatulence, and crampy abdominal colic.
Stool test for reducing substances: Positive >0.5%.
Intestinal mucosal biopsy for direct lactase assay.
Reduction or temporary elimination of lactose from the diet.
Switch to lactose-free formula (soya milk) in secondary lactose intolerance.
Yogurt (contains bacteria producing endogenous lactase) can be tolerated.
Evaluation of the Patient with Chronic Diarrhea (Phased Approach)

Phase I: Detailed history (including fluid intake), physical exam with nutritional assessment, stool examination (pH, reducing substances, fat, ova, parasites, cultures), CBC, ESR, serum electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine.
Phase II: Sweat chloride test (to rule out Cystic Fibrosis), 72-hour quantitative stool fat collection, stool electrolytes.
Phase III: Endoscopic evaluation with small and large bowel mucosal biopsies, barium contrast studies.
Phase IV: Hormonal assays (Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide [VIP], gastrin, secretin, 5- HIAA).

sections.title: Hepatomegaly
blocks: The liver may be normally palpable 1–2 cm below the costal margin (soft with a rounded border) in healthy newborns and infants. In older children, the lower border should not be palpable below the costal margin.
Defined as an increase in liver span beyond age-matched normal values (normal span ranges from 4.5–5 cm at 1 week of age to 7–8 cm in boys 6–6.5 cm in girls by 12 years of age.
1. Increase in the number or size of intrinsic liver cells (storage or inflammation).
2. Infiltration by extrinsic cells (neoplastic or inflammatory).

sections.title: Causes of Hepatosplenomegaly
blocks: Neonates: Neonatal hepatitis, biliary atresia, congestive heart failure (CHF), erythroblastosis fetalis, congenital infections (TORCH), septicemia.

Infants: Systemic infections (viral, bacterial, parasitic), inborn errors of metabolism (galactosemia, glycogen storage disease), protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), CHF, hepatic tumors (hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma, lymphoma), veno-occlusive disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome.

Children: Viral/bacterial hepatitis, drug and toxin exposure, metabolic liver disease (Reye's syndrome, α₁-antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease), primary or metastatic tumors (leukemia, lymphoma), CHF.
Common: Congenital heart failure, metabolic storage disorders, neonatal sepsis, TORCH intrauterine infections.
Uncommon: Systemic hemangiomatosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

Common: Chronic hemolytic anemias (Thalassemia, Sickle Cell Disease), biliary obstruction, congestive heart failure, acute leukemias / lymphomas, parasitic infections (Amebiasis, Schistosomiasis, Malaria, Leishmaniasis), bacterial sepsis, systemic chronic infections.
Uncommon: Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis, Gaucher disease, primary immunodeficiencies, Niemann-Pick disease, veno-occlusive disease.

sections.title: Common Symptoms of Upper Respiratory Tract
blocks: Upper Respiratory Airway: Comprises the nose, pharynx, tonsils, epiglottis, larynx, and trachea, as well as the paranasal sinuses and the middle ear.
Lower Respiratory Airway: Comprises the bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs, along with the pleura, diaphragm, and intercostal muscles.
Extrathoracic Airway: Upper airway structures located outside the thoracic cavity like pharynx, larynx and adenoids.
Intrathoracic Airway: Lower airway structures situated within the chest wall. Like lungs, bronchi and diaphragm.
2. COMMON SYMPTOMS OF THE UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT
Upper Respiratory Symptoms: Snoring, nasal discharge, hoarseness of voice, brassy cough, stridor, obstructive apnea, and respiratory distress.
Definition: An inspiratory harsh sound caused by partial obstruction of the larynx or trachea.

sections.title: Upper Respiratory Tract Infections
blocks: Acute stridor (croup) is a heterogeneous group of acute infectious conditions causing varying degrees of laryngeal obstruction. They are characterized by a distinctive brassy cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and signs of respiratory distress.

Etiology: Most common cause of croup; viral in origin. Parainfluenza viruses (types 1, 2, and 3) account for ~75% of cases. Other causative viruses include Influenza A and B, Adenovirus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and Measles. (Note: Influenza A causes severe ALTB).
Begins following symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) and typically lasts < days.
Slow or acute onset of brassy/barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor, and respiratory distress.
As obstruction progresses, the child becomes extremely restless with elevated respiratory rate (RR) and heart rate (HR).
Cyanosis is a late sign denoting complete airway obstruction.
Symptoms are characteristically worse at night.
Radiography: Neck X-rays display subglottic narrowing known as the classic "Steeple Sign".
Humidification: Cool night air or warm bathroom steam provides symptom relief in mild cases.
Nebulized Epinephrine: Racemic epinephrine (2.25% solution; 0.25 mL for < months, 0.5 mL for > months in 2.5 mL normal saline nebulized over 15 min) temporarily reduces mucosal edema.
Corticosteroids: Oral Dexamethasone as a single dose of 0.6 mg/kg.
Airway Control: Nasotracheal intubation or tracheostomy for severe obstruction.
Definition & Etiology: A dramatic, potentially lethal condition; the most serious form of croup syndromes. Affects children aged 2–7 years and is caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).
Abrupt onset of high fever (39–40°C), aphonia, drooling of saliva, and severe respiratory distress with stridor.
The child assumes a characteristic tripod sitting position, leaning forward with the mouth open and tongue protruded.
The inflamed airway may suddenly progress to total, fatal obstruction.
Auscultation reveals bilaterally diminished breath sounds, wheezing, and scattered rales.
Direct Laryngoscopy: Visualizes swollen, cherry-red supraglottic structures and epiglottis.
Lateral Neck X-Ray: Demonstrates the classic "Thumb sign" of a swollen epiglottis.
CBC & Blood Culture: Leukocytosis; blood cultures are positive for Hib in > 80% of cases.
Immediate emergency nasotracheal intubation or tracheostomy.
Parenteral Antibiotics: Immediate administration of IV Ceftriaxone, Cefotaxime, or Ampicillin-sulbactam. (Epinephrine and steroids are of limited value).
Prevention: Active immunization with the Hib vaccine.

Definition & Etiology: An acute bacterial infection of the trachea (sparing the epiglottis) capable of causing life-threatening airway obstruction. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and H. influenzae. Usually follows a primary viral URTI as a secondary bacterial complication.
Acute Diphtheritic Laryngitis (Diphtheritic Croup): A rare, severe laryngeal obstruction caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
Acute Spasmodic Laryngitis (Spasmodic Croup): Recurrent allergic/spasmodic upper airway obstruction.
Definition: An acute viral infection of the upper respiratory tract dominated by rhinorrhea and nasal obstruction. Systemic symptoms like fever, myalgia, and headache are mild or absent.
Etiology: Rhinoviruses cause > 50% of colds. Other agents include RSV, Human Metapneumovirus, Parainfluenza viruses, and Adenoviruses.
Noninfectious: Tobacco smoke, periodic fever, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD).
Infectious: Bacteria Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus [GABHS / S. pyogenes]) and Viruses (Adenovirus, Coronavirus, CMV, EBV).
Causes of Recurrent GABHS Pharyngitis: Reinfection with the same M type, poor compliance with oral antibiotics, macrolide resistance, or infection with a new M type strain.
Treatment: Non-specific analgesics/antipyretics, anesthetic sprays/lozenges, and a 10- day course of oral Penicillin V or Amoxicillin for GABHS.
Etiology: Primarily caused by Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus(GABHS).

Acute Infection: Odynophagia, dry throat, malaise, fever, chills, dysphagia, referred otalgia, headache, dry tongue, erythematous enlarged tonsils with exudate, palatine petechiae, and enlarged, tender jugulodigastric lymph nodes.
Chronic Infection: Halitosis (foul breath odor), chronic sore throat, foreign-body sensation, and history of expelling foul-smelling cheesy material.
Treatment: 10-day oral Penicillin V or Amoxicillin; Tonsillectomy is indicated to reduce recurrent infections and chronic symptoms.
Etiology: Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis.

Clinical Picture: Nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge (unilateral or bilateral), fever, cough, halitosis, hyposmia, periorbital edema, and maxillary tooth discomfort/facial pressure exacerbated by bending forward.

Diagnosis & Treatment: Sinus aspirate culture (gold standard), CT Sinus view. Treated with oral Amoxicillin (45 mg/kg /day), Amoxicillin-clavulanate (80–90 mg/kg/day), or IV/IM Ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg/day) for a minimum of 10 days.
Etiology: S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, and M. catarrhalis (less commonly GABHS and S. aureus).
Clinical Picture: Severe ear pain, fever (may be sole sign), systemic symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea); tympanic membrane rupture leads to purulent otorrhea.

Treatment: Pain relief/analgesia, oral Amoxicillin (90 mg/kg/day) in 2 divided doses for 10 days, Amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day) of amoxicillin component), or IM/IV Ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg/day) for 1–3 days.

sections.title: Common Symptoms of Lower Respiratory Tract
blocks: Accepted age-specific cutoffs defining tachypnea in children:
Fever Effect: Fever increases respiratory rate by up to 10 breaths/min for each 1°C rise in temperature.
Severe: Orthopnea (difficulty breathing when lying flat).
Stoppage of breathing for ≥ 20 seconds, or any respiratory pause accompanied by cyanosis or bradycardia. Classified into Central, Obstructive, and Mixed types.

Deep breathing occurring with fever, metabolic acidosis, salicylism, cardiac/pu lmonary disease, or hyperventilation/panic attacks. Hyperpnea without signs of respiratory distress strongly points to a nonpulmonary cause (acidosis, fever, or salicylism).
Forced expiration against a partially closed glottis. Characteristically suggests pneumonia, hypoxia, atelectasis, or pulmonary edema.
Clinical composite including rapid breathing (tachypnea), alae nasi (nasal flaring), cyanosis, and chest wall retractions (intercostal and subcostal indrawing).
Used for clinical diagnosis and severity scoring of acute respiratory failure:

sections.title: Bronchitis
blocks: Acute Bronchitis: An acute infection that typically improves within 7 to 10 days.
Chronic Bronchitis: Defined as a productive cough lasting for 3 months or more per year for at least 2 consecutive years.
Etiology: In children, bronchitis is almost exclusively caused by viral infections.
Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs): Demonstrate variable degrees of airway obstruction in chronic cases.
Chest X-ray: Shows mildly prominent bronchovascular markings.
Complications: Otitis media, sinusitis, and post-viral secondary bacterial pneumonia.
Treatment: Adequate hydration and avoidance of environmental irritants; expectorants or cough suppressants are rarely indicated.

sections.title: Bronchiolitis
blocks: Epidemiology: Affects children under 2 years of age, with a peak seasonal incidence in winter.
Etiology: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the most common cause. Other causative agents include Parainfluenza virus, Influenza virus, Adenovirus, Mycoplasma, and Chlamydia.
Clinical Picture: Begins with upper respiratory rhinorrhea followed by tachypnea, severe respiratory distress, expiratory wheezing, and frequently apnea.
Complications: Otitis media, dehydration, pneumonia, and recurrent wheezy chest episodes.
Investigations: Chest X-ray reveals hyperinflation or segmental atelectasis.
Hospitalization: Indicated for severe distress or hypoxemia.
Oxygenation: Humidified oxygen targeting adequate saturation monitored via pulse oximetry or ABG.
Supportive Care: Intravenous fluid hydration and mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure occurs.
Pharmacotherapy: Trial of inhaled β-agonists or theophylline; empiric corticosteroids; and inhaled Ribavirin as specific antiviral therapy.

sections.title: Bronchiectasis
blocks: Definition & Pathophysiology: A chronic condition characterized by irreversible bronchial dilation resulting from tissue destruction combined with chronic pulmonary infection.

Clinical Picture: Chronic productive cough with purulent sputum, recurrent fever, dyspnea, digital clubbing, signs of co-existing sinusitis, recurrent pneumonia, and persistent moist rales and rhonchi over the affected lung segments.
Bacteriology: Haemophilus influenzae type b is the most common isolated pathogen.
Chest Radiography: Shows areas of atelectasis with cystic changes.
High-Resolution CT Scan: Diagnostic test of choice.
Bronchogram: Rarely performed except during pre-surgical planning.
PFTs: Demonstrate an obstructive ventilatory pattern.

sections.title: Pneumonia
blocks: Definition: Inflammation of the lung parenchyma accompanied by alveolar exudation leading to pulmonary consolidation.
1. Lobar Pneumonia: Consolidation localized to and completely involving one or more lobes.
2. Lobular Pneumonia (Bronchopneumonia): Patchy consolidation involving scattered lobules across both lung fields.
3. Interstitial Pneumonia: Inflammation primarily involving the alveolar walls, sacs, ducts, and interstitium (typical of viral infections).
1. Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, Group B Streptococcus, S. aureus, Klebsiella, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas, M. tuberculosis.
2. Viral: RSV, Adenovirus, Parainfluenza, Influenza, SARS, Avian flu (H5N1), Swine flu (H1N1), Measles.
4. Aspiration: Infected amniotic fluid or regurgitated milk feeds.
Neonate: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli.
4 to 16 Weeks: S. aureus, H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae.
Up to 5 Years: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae.
Overview: S. pneumoniae causes >90% of childhood bacterial pneumonias.

Clinical Presentation in Infants: Rapid onset preceded by URTI; high fever (39–40°C), restlessness, tachypnea, and severe respiratory distress. Physical exam reveals localized dullness, diminished breath sounds or bronchial breathing, fine crackles/rales over the affected lobe, abdominal distension (secondary to swallowed air or paralytic ileus), and nuchal rigidity (meningism)—especially with right upper lobe consolidation.

Clinical Presentation in Children & Teenagers: Abrupt onset with shaking chills, high fever (39°C), dry hacking cough progressing to productive blood- tinged sputum, and pleuritic chest pain. Classic physical signs of consolidation are evident by days 2–3.
Complications: Pleural effusion, empyema, and lung abscess.
Antibiotic Therapy: Oral Amoxicillin (50 mg/kg/day) or parenteral Ceftriaxone (50–100 mg/kg/day) for a minimum of 10 days.
Supportive Care: Oxygen therapy, fluid hydration, and antipyretics.

sections.title: Pleural Disorders
blocks: Definition: Inflammatory reaction involving the pleural sac.
Dry Pleurisy: Secondary to pneumococcal or viral pneumonia, tuberculosis, or connective tissue disorders.
Clinical Presentation: Characterized by localized pleural pain and a audible pleural friction rub.
Definition: Fluid accumulation within the pleural space.

Etiology: Bacterial pneumonia, congestive heart failure (CHF), metastatic intrathoracic malignancies, subphrenic abscesses, collagen vascular diseases (SLE, Rheumatic Fever), nephrotic syndrome, and liver cirrhosis.
Symptoms: Fever, cough, dyspnea, and orthopnea (child lies preferentially on the affected side).

Physical Signs: Bulging of the affected chest wall, fullness of intercostal spaces, diminished chest wall movement, mediastinal shift (trachea and apex beat pushed to opposite side), stony dullness on percussion, and markedly diminished or absent breath sounds. (Bronchial breathing and aegophony above the fluid level signify compression lung collapse).
Chest X-Ray: Homogeneous dense opacity obliterating the costophrenic angle and rising toward the axilla.
Workup: Diagnostic thoracocentesis, pleural fluid culture, and tuberculin skin testing.
Management: Treatment of underlying cause, repeated therapeutic thoracocentesis, and chest tube drainage.
Definition: Accumulation of gross pus within the pleural space.
Etiology: Pyogenic infection spreading from underlying pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae), lung abscess, trauma/thoracic surgery, mediastinitis, or subdiaphragmatic infection.

Clinical Picture: Features identical to pleural effusion, but the child appears markedly more toxic with higher fever, severe respiratory distress, intercostal edema, and significant chest wall tenderness.

Complications: Chronic empyema (thick, rigid pleural walls preventing lung re- expansion), bronchopleural fistula (S. aureus), pyopneumothorax (S. aureus), empyema necessitans (pus burrowing through the chest wall), rib osteomyelitis, purulent pericarditis, and peritonitis.
Treatment: High-dose parenteral antibiotics, chest tube drainage, and thoracocentesis.

sections.title: Wheezy Chest (DD)
blocks: A wheezy chest in children requires differentiation across anatomical levels:
Upper Respiratory Tract Conditions: Allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinitis, sinusitis, adenotonsillar hypertrophy, and nasal foreign body.

Middle Respiratory Tract Conditions: Laryngotracheobronchomalacia, laryngotracheobronchitis (e.g., pertussis), laryngeal web/cyst/stenosis, chronic bronchitis secondary to tobacco smoke exposure, vocal cord paralysis, tracheoesophageal fistula, vascular rings/slings/masses, and foreign body aspiration.

Lower Respiratory Tract Conditions: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), viral bronchiolitis, gastroesophageal reflux (GERD), tuberculosis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, and causes of bronchiectasis (Cystic Fibrosis, primary immunodeficiency, chronic aspiration, primary ciliary dyskinesia).

sections.title: Rheumatic Fever
blocks: Definition: An immunologic inflammatory disease that occurs as a delayed sequela following Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) pharyngitis.
Predisposing Factors: Family history of ARF, low socioeconomic status (overcrowding, poor hygiene, healthcare deprivation), and age between 5 and 15 years.
Streptococcal Link: Pharyngitis precedes the onset of ARF by 2 to 6 weeks.
Rheumatogenic Strains: Specific GABHS M serotypes (types 1, 3, 5, 6, 18, 19, and 24) carry high rheumatogenic potential.
Immune-Mediated Injury (Accepted Theory): Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and human host tissues triggers autoantibody production.

Pathology: Inflammatory lesions in joints, heart, brain, and skin. Valvular damage predominantly targets the mitral valve, followed by the aortic valve, and rarely tricuspid or pulmonary valves. Aschoff bodies (granulomatous inflammatory lesions) within the atrial myocardium are pathognomonic.
Diagnosis requires evidence of preceding GABHS infection PLUS either 2 Major Criteria OR 1 Major + 2 Minor Criteria:
Involves large joints (knees, ankles, elbows, wrists).
Classic migratory polyarthritis featuring swelling, heat, redness, severe pain, and restricted movement.
Characterized by a dramatic clinical response to salicylates within 48 hours and resolves without residual joint deformities.

Features: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever; valvulitis murmurs (Mitral Regurgitation [MR] or Aortic Regurgitation [AR]); pericarditis (friction rub, pericardial effusion, chest pain, ECG changes); cardiomegaly; and congestive heart failure (gallop rhythm, muffled heart sounds, hepatomegaly, pulmonary/peripheral edema).
Diagnostic Triad: Choreic movements + Hypotonia + Emotional lability.
Begins with emotional changes, followed 1–4 weeks later by involuntary, purposeless, irregular choreic movements.
Movements are exacerbated by stress and disappear during sleep; accompanied by motor weakness and facial grimacing. Associated with elevated anti-neuronal antibodies affecting the basal ganglia.
Non-pruritic, erythematous, serpiginous or annular rash located on the trunk and inner proximal extremities.
Evanescent: Fades with cold exposure and r eappears after warm baths or under warm blankets.
Firm to hard, painless, non-pruritic, freely mobile nodules (0.2–2 cm).
Found symmetrically over extensor surfaces of large and small joints, the scalp, and along the spine.
Laboratory: Elevated acute-phase reactants (increased ESR and CRP) and prolonged PR interval on ECG.
C. Supporting Evidence of Preceding GABHS Infection
Positive throat culture or positive rapid streptococcal antigen test.
Elevated or rising streptococcal antibody titers: ASO titer >330 Todd units in children (Anti-DNase B >25 Todd units).
D. Exceptions to Jones Criteria (3 Exceptions)
1. Sydenham's chorea occurring as the sole presenting manifestation.
2. Indolent carditis presenting months after the initial streptococcal infection.
Complete Blood Count (CBC), elevated ESR, elevated CRP, positive throat culture, elevated ASO titer (>330 Todd units), chest X-ray, ECG, and Echocardiography with Doppler studies.
1. Bed Rest: Strict bed rest during acute inflammation.
Single IM dose of Benzathine Penicillin OR a 10-day course of oral Erythromycin.
Arthritis & Mild Carditis: Aspirin at 50–70 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 3–5 days, then 50 mg/kg/day for 2–3 weeks, followed by half the dose for 2–4 weeks.
Moderate to Severe Carditis / CHF: Oral Prednisone at 2 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 2–3 weeks, followed by half the dose for 2–3 weeks, then tapered by 5 mg/day every 2–3 days.
4. Management of Congestive Heart Failure: Complete bed rest, cool humidified oxygen, sodium and fluid restriction, IV Prednisolone, Digoxin, and IV Furosemide (1 mg/kg).

5. Management of Chorea: Streptococcal eradication, monthly penicillin prophylaxis, and motor control drugs (Phenobarbital, Haloperidol, Valproic acid, Chlorpromazine, Diazepam, or Steroids). (Plasma exchange and IVIG are under clinical trial).
Primary Prophylaxis: A 10-day course of oral Penicillin V or Erythromycin given for acute GABHS pharyngitis.
Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin: 1.2 million units IM every 3 to 4 weeks (Drug of Choice).
Oral Alternatives: Oral Penicillin V (250 mg BD), oral Sulfadiazine (1 g OD), or oral Erythromycin (250 mg BD or 20 mg/kg/day).
Clinical Category Mandatory Duration of Prophylaxis
ARF Without Carditis 5 years OR until 21 years of age (whichever is
10 years OR until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)
