sections.title: Infective Endocarditis
blocks: Infective endocarditis requires three core predisposing factors:
Rheumatic Heart Disease (R HD): Most commonly aortic stenosis, aortic insufficiency, and mitral insufficiency.

Congenital Heart Disease (CHD): Ventricular septal defects (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and pulmonary stenosis (PS). It does not occur in simple atrial septal defects (ASD). It is rare in mitral valve prolapse or cyanotic CHD unless a shunt procedure has been performed.
Other: May occur on normal tricuspid valves in immunosuppressed patients or on prosthetic heart valves.
Streptococcus viridans: Accounts for 50% of cases.
Staphylococcus aureus: Accounts for 30% of cases.
Other Agents: Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, or fungal pathogens (e.g., Candida).
3. Route of Entry / Source of Infection:
Transient bacteremia following dental extractions or poor oral hygiene.
Cardiac surgery, cardiac catheterization, or indwelling intravenous lines.
Symptoms and signs arise from systemic toxemia, secondary autoimmune responses, cardiac
Pyrexia (fever), anorexia, profuse sweating, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, splenomegaly, and digital clubbing.
Splenic Infarction: Causes left flank pain.
Cerebral Infarction: Produces stroke-like focal neurological deficits.
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: Leads to sudden monocular blindness.
Pulmonary Embolism: Causes pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath.
Splinter Hemorrhages: Linear subungual hemorrhages under finger or toe nails.
Petechiae: Small hemorrhagic lesions with pale centers on the conjunctiva, oral mucosa, dorsum of hands, and trunk.
Osler's Nodules: Painful, small, red or purple raised nodules located on the pulps of the terminal phalanges of fingers and toes.
Janeway Lesions: Flat, non-tender erythematous macules on the thenar a nd hypothenar eminences of the palms and soles.
Roth's Spots: White-centered retinal hemorrhages seen on fundoscopy.
Diffuse Glomerulonephritis: Results in microscopic hematuria.
Signs of pre-existing valvular or shunt lesions (present in 85% of cases).
Sudden appearance of a new heart murmur or a change in the character of a pre- existing murmur.
Signs of acute congestive heart failure (tachycardia, hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm).
Blood Cultures: The gold standard; 2 to 5 blood samples drawn on 2 to 3 successive days before starting antibiotics.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Demonstrates normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, or occasional leukopenia.
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): Characteristically markedly elevated.
Echocardiography (with Doppler): Visualizes valvular vegetations, perivalvular abscesses, and underlying congenital/acquired structural defects.
Renal failure (secondary to embolic infarction or immune-complex glomerulonephritis).
Myocardial and perivalvular abscesses, which may rupture to produce purulent pericarditis.
Indicated 1 hour prior to invasive procedures in high-risk patients:
Dental Procedures: Oral Amoxicillin (50 mg/kg as a single dose).
GU / GI Procedures: Amoxicillin combined with Gentamicin (1.5 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours).
General Measures: Maintain strict oral hygiene and perform surgical correction of structural defects (e.g., closure of PDA) when feasible.
Blood cultures must be drawn immediately prior to starting therapy.
Empiric Regimen: Intravenous Crystalline Penicillin G (200,000–300,000 U/kg/day) combined with IV Gentamicin (4 mg/kg/day).
Regimens are subsequently tailored according to culture and sensitivity results and continued for 4 to 6 weeks.
Surgical Intervention: Indicated for refractory heart failure, persistent bacteremia, or perivalvular/aortic root abscesses.

sections.title: CBC Interpretation
blocks: MCV: 80–95 fL, MCH: 27–31 pg, MCHC: 32–36 g/dL
B. Clinical Indications for Requesting a CBC

Suspected infection/s epsis, anemia, bleeding disorders, nutritional deficiencies, concerning weight loss, bone marrow failure, acute trauma/hemorrhage, active hemolysis, renal failure, or chronic systemic illness.

Clinical Assessment: Children often remain asymptomatic until Hb < 7 g/dL. Evaluation includes family history (SCD, Thalassemia, Spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency), dietary history (iron intake), and physical signs (mucous membrane pallor, excessive bruising, splenomegaly, jaundice).
Normal or Elevated: Indicates hemorrhage, splenic sequestration (SCD), or active hemolysis (Hereditary Spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency).
Low: Indicates bone marrow failure (aplastic anemia, marrow infiltration, Parvovirus B19 infection, chemotherapy), hematinic deficiency, ineffective erythropoiesis, or reduced erythropoietin drive.
2. Red Cell Indices (MCV, MCH): Categorizes anemia into Normocytic normochromic, Microcytic hypochromic, or Macrocytic.
Peripheral Blood Film (PBF): Evaluates diagnostic red cell morphology (e.g., spherocytes, sickle cells, schizocytes/fragments, target cells).
Leukocytosis: Indicates infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, or leukemic neoplasia. Eosinophilia points to allergic conditions, asthma, or parasitic infections.
Neutropenia Definition: Reduction in absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below normal for age, sex, and ethnic origin.

Etiology: Congenital (Kostmann syndrome, severe chronic neutropenia); Acquired (drug- induced, toxins, post-viral marrow suppression, immune-mediated, hypersplenism). Viral infection is the most common cause of transient neutropenia in children.

Management: Workup includes viral screening, neutrophil antibodies, B12/folate levels, immunoglobulins, and lymphocyte subsets. Managed with G-CSF therapy or bone marrow transplantation for severe persistent cases.
Normal Range: 150–450 × 10⁹/L (average lifespan 7–10 days; cleared by the spleen).
Impaired Production: Inherited (Fanconi anemia) or Acquired (aplastic anemia, bone marrow infiltration).
Decreased Survival: Immune-mediated (ITP) or Non-immune mediated (DIC).
Defined as a hemoglobin concentration or red cell mass falling below the lower limit of normal for age and sex.
B. Essential Nutritional Requirements for Erythropoiesis
Vitamins: Vitamin B₁₂, folic acid, Vitamin C, B₆, Vitamin E, Riboflavin.
Microcytic Hypochromic: Iron deficiency anemia, Thalassemia, Sideroblastic anemia, Lead poisoning.
Normocytic Normochromic: Acute blood loss, early chronic disease.
Blood Loss: Acute or chronic hemorrhage.
Cytoplasmic Maturation Defect: Defective heme synthesis (IDA) or globin synthesis (Thalassemia).
Stem Cell Proliferation Defect: Aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia.
Anemia of Chronic Diseases: Chronic renal failure, leukemia, lymphoma, myelosclerosis.

sections.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia
blocks: Anemia resulting from inadequate body iron required for hemoglobin synthesis; it represents the most common type of anemia in childhood.
Body Iron Content: A full-term newborn contains 0.5 g of iron, whereas an adult contains 5 g.
Peak Age Incidence: Most common between 9 and 24 months of age.
Daily Requirement: 1 mg/kg/day of elemental iron up to 15 years of age.
Occurs primarily in the proximal small intestine (duodenum) via specialized transport proteins, with an overall absorption rate of 10% to 20%.
Human Milk Advantage: Iron in human breast milk is absorbed 3 times more efficiently than iron in cow's milk.
C. Causes of Iron Deficiency Anemia
Dietary intake poor in bioavailable iron.
Low birth weight (LBW) and prematurity (depleted neonatal iron stores).
Cow's milk protein allergy causing occult GI blood loss.
Delayed introduction of iron-fortified complementary foods (cereals) beyond 6 months of age.
Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss: Peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic diarrhea, hookworm infestation (Ancylostoma), or menorrhagia.
Pallor: The most important and consistent clinical sign.
Pica: An abnormal craving to ingest non-nutritive substances (e.g., ice, dirt, clay, plaster).
General Symptoms: Irritability, anorexia, fatigue, tachycardia, functional hemi c murmurs, and glossitis.
CNS & Behavioral Effects: Decreased attention span, impaired alertness, cognitive/learning difficulties, and an increased frequency of breath-holding spells.
Serum Ferritin: Decreased (the most sensitive marker of depleted body iron stores).
Peripheral Blood Film (PBF): Microcytic hypochromic red cells, marked anisocytosis (variation in size), poikilocytosis (variation in shape), and nucleated RBCs.
Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW): Markedly increased (a key feature distinguishing IDA from Thalassemia trait).
Reticulocyte Count: Normal or slightly elevated.
Platelets: Reactive thrombocytosis is frequently present.
Bone Marrow: Hypercellular with marked erythroid hyperplasia.
β-ThalassemiaTrait: RBC count is characteristically elevated; RDW is normal or only slightly raised.
Lead Poisoning: Characterized by prominent basophilic stippling on PBF.
Administer oral ferrous salts providing 3 to 6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron.
Duration: Continued for 3 months (1 month to restore normal Hb levels, followed by 2 additional months to fully replenish tissue iron stores).
Calculated via the formula: Iron Deficit (mg) = Hb Deficit × Weight (kg) × 4.
Administered as 50 mg iron IM daily.
Reduce whole cow's milk consumption to ≤ 500 mL/day.
Encourage iron-rich foods (iron-fortified cereals, green leafy vegetables, bananas, apples, liver, red meat, fish).
Reserved strictly for severe anemia (Hb <4 g/dL) or cardiac decompensation, using packed RBCs at 2 to 3 mL/kg.
5. Treat Underlying Cause: Eradicate intestinal parasites (hookworm), treat peptic ulcer disease, or manage dietary allergies.
H. Chronological Response Timeline to Oral Iron Therapy
12 to 24 Hours: Rapid replacement of intracellular iron-containing enzymes; clinical improvement marked by increased appetite and decreased irritability.
36 to 48 Hours: Initial bone marrow response with marked erythroid hyperplasia.
48 to 72 Hours: Reticulocytosis begins, reaching a peak at 5 to 7 days.
4 to 30 Days: Steady rise in hemoglobin levels.
1 to 3 Months: Full repletion of internal iron stores.

sections.title: Megaloblastic Anemia
blocks: Megaloblastic anemia is a nuclear maturation defect characterized by:
Abnormally large red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow called megaloblasts.
Prominent macro-ovalocytosis with a Mean Corpuscular Volume MCV >100 fL.
Primary Causes: Deficiency of Vitamin B₁₂ or Folic acid (folate). Both human milk and cow's milk are naturally poor sources of folic acid.

Pathogenesis: Vitamin B₁₂ and folic acid are essential cofactors for cellular DNA synthesis. Deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, causing delayed nuclear maturation, while RNA and protein synthesis remain unaffected (resulting in normal cytoplasmic maturation and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchronous development). Both vitamins are required for rapidly dividing cells, including myeloid bone marrow precursors and gastrointestinal mucosal epithelial cells.
Folate Deficiency: Peaks in infants aged 4 to 7 months; presents with generalized anemia, irritability, and failure to gain weight.

Neurological Features: Peripheral neuropathy manifesting as weakness, paresthesia, sensory deficits, hypotonia, seizures, and developmental delay. In adults, it causes sub-acute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

Systemic & Epithelial Features: Angular stomatitis, glossitis (beefy red tongue), purpura, anorexia, weight loss, malabsorption, irritability, tremors, and hyperpigmentation on the dorsum of the limbs, fingers, and nose.
Complete Blood Count (CBC) & Peripheral Blood Film:
Blood film displays marked macrocytosis, macro-ovalocytes, anisocytosis, and poikilocytosis.
Red cell indices show ↑ MCV, ↑ MCH, with normal or ↓ MCHC.
Leukopenia with characteristic hypersegmented neutrophils (5 or more lobes).
Bone Marrow Examination: Hypercellular marrow showing classic megaloblastic erythroid precursors.
Biochemical Assays: Reduced serum Vitamin B₁₂ levels (< 200 pg/mL; normal is 200– 700 pg/mL) and radio-assays.
Folic Acid Therapy: Administered at a dose of 1 to 2.5 mg/day orally for 3 to 4 weeks.
Vitamin B₁₂ Therapy: Administered at a dose of 5 mg/day; if neurological symptoms are present, give 1 mg IM daily for 7 days, followed by weekly doses.
Blood Transfusion: Reserved for severe, life-threatening anemia.

sections.title: Aplastic Anemia
blocks: A primary bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by the suppression or destruction of multipotent myeloid stem cells, resulting in profound pancytopenia (neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia).
Idiopathic: Accounts for the majority of cases.
Myelotoxic Drugs & Chemicals: Benzene, alkylating agents, antimetabolites (e.g., vincristine).
Infectious Agents: Hepatitis viruses, HIV/AIDS, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Inherited Bone Marrow Failure Disorders: Fanconi anemia and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (pure red cell aplasia).
Anemia Signs: Progressive pallor, weakness, and fatigue.
Granulocytopenia Signs: Recurrent, severe bacterial or fungal infections.
Thrombocytopenia Signs: Mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and gum bleeding.
Physical Finding: The spleen is characteristically NOT enlarged.
Peripheral Blood: Marked reduction in Hb, total WBC, absolute neutrophil count, and platelet count.
Bone Marrow Aspirate & Biopsy: Yields a "dry tap" or demonstrates hypocellular/aplastic marrow replaced by fat cells.
Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), Acute Leukemia, and Myeloid Metaplasia.
Definitive Treatment of Choice: Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplantation (BMT).
Supportive Care: Transfusion of packed RBCs and platelets, aggressive treatment of bacterial infections with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and IV Amphotericin B for fungal infections.
Anti-Lymphocyte Globulin (ALG) or Anti-Thymocyte Globulin (ATG; 10–15 mg/kg/day for 4 days).
Hematopoietic Growth Factors: Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor (G-CSF) and Recombinant Human Erythropoietin.

sections.title: Hemolytic Anemia
blocks: Hemolytic anemias are a diverse group of conditions characterized by:
1. Premature destruction of red blood cells (shortened RBC lifespan <120 days).
3. Compensatory erythroid hyperplasia and increased erythropoiesis within the bone
Autoimmune HA: Warm antibody or cold antibody type.
Isoimmune HA: Rh or ABO incompatibility.
Direct Toxic Infection: Malaria, severe bacterial sepsis.
Acquired Membrane Abnormality: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH).
RBC Membrane Abnormalities: Hereditary spherocytosis, hereditary elliptocytosis.
RBC Enzyme Deficiencies: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency.
Hemoglobin Disorders: Hemoglobinopathies (Sickle cell syndromes) and Thalassemias.
Positive family history with a lifelong history of anemia.
Splenomegaly and development of pigment gallstones.

Tests Demonstrating Increased Hemolysis: Elevated unconjugated (indirect) serum bilirubin, increased urine urobilinogen, decreased serum haptoglobins and hemopexins, elevated plasma lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria.

Tests Demonstrating Increased Erythropoiesis: Elevated reticulocyte count, peripheral blood smear showing macrocytosis, polychromasia, normoblasts, and microspherocytes; bone marrow showing erythroid hyperplasia with increased iron stores.
Special Tests: Osmotic fragility test, Direct and Indirect Coombs' tests, Hb electrophoresis, fetal Hb estimation, sickling test, and G6PD screening assay.

sections.title: Thalassemia Syndrome
blocks: A heterogeneous group of single-gene Mendelian disorders characterized by defective or absent synthesis of specific globin polypeptide chains α-globin or β-globin of adult Hemoglobin A (α₂β₂).
Gene Loci: β-globin chains are encoded by a single pair of genes on chromosome 11; α- globin chains are encoded by two pairs of genes on chromosome 16.
Classified according to the number of deleted α-globin genes:
4. Hydrops Fetalis: 4 genes deleted (fatal in utero or at birth).
Classified by genetic defect (β⁰: complete absence of β-chain synthesis; β⁺: reduced β-chain synthesis) and gene dosage:
1. Thalassemia Major (Cooley's Anemia): Homozygous state (β⁰/β⁰ or β⁺/β⁺).
2. Thalassemia Intermedia: Genetically heterozygous β⁰/β⁺ presenting with clinical features between major and minor.
3. Thalassemia Minor (Trait): Heterozygous state with one normal β-gene.

sections.title: Thalassemia Major
blocks: Pathogenesis: Complete absence or severe reduction of β-chain synthesis leads to an excess of un-paired α-chains, which precipitate within developing erythroblasts causing ineffective erythropoiesis and severe peripheral hemolysis. This stimulates excessive production of alternate hemoglobins: Fetal HbF (α₂γ₂)or HbA₂ (α₂δ₂).
Infants appear normal at birth; severe anemia manifests between 4 and 6 months of age as fetal hemoglobin declines.
Classic Thalassemia Facies: Caused by severe medullary erythroid hyperplasia expanding facial bones (f rontal bossing, prominent maxilla, dental malocclusion, and depressed nasal bridge).
Features of Systemic Iron Overload: Physical growth retardation, delayed puberty, diabetes mellitus, and fatal iron-overload cardiomyopathy.
CBC: ↓ Hb/Hct, marked ↓ MCV & MCH, ↑ reticulocytes, and reactive leukocytosis.
Peripheral Blood Film: Microcytic hypochromic anemia, marked anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, fragmented RBCs, nucleated RBCs, polychromasia, basophilic stippling, and target cells.
Biochemical: Elevated indirect serum bilirubin and markedly increased serum ferritin.
Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: Demonstrates elevation of HbF (50–98%) or increased HbA₂, with absent or markedly decreased HbA1.
Radiology: Hand X-rays show a rectangular appearance of metacarpals; skull X - ray shows the classic "hair-on-end" trabecular pattern. Bone marrow exhibits normoblastic erythroid hyperplasia.
1. Bone Marrow Transplantation: Curative treatment for children < 15 years of age without severe iron overload or hepatomegaly.
2. Hypertransfusion Therapy: Regular packed RBC transfusions (10–15 mL/kg every 3 to 4 weeks) targeting a baseline Hb level of 9.5 to 10 g/dL.
3. Iron Chelation Therapy: Essential to treat transfusion-induced iron overload using parenteral Desferrioxamine or oral Deferiprone (75 mg/kg/day) in 2–3 divided doses).
4. Splenectomy: Indicated when annual blood transfusion requirements exceed 240 mL/kg/year.
Thalassemia Intermedia: Heterozygous (β⁰/β⁺) with baseline Hb levels between 5 and 10 g/dL. Anemia is detected around 4 to 5 years of age with mild hepatosplenomegaly.

Thalassemia Minor (Trait): Heterozygous state with moderate β-chain suppression. Usually asymptomatic with mild anemia (Hb 10–12 g/dL), normal free erythrocyte protoporphyrin, elevated HbA₂, and a slight increase in HbF.

sections.title: Sickle Cell Disease
blocks: A autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the β- globin gene on chromosome 11, resulting in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the 6th position of the β-polypeptide chain, forming sickle hemoglobin (HbS).
Mixed Hemoglobinopathies: Sickle β-thalassemia, Sickle C disease, and Sickle D disease.
During deoxygenation, HbS molecules aggregate and polymerize into rigid polymers, altering the normal biconcave RBC into an elongated crescent or sickle-shaped cell.
Sickling is exacerbated by dehydration (elevated MCHC accelerates polymerization), hypoxia, and acidosis.

Chronic hemolytic anemia, chronic hyperbilirubinemia (lemon-yellow skin hue), gallstones, early hepatosplenomegaly progressing to auto-splenectomy, non-healing leg ulcers, physical growth retardation, delayed puberty, and digital clubbing.
Micro-infarctions in the abdomen, chest, back, and joints causing acute painful crises.
Macro-infarctions in heart valves, spleen, bones, lungs, kidneys, liver, and skin.
Auto-splenectomy: Repeated splenic infarctions reduce the spleen to a fibrotic nodule.
Acute Chest Syndrome: Pulmonary infarction accompanied by pneumonitis and fat embolism.
Stroke: Most common in children aged 6 to 9 years.
Acute Sickle Dactylitis: Hand-foot syndrome occurring in infants.
2. Aplastic Crises: Acute bone marrow suppression triggered by Parvovirus B19 infection or folate deficiency.
3. Splenic Sequestration Crises: Massive pooling of blood in the spleen.

Infection Susceptibility: Loss of splenic function creates high susceptibility to severe encapsulated bacterial infections, particularly Salmonella osteomyelitis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and H. influenzae.
Peripheral blood film demonstrates sickled RBCs and target cells.
Positive Sickling Test: Demonstrates sickling when exposed to reducing agents like sodium metabisulfite.
Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: Confirms presence of HbS (2–20% HbA₂/HbF/HbS).
Prenatal diagnosis via fetal DNA analysis.
1. Immunization: Mandatory vaccination with conjugate pneumococcal vaccine and all routine childhood vaccines.
2. Prophylactic Penicillin: Initiated at 2 months of age (125 mg BD from 2 months to 3 years; 250 mg BD above 3 years).
4. Analgesic Therapy: Acetaminophen with codeine for painful crises.
5. Blood Transfusion: Indicated for acute chest syndrome, stroke, severe aplastic anemia, splenic sequestration, and pre-surgical preparation.
6. Disease-Modifying Drug: Hydroxyurea (increases protective HbF levels).
7. Curative Therapy: Bone marrow transplantation in patients <16 years of age.

sections.title: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency
blocks: An X-linked recessive enzymopathy affecting males, while females are usually asymptomatic heterozygous carriers.
Oxidant Drugs: Antimalarials (primaquine), sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, aspirin, large doses of vitamin K, and nalidixic acid.
Favism: Ingestion of fava beans (Vicia faba).
Deficiency of G6PD impairs the hexose monophosphate shunt, leading to inadequate production of reduced glutathione (GSH).
Under oxidant stress, hemoglobin undergoes oxidation and denaturation, forming insoluble inclusions called Heinz bodies.

Heinz bodies attach to the inner erythrocyte membrane, reducing cell flexibility; as these damaged cells pass through the spleen, splenic macrophages bite out the inclusions, leading to intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.
Type I: Sensitive to strong oxidants (primaquine, sulfonamides, high-dose vitamin K).
Type II: Hemolysis continues during continuous drug exposure; enzyme activity is reduced to 8–15%.
Type III: Severe enzyme deficiency presenting with neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, severe jaundice during viral hepatitis, or chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia without drug exposure.
Onset of acute hemolytic anemia occurs within hours after exposure to oxidant stress. Symptoms include sudden jaundice, dark urine, pallor, and fatigue.
The episode is self-limiting because hemolysis preferentially destroys older, enzyme - depleted RBCs while sparing younger reticulocytes with higher enzyme activity.
Demonstration of Heinz bodies on special blood film stains during acute crisis.
Direct quantitative assay of G6PD enzyme activity in RBCs (performed after the acute hemolytic episode has resolved).
Strict avoidance of known oxidant drugs, chemicals, and fava beans.
Packed RBC transfusions for severe, symptomatic acute anemia.

sections.title: Hereditary Spherocytosis
blocks: Definition: A hereditary intrinsic hemolytic anemia characterized by a fundamental defect in the red blood cell (RBC) membrane.
Inheritance: Transmitted predominantly as an autosomal dominant trait.
Results from a deficiency or structural abnormality in spectrin (or associated membrane proteins like ankyrin), which is a key structural protein of the RBC cytoskeleton.
Cytoskeletal instability causes progressive loss of membrane lipid surface area relative to intracellular volume, converting the normal biconcave disc into a rigid, spherical cell (microspherocyte).
Microspherocytes lack flexibility and are prematurely trapped and destroyed during transit through the narrow cords of the spleen.
Classic Triad: Hemolytic anemia, jaundice (mild and fluctuating), and splenomegaly.
Pigment gallstones (cholelithiasis) secondary to chronic hyperbilirubinemia.
Positive family history of lifelong anemia, early gallstones, or splenectomy.
CBC: Decreased hemoglobin Hb; elevated reticulocyte count (typically 5% to 20%).
Peripheral Blood Film (PBF): Demonstrates abundant hyperchromic microspherocytes (small, round RBCs lacking central pallor).
Osmotic Fragility Test: Markedly increased (spherocytes lyse in higher concentrations of hypotonic saline than normal cells).
EMA (Eosin-5-Maleimide Binding) Test: Flow cytometric dye-binding assay used as a highly sensitive diagnostic test.
Folic Acid Supplementation: 1 mg/day daily to support elevated erythropoiesis and prevent aplastic crises.
Eliminates the site of RBC destruction, resolving anemia and jaundice (though membrane defect persists).
Timing: Recommended after 5 years of age to minimize the risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI).
Under 5 years: Partial splenectomy is preferred if severe anemia requires intervention.
Vaccinations: Pre-operative administration of pneumococcal, H. influenzae type b, and meningococcal vaccines 2 weeks prior to surgery.
Antibiotics: Daily oral Penicillin V (125-250 mg twice daily) for life.

sections.title: Generalized Lymphadenopathy
blocks: Enlargement of more than two contiguous lymph node regions; usually caused by systemic infections, immune disorders, or hematological malignancies, and often accompanied by abnormal findings in other organ systems.
B. Characteristics of Enlarged Lymph Nodes
Infectious / Inflammatory: Tender, warm, with overlying skin erythema (suggests acute pyogenic infection).
Tuberculous: Typically matted, firm, and may form cold abscesses or sinus tracts.
Malignant: Firm to stony hard, non-tender, rubbery, matted, or fixed to adjacent skin/underlying deep structures.
Abnormal Size Thresholds: Diameter exceeding >1.5 cm for cervical or axillary nodes, and >2.5 cm for inguinal nodes. Nodes >2 cm raise heightened suspicion of neoplasia.
C. Indications for Lymph Node Biopsy
1. Persistent, unexplained fever, weight loss >10%, night sweats, or a fixed node.
2. Failure to decrease in size after 2 weeks of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
3. Persistent lymphadenopathy lasting longer than 4 to 6 weeks.
4. Enlargement of supraclavicular lymph nodes (associated with a high risk of
Infectious Causes of Generalized or Prominent Cervical Lymphadenopathy:
Viral: Epstein-Barr Virus (Infectious Mononucleosis), Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Rubella, Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), Adenovirus, Coxsackievirus, HIV.
Bacterial & Others: Streptococcal pharyngitis, Tuberculosis, Brucellosis, Toxoplasmosis, Cat-scratch disease.
Cervical: Streptococcal adenitis, Infectious Mononucleosis, Toxoplasmosis, Kawasaki disease, Tuberculosis, Lymphoma/Leukemia.
Mediastinal: Tuberculosis, Lymphoma, Leukemia, Sarcoidosis, Fungal infections.
Abdominal / Mesenteric: Mesenteric adenitis (right iliac fossa pain mimicking appendicitis), Lymphoma, HIV.
Axillary: Cat-scratch disease, chest wall/arm infections, Lymphoma/Histiocytosis, HIV.
Occipital / Submandibular: Scalp infections, rubella, viral exanthems, throat infections, TB.
Inguinal: Lower extremity or groin infections, STDs.
1. Detailed History: Contact with TB cases, animal/cat exposure, B-symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).
2. Physical Examination: Assess node consistency, mobility, fixation, and examine for hepatosplenomegaly or systemic bleeding signs.
Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential, Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR).
Tuberculin Skin Test (TST), serology for EBV (heterophile/VCA antibodies), Toxoplasma (IgM/IgG), HIV.
Chest X-ray (to screen for mediastinal masses or hilar lymphadenopathy).
Excisional lymph node biopsy or fine-needle aspiration for histopathology and culture.

sections.title: Functions of the Spleen
blocks: 1. Reservoir: Normally stores ~25 mL of blood.
2. Hematopoiesis: Active site of RBC production during the 1st 3–6 months of fetal life; resumes extramedullary hematopoiesis in chronic severe hemolytic anemias (Thalassemia) or myelofibrosis.
3. Storage: Stores Factor VIII and up to one-third of body platelets (released during stress or epinephrine stimulation).
4. Filtration & Culling: Filters blood, removing old, rigid, damaged, or antibody-coated RBCs.

5. Immunological Defense: Key site of specific antibody synthesis (e.g., in ITP), production of immunoglobulins and properdin, phagocytosis, and trapping/destroying encapsulated bacteria and intra-erythrocytic parasites (malaria).

sections.title: Clinical Splenomegaly
blocks: Spleen must enlarge 2 to 3 times its normal size before becoming clinically palpable.
Soft, palpable splenic tips occur in 15% of healthy neonates, 10% of infants, and 5% of healthy adolescents.
Detection Methods: Physical examination via abdominal palpation; confirmed by Abdominal Ultrasonography, CT scan, or Technetium-99m sulfur colloid scan.
Grade 1: Palpable only on deep inspiration.
Grade 2: Palpable below the costal margin, extending up to halfway to the umbilicus along the mid-clavicular line.
Grade 3: Spleen extends towards the umbilicus.
Grade 4: Spleen extends past the umbilicus (halfway between umbilicus and symphysis pubis).
Grade 5: Massive splenomegaly extending down towards the symphysis pubis.

sections.title: Causes of Splenomegaly
blocks: Bacterial: Typhoid fever, infective endocarditis, bacterial sepsis.
Protozoal / Parasitic: Malaria, Toxoplasmosis, Visceral Leishmaniasis, Schistosomiasis.
Hematological: Congenital and acquired hemolytic anemias (Spherocytosis, Thalassemia, Sickle Cell Disease), extramedullary hematopoiesis (Osteopetrosis, Myelofibrosis).
Neoplasms: Benign (hemangiomas); Malignant (Acute/Chronic Leukemias, Hodgkin & Non-Hodgkin Lymphomas, Histiocytosis).
Metabolic / Storage Diseases: Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, Mucopolysaccharidoses.
Congestive: Portal hypertension (hepatic cirrhosis, extrahepatic portal vein thrombosis, splenic vein obstruction), Congestive Heart Failure.
Cysts: Congenital or post-traumatic false cysts.

sections.title: Hypersplenism
blocks: 1. Increased splenic destruction and sequestration of circulating blood cells.
2. Peripheral blood cytopenia involving one or more cell lines (anemia, leukopenia, or
3. Compensatory hypercellular bone marrow responding to the specific cytopenia.

sections.title: Splenectomy
blocks: Indications: Traumatic or non-traumatic splenic rupture, severe hereditary spherocytosis, refractory immunocytopenias (severe ITP), metabolic storage disease, or secondary hypersplenism.

Post-Splenectomy Complications & Risks: High risk of Overwhelming Post - Splenectomy Sepsis (OPSS) / fulminant bacteremia caused by encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b); increased severity of malaria; post-operative reactive thrombocytosis and leukocytosis.
Avoid splenectomy before 5 years of age whenever possible.
Pre-operative immunization against S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and Hib administered at least 2 weeks prior to elective surgery.
Long-term daily oral Penicillin V (250 mg twice daily) post-operatively.

sections.title: Hemostasis
blocks: The spontaneous physiological arrest of bleeding from a injured blood vessel through complex, coordinated vascular, platelet, and plasma factors.
Immediate reflex local vasoconstriction of the damaged blood vessel, mediated by von Willebrand factor (vWF), endothelin, and thromboxane A2.
2. Stage II: Formation of Temporary Hemostatic Plug (Primary Hemostasis):
Platelet Adhesion & Activation: Platelets adhere to exposed subendothelial collagen via vWF binding to glycoprotein Ib/IX receptors.
Platelet Aggregation: Platelets change shape, release dense/alpha granules (ADP, thromboxane), and aggregate via fibrinogen binding to GP IIb/IIIa receptors.
Plug Formation: Creates a primary platelet plug to transiently stop microvascular bleeding.
3. Stage III: Clot Formation (Secondary Hemostasis / Coagulation Cascade):
Sequential activation of plasma clotting factors culminating in the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to an insoluble fibrin clot meshwork.
Factor IX: Christmas Factor / Plasma Thromboplastin Component (PTC)
Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency (X-linked recessive).
Hemophilia B: Factor IX deficiency (X-linked recessive).
Hemophilia C: Factor XI deficiency (Autosomal recessive).
von Willebrand Disease (vW D): Deficiency or qualitative defect of vWF (Autosomal dominant/recessive).
Other Factor Deficiencies: Congenital deficiencies of Factors V (Parahemophilia), VII, X, XII, or XIII.
Vitamin K Deficiency: Impairs synthesis of functional factors II, VII, IX, and X (e.g., Hemorrhagic Disease of the Newborn [HDN], obstructive jaundice, malabsorption).
Severe Parenchymal Liver Disease: Impaired synthesis of all coagulation factors except Factor VIII.

sections.title: Approach to Bleeding Disorders
blocks: Plasma coagulation factor deficiencies manifest early in life (e.g., persistent umbilical stump bleeding, severe intramuscular hematomas following immunizations, or prolonged bleeding after neonatal circumcision).
Vascular and platelet disorders (purpuras) tend to present later in childhood.
Hemophilia A and B occur almost exclusively in males (X-linked recessive).
von Willebrand disease affects males and females equally (autosomal inheritance).
3. Family History: A positive family history of sex-linked or autosomal bleeding confirms an inherited plasma coagulation defect.
Platelet / Vascular Disorders: Spontaneous appearance of petechiae, superficial mucous membrane bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding), or small multiple ecchymoses.
Coagulation Disorders: Deep tissue bleeding, extensive spreading subcutaneous hematomas, or intra-articular bleeding (hemarthrosis).
5. Menstrual History: Menorrhagia in adolescent females strongly suggests von Willebrand disease or platelet dysfunction.
Petechiae: Pinpoint (1–2 mm) non-blanching hemorrhagic macules in skin or mucous membranes; pathognomonic for thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, or vasculitis.
Purpura: Larger purpuric skin hemorrhages (>2 mm); observed in platelet disorders and allergic/infectious vasculitis (e.g., HSP).
Ecchymosis: Subcutaneous extravasation of blood (>1 cm); small multiple ecchymoses occur in purpura, whereas large, spreading, painful ecchymoses signify plasma coagulation factor deficiencies.
Hematoma: Palpable collection of blood within muscle or soft tissue (>1 cm); classic feature of coagulation factor deficiencies.
Hemarthrosis: Extravasation of blood into joint spaces (knees, ankles, elbows); hallmark sign of severe Hemophilia A or B.
Systemic Disease Screening: Always exclude systemic etiologies presenting with bleeding diathesis, such as acute leukemia, DIC, aplastic anemia, meningococcemia, or severe sepsis.
Bleeding Time (BT) (Normal: 4 to 8 minutes): Evaluates primary hemostasis (vascular response and platelet function).
Clotting Time (CT) (Normal: 3 to 6 minutes): Evaluates intrinsic and common secondary coagulation pathways.
CBC & Peripheral Blood Film: Excludes pancytopenia, acute leukemia, or DIC.
Prolonged Bleeding Time (BT) WITH Low Platelet Count:
Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), drug-induced thrombocytopenia, acute leukemia, aplastic anemia, or DIC.
Prolonged Bleeding Time (BT) WITH Normal Platelet Count:
von Willebrand Disease (vWD), Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), or functional qualitative platelet defects (thrombasthenia).
Prolonged Clotting Time (CT) WITH Normal BT & Platelets:
Plasma coagulation factor deficiencies (Hemophilia A, B, or C), Vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, or DIC.
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) (Normal: 20 to 45 seconds): Measures factors in the intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and common pathways.
Isolated Prolonged APTT: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII), Hemophilia B (Factor IX), Hemophilia C (Factor XI), von Willebrand Disease, or Factor XII deficiency.
Prothrombin Time (PT) (Normal: 10 to 13 seconds): Measures factors in the extrinsic (Factor VII) and common pathways.
Isolated Prolonged PT: Congenital Factor VII deficiency.
Acquired disorders affecting common pathway factors (Vitamin K deficiency, severe chronic liver disease, DIC, or congenital deficiencies of Factors V, X, II, or I).
Thrombin Time (TT) (Normal: 11 to 15 seconds): Evaluates conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin; prolonged in hypofibrinogenemia, dysfibrinogenemia, or in the presence of heparin.

sections.title: Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura
blocks: Definition: An immune-mediated thrombocytopenic purpura caused by autoantibodies directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins.

Acute ITP: Most common form in children (peak incidence at 1 to 4 years of age); typically follows 1 to 4 weeks after a viral infection. Spontaneous recovery occurs within 6 months in 70% to 80% of cases.
Chronic ITP: Persistent thrombocytopenia lasting longer than 6 months (occurs in 10% to 20% of cases); more common in females and older children/adults, usually without a preceding viral illness.
Caused by autoantibodies that bind to antigens on the platelet membrane.
These antibody-coated platelets bind to Fc receptors on macrophages in the spleen, where they are ingested and prematurely destroyed.
Sudden appearance of generalized petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses in a child who was recently healthy.
Mucocutaneous bleeding from the gums and nose (epistaxis).
Splenomegaly is rare; the presence of significant splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, or lymphadenopathy strongly suggests an alternative diagnosis (such as leukemia).
Less than 1% of children develop severe intracranial hemorrhage.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Severe isolated thrombocytopenia (often <20,000/μL).
Bone Marrow Examination: Performed to exclude aplastic anemia or leukemia before initiating steroid therapy; demonstrates increased megakaryocytes with normal myeloid and erythroid lineages.
Antinuclear Antibodies (ANA): May be positive in adolescent females with underlying autoimmune disease.
Asymptomatic / Mild (Platelets >20,000/μL): Observation ("wait and see") with avoidance of trauma.
1. Oral Prednisone: 1–2 mg/kg/day for 2 to 4 weeks until platelet count rises above 20,000/μL.
2. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (I VIG): Single dose of 1 g/kg; blocks Fc receptors on splenic macrophages to stop platelet destruction.
3. IV Anti-D Therapy: Administered to Rh-positive individuals at 50–75 μg/kg; binds Fc receptors via transient, mild hemolysis of Rh-D positive RBCs.
Splenectomy: Indicated for severe chronic ITP lasting longer than 1 year in children older than 4 years of age whose symptoms are not controlled by medical therapy.

sections.title: Hemophilia
blocks: Congenital bleeding disorders caused by inherited deficiencies of specific plasma coagulation factors.
Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency; inherited as an X-linked recessive trait (sufferers are males, females are carriers). Represents the most common severe inherited coagulation disorder in males.
Hemophilia B (Christmas Disease): Factor IX deficiency; inherited as an X- linked recessive trait.
Hemophilia C: Factor XI deficiency; inherited as an incomplete autosomal recessive trait affecting both males and females equally.
Factors VIII and IX are required to activate Factor X, which generates thrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin.
Deficiency causes a slowing of the rate of clot formation and produces a weak clot (patients do not bleed faster, but bleed for a prolonged duration).
C. Grading of Severity (Based on Clotting Factor Levels)
Severe Hemophilia: Factor level (< 1%) of normal (causes spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles).
Moderate Hemophilia: Factor level (1% to 5%) of normal (bleeding follows mild trauma).
Mild Hemophilia: Factor level (> 5% to 30%) of normal (bleeding follows major trauma or surgery).

Clotting factors do not cross the placenta, but neonates may be asymptomatic at birth unless challenged by procedures (e.g., severe bleeding following neonatal circumcision or intracranial hemorrhage).
Easy bruising becomes apparent when the infant begins to crawl and walk.
Intramuscular Hematomas: Develop after minor trauma or IM injections.
Hemarthrosis (Hallmark Sign): Spontaneous or post-traumatic bleeding into joint spaces (most commonly affecting ankles, knees, and elbows). Recurrent hemarthrosis can cause permanent joint damage.
Life-Threatening Bleeding: Hemorrhage into critical anatomic sites, such as the CNS, upper airway (sublingual/neck hematomas), GI tract, or iliopsoas muscle.
Prolonged bleeding following minor dental procedures or tonsillectomy.
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT): Characteristically prolonged.
Normal Screening Parameters: Platelet count, Bleeding Time (BT), Prothrombin Time (PT), and Thrombin Time (TT) are all normal.
Mixing Studies: Mixing patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma corrects the prolonged APTT.
Specific Factor Assays: Quantitative measurement of Factor VIII or Factor IX activity confirms the specific diagnosis and severity.
Bethesda Assay: Quantitative assay to detect specific factor inhibitors (antibodies) against Factor VIII or IX.

Replacement Therapy (Mainstay): Administer factor concentrates to raise plasma levels to 35–40 U/dL for mild/moderate bleeding, and to 100 U/dL for major, life - threatening hemorrhages or head trauma.

Factor VIII Replacement: Recombinant Factor VIII concentrate (e.g., octocog alfa), Cryoprecipitate (contains Factor VIII, vWF, and fibrinogen), or Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP; 1 unit contains ~200 units of Factor VIII/IX).
Factor IX Replacement: Recombinant Factor IX concentrate (e.g., nonacog alfa) or Fresh Frozen Plasma.
Antenatal Diagnosis: Fetal blood Factor VI IIc assay at 18–20 weeks gestation, amniocentesis for DNA probes, or Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS).

sections.title: von Willebrand Disease
blocks: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of von Willebrand Factor (vWF).
The vWF gene is located on chromosome 12. Transmitted predominantly as an autosomal dominant trait (affecting males and females equally), though autosomal recessive types exist.
B. Functions of von Willebrand Factor (vWF)
1. Promotes platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen via glycoprotein
2. Acts as a stabilization carrier protein for Factor VIII in plasma.
Type I (70% of cases): Autosomal dominant; partial quantitative reduction of vWF.
Type II (25% of cases): Qualitative structural/functional abnormality of vWF.
Type III: Autosomal recessive; severe form characterized by complete absence of vWF.
Spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding: recurrent epistaxis, gingival bleeding.
Excessive bleeding from superficial cutaneous wounds and surgical procedures.
Joint bleeding (hemarthrosis) is uncommon (unlike hemophilia), except in severe Type III disease.
Bleeding Time (BT): Prolonged (with a normal platelet count).
APTT: Prolonged (secondary to decreased Factor VIII carrier activity).
vWF Assays: Reduced plasma vWF level, reduced Ristocetin Cofactor Activity, and low Factor VIII coagulant activity.
DDAVP (Desmopressin): Treatment of choice for mild-to-moderate Type I vWD; stimulates the release of stored vWF and Factor VIII from endothelial cells.
vWF Concentrates (e.g., Humate-P): Indicated for severe vWD (Type II and Type III) or non-responders to DDAVP.
Antifibrinolytic Therapy: Epsilon Amino Caproic Acid (EACA) or Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding.

sections.title: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulopathy
blocks: An acquired thrombohemorr hagic syndrome characterized by systemic activation of the coagulation cascade in microvessels, leading to microthrombi formation, consumption of platelets and clotting factors, and severe multiorgan bleeding.
1. Release of tissue factor / thromboplastic substances into the circulation (massive trauma, severe sepsis).
2. Widespread direct injury to vascular endothelial cells.
Microvascular Thrombosis: Microthrombi occlude small v essels, causing tissue ischemia and acute organ failure.
Consumptive Coagulopathy: Depletion of platelets, fibrinogen, and plasma clotting factors causes diffuse multiorgan hemorrhage.
Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia: Mechanical fragmentation of circulating RBCs as they squeeze through fibrin-occluded microvessels.
Extensive tissue injury: crush injuries, major fractures, severe thermal burns.
Venoms and toxins: poisonous snake bites.
Neonatal triggers: severe perinatal asphyxia, neonatal sepsis.
Purpura fulminans and severe systemic vasculitis.
Spontaneous Bleeding: Generalized purpura, ecchymoses, petechiae, oozing from venipuncture/wound sites, epistaxis, gum bleeding, hematuria, and GI bleeding.
Thromboembolic / Ischemic Features: Acute renal failure (oliguria, hematuria), respiratory distress (ARDS, cyanosis), seizures, altered consciousness, and peripheral gangrene (purpura fulminans).
Coagulation Profile: Prolonged PT, APTT, and Thrombin Time (TT).
Fibrin Degradation Products (FDPs) / D-Dimer: Markedly increased.
Peripheral Blood Film: Demonstrates fragmented RBCs (schistocytes).
1. Treat the Underlying Cause: Primary focus (e.g., IV antibiotics for sepsis, debridement, fluid resuscitation).
2. Correct Aggravating Factors: Treat hypoxia, metabolic acidosis (Sodium Bicarbonate), and electrolyte imbalances.
Packed RBCs: To correct severe anemia.
Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): To replenish depleted plasma coagulation factors.
Platelet Transfusions: To correct severe consumptive thrombocytopenia.
Hydrocortisone: Administered for purpura fulminans or meningococcemia.
4. Anticoagulant Therapy (Heparin): Controversial; strictly reserved for cases dominated by severe thromboembolic complications (e.g., purpura fulminans).

sections.title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)
blocks: A malignant neoplasm of hematopoietic stem cells characterized by the clonal proliferation and expansion of immature white blood cells (lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow, blood, and extramedullary tissues.
Represents 25% of all childhood cancers and 75% of all childhood leukemias.
Genetic Factors: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Fanconi anemia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
Environmental & Viral: Ionizing radiation, drugs, viral infections (e.g., EBV), advanced maternal age.
L1: Small, uniform blasts (most common in childhood; ~85% of cases).
L3: Burkitt-type blasts with prominent cytoplasmic vacuolation.
WHO Classification: Categorizes ALL into precursor B-cell ALL and T-cell ALL based on genetic and immunophenotypic markers.
Early Features: Anorexia, fatigue, irritability, low-grade intermittent fever, and a history of a preceding upper respiratory tract infection 1 to 2 months prior.
Marrow Failure Features (Replacement of Normal Hematopoiesis):
Neutropenia: Recurrent, persistent, or severe infections and fever.
Thrombocytopenia: Petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and mucosal bleeding.
Musculoskeletal: Bone and joint pain (frequently causes a limp or refusal to walk).
CNS Infiltration: Symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure (headache, vomiting, papilledema), neck stiffness, and cranial nerve palsies.
Other Sites: Testicular swelling (painless mass), mediastinal mass (T-cell ALL), renal, skin, or cardiac involvement.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): Anemia, thrombocytopenia, and a variable WBC count (may be leukopenic, normal, or markedly elevated >50,000/μL).
Peripheral Blood Smear (PBS): Demonstrates circulating atypical lymphoblasts and immature WBCs.
Bone Marrow Examination (Gold Standard): (>25%) leukemic lymphoblasts in the marrow is diagnostic.
CSF Examination: Presence of single or multiple leukemic blasts confirms CNS involvement.
Radiology: Chest X-ray to detect mediastinal mass.
Metabolic Studies: Elevated blood uric acid, altered serum electrolytes, and elevated serum phosphate (risk of Tumor Lysis Syndrome).
Initial WBC count (< 50,000/μL) (single most important prognostic factor).
Rapid early clinical response to induction chemotherapy.
Presence of a mediastinal mass or CNS involvement at presentation.
Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): Gingival infiltration, subcutaneous "blueberry muffin" nodules, discrete masses, or features of DIC strongly suggest AML.
Infectious Mononucleosis, Aplastic Anemia, Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP), Pertussis, Acute Infectious Lymphocytosis, Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA), Myelofibrosis, and Neuroblastoma.
Remission Induction (4 to 6 weeks): Prednisolone (or Dexamethasone), Vincristine, and Pegaspargase (L-asparaginase).
CNS Prophylaxis: Intrathecal chemotherapy using Methotrexate.
Consolidation (Intensification Phase): High-dose multidrug therapy administered shortly after induction to eliminate residual subclinical disease.
Maintenance Phase: Long-term daily oral 6-Mercaptopurine (6-MP) and weekly oral Methotrexate for 2 to 3 years.
2. Supportive Care: Transfusions, infection control, metabolic management.
3. Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplantation (BMT): Indicated for high-risk ALL or relapsed disease.

sections.title: Hodgkin's Disease
blocks: Definition: A malignancy of lymphoid tissue arising from activated B or T lymphocytes.
Initially spreads to adjacent lymph nodes.
Hematogenous spread can involve the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and brain.
The Reed-Sternberg cell is considered the hallmark of Hodgkin's disease, and positivity for CD15 and CD30 is diagnostic.
Childhood form typically affects children < 14 years of age.
Characterized by progressive, painless enlargement of lymph nodes.
Systemic ("B") Symptoms: Unexplained fever, night sweats, and significant weight loss (> 10% of body weight).
Rare Features: Signs of airway obstruction, pleural or pericardial effusion, liver dysfunction, and features of bone marrow infiltration.
Chest X-ray and CT scan to evaluate for mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR).
Histopathological identification of CD15/CD30-positive Reed-Sternberg cells.
Ultrasound of the thorax and abdomen.
Treatment: Combination chemotherapy and radiation therapy.

sections.title: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
blocks: Definition: A malignant clonal proliferation of T or B lymphocytes.
Classification: Classified according to WHO 2016 guidelines (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma).
Age & Gender: Peak incidence between 5 and 15 years of age, with a strong male predominance (M:F ratio = 3:1).
Typically presents with extranodal disease involving the mediastinum, abdomen, or head and neck region.
Laboratory tests: CBC, Kidney Function Tests (KFTs), Liver Function Tests (LFTs), serum electrolytes, and Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
Imaging: Chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, and CT scan.
T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma is treated according to Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) protocols.

sections.title: Brain Tumors
blocks: Overview: Brain tumors represent the second most common malignancy during childhood and adolescence.
Etiology & Risk Factors: Etiology is largely unknown. Identified risk factors include familial and genetic associations, occupational exposures, postnatal irradiation, and viral exposures.

sections.title: Neuroblastoma
blocks: Definition: An embryonal cancer of the peripheral sympat hetic nervous system. It is unique in its ability to undergo spontaneous regression and maturation.
Age: Occurs in children 1 to 6 years of age, with a median age of 2 years.
Signs and symptoms depend on the site of the primary tumor and metastatic spread.
Primary Sites: Abdominal mass, thoracic mass, or pelvic mass (which presents as bowel and bladder dysfunction).
Nonspecific Features: Intermittent fever, weight loss, and generalized pain.
Catecholamine Metabolic Effects: Bouts of profuse sweating, pallor, diarrhea, and hypertension due to high circulating catecholamine levels.
Biopsy of primary mass or metastatic tissue.
Elevated urine catecholamine metabolites: Vanillylmandelic Acid (VMA) and Homovanillic Acid (HVA).
Demonstration of neuroblasts in bone marrow aspirate/biopsy.
CT or MRI demonstrating mass calcification (a key feature distinguishing it from Wilms' tumor).
Treatment: Surgical resection, radiation therapy, and systemic chemotherapy.

sections.title: Wilm's Tumor (Nephroblastoma)
blocks: Definition: A mixed embryonal neoplasm of the kidney. It is the second most common abdominal tumor in pediatric patients.
Age: Peak incidence between 2 and 5 years of age.
Etiology: Familial forms show an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern associated with mutations in the Wilms' tumor suppressor gene.
Asymptomatic abdominal mass bulging in the flanks.
Gross or microscopic hematuria and hypertension occur in > 5% of cases.
Nonspecific symptoms: fever, malaise, constipation, and anorexia.
Physical Examination: Reveals a smooth, non-tender, firm abdominal mass.
Metastasis: Spreads hematogenously, primarily to the lungs (85%) and liver (7%).
Differential Diagnosis: Neuroblastoma, hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney disease, and lymphoma.
Laboratory & Imaging Investigations: Complete blood count, urinalysis, abdominal ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, and biopsy.
Management: Multimodal therapy combining surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy.

sections.title: Retinoblastoma
blocks: Definition: A malignant tumor of the embryonic neural retina.
Age: Occurs in early childhood before 4 years of age, with a median age of 2 years.
Common Presenting Signs: Leukokoria ("cat's eye reflex" / abnormal white pupillary reflex) and squint (strabismus).
Rare Presenting Signs: Orbital inflammation, hyphema, fixed pupil, heterochromia iridis, and poor vision.
CT and MRI of the orbit and brain.
Bone marrow examination, lumbar puncture (CSF analysis), and bone scan.
Focal Therapies: Transpupillary thermal therapy, laser therapy, and cryotherapy.
Enucleation (surgical removal of the eye) when conservative therapies fail.

sections.title: Hematuria
blocks: Definition: Persistent presence of more than 5 red blood cells (RBCs) per high-power field (HPF) in centrifuged urine.
Isolated Renal Diseases: IgA nephropathy, Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis), thin glomerular basement membrane nephropathy, and postinfectious glomerulonephritis.
Multisystem Diseases: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) nephritis, Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP) nephritis, polyarteritis nodosa, Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS), and sickle cell glomerulopathy.

Extraglomerular Causes: Pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis, acute tubular necrosis, vascular disorders, thrombocytopenia, polycystic kidney disease, hydronephrosis, and tumors (e.g., Wilms' tumor).
Lower Urinary Tract Disorders: Inflammation (infectious and noninfectious cystitis or urethritis), urolithiasis, and trauma.
Glomerular Hematuria: Characterized by brown/tea-colored urine, significant proteinuria, RBC casts, and dysmorphic RBCs.

Workup: CBC with differential, serum electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca⁺⁺), BUN, serum creatinine, serum protein/albumin, cholesterol, complement levels (C3/C4), ANA, ASO/Anti-DNAse B titers, and spot urine protein/creatinine ratio.
Step II: Urine calcium/creatinine ratio, renal ultrasonography, and CT urogram.

Step III: Serum electrolytes. If crystalluria is present, evaluate for urolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis with 24-hour urine collection for calcium, creatinine, uric acid, and oxalate. If hydronephrosis is present, obtain a cystogram, renal scan, or voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG).

sections.title: Proteinuria
blocks: Normal protein excretion in healthy children is < 150 mg/day or < 4 mg/m²/hr.
Abnormal protein excretion is 4 to 40 mg/m²/hr.
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is defined as > 40 mg/m²/hr or > 50 mg/kg/day.
Glomerular Proteinuria: Disruption of the glomerular capillary wall barrier.
Tubular Proteinuria: Tubular injury or dysfunction leading to ineffective reabsorption of low-molecular-weight proteins.
Increased Production of Plasma Proteins: Overproduction overwhelms proximal tubular reabsorptive capacity (e.g., rhabdomyolysis).
Dipstick Testing: Reported as Negative, Trace (10–29 mg/dL), 1+ (30–100 mg/dL), 2+ (100–300 mg/dL), 3+ (300–1000 mg/dL), or 4+ (> 1000 mg/dL).
Spot Urine Protein/Creatinine Ratio: Preferably measured on a first morning void (a ratio > 0.2 mg/mg is abnormal in children).
Transient Proteinuria: Triggered by fever, strenuous exercise, dehydration, cold exposure, congestive heart failure, seizures, or acute stress.
Postural (Orthostatic) Proteinuria: Proteinuria present only in the upright position and absent when supine; benign condition common in adolescents.
Glomerular Diseases (Isolated Proteinuria): Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome, secondary nephrotic syndrome, renal amyloidosis, diabetic nephropathy, and sickle cell nephropathy.
Glomerular Diseases (Prominent Proteinuria): Acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, HSP nephritis, lupus nephritis, serum sickness, and Alport syndrome.

Tubular Diseases: Cystinosis, Fanconi syndrome, Wilson disease, reflux nephropathy, drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, penicillamine, lithium, cyclosporine), and heavy metal exposure (lead, gold, mercury).

sections.title: Nephrotic Syndrome
blocks: Definition: A clinical manifestation of glomerular disease characterized by heavy (nephrotic-range) proteinuria.
Primary Causes: Idiopathic Nephrotic Syndrome and Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome.
Infections: Endocarditis, Hepatitis B and C, HIV, Infectious Mononucleosis, CMV, and Malaria.
Drugs: Captopril, penicillamine, gold, lithium, and NSAIDs.
Role of the Podocyte: Podocyte injury or genetic mutations in genes coding for podocyte structural proteins lead directly to nephrotic-range proteinuria.

Role of the Immune System: Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS) often follows viral infections or allergen exposure, and dramatic response to immunosuppression supports an immune-mediated pathogenesis.

1. Edema Formation: Urinary protein loss causes hypoalbuminemia, which lowers plasma oncotic pressure. Fluid transudates into the interstitial space, triggering activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) to increase tubular Na⁺ reabsorption and stimulating ADH release to increase water retention.
2. Hyperlipidemia: Resulting from increased compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis combined with decreased clearance due to urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase enzyme.

3. Increased Susceptibility to Infections: Driven by hypogammaglobulinemia (urinary loss of IgG), defects in the alternative complement cascade (urinary loss of complement factors), and the use of immunosuppressive drugs.
4. Hypercoagulability: Caused by vascular stasis, increased hepatic production of fibrinogen, and urinary losses of natural antithrombotic factors such as antithrombin III and proteinS.
Here is a detailed, source-grounded breakdown of every element from Idiopathic Nephrotic

Syndrome in Chapter 15 (Nephrology), through Short Stature in Chapter 16 (The Endocrine System), and concluding with Microcephaly in Chapter 17 (The Nervous System), stopping right before Cerebral Palsy:
Incidence: Represents 90% of all cases of nephrotic syndrome in children.
Age: Peaks between 2 and 6 years of age (ranges from 6 months to childhood).

Generalized Edema (Anasarca): Initially presents as mild periorbital edema around the eyes and in lower extremities, progressing over time to generalized edema with ascites, pleural effusion, and scrotal/labial edema.
Systemic Symptoms: Anorexia, irritability, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
Atypical Signs: Hypertension and hematuria are rare.
Serum complement levels (C3 and C4): Characteristically normal.
General Measures: Dietary salt restriction, high-protein diet, and low-fat diet.
Steroid Induction Therapy: Oral Prednisone or Prednisolone at 60 mg/m²/day or 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 60 mg daily) for 4 to 6 weeks.
Steroid Maintenance Therapy: Alternate-day Prednisone at 40 mg/m² or 1.5 mg/kg as a single daily dose for 4 to 6 weeks, followed by gradual tapering over 2 to 5 months.
Intravenous Albumin & Diuretics: Administer IV 25% Albumin (0.5–1.0 g/kg) as a slow infusion followed by IV Furosemide (1–2 mg/kg/dose) for severe symptomatic edema.
Remission: Urine protein is negative or trace for 3 consecutive days.
Relapse: Urine protein ≥ 3+ by dipstick for 3 consecutive days.
Frequent Relapses: 2 or more relapses in 6 months of initial response, or 4 relapses in any 12-month period.
Steroid D ependence: Occurrence of 2 consecutive relapses during steroid therapy or within 2 weeks of stopping steroids.
Steroid Resistance: Failure to achieve remission after 4 weeks of daily oral prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day.
Management of Relapse, Frequent Relapses, & Steroid Dependence:
Alternative immunosuppressive agents include: Cyclophosphamide, Levamisole, Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF), Rituximab, Cyclosporine, and Tacrolimus.
Infections: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP) is the most common serious complication (Streptococcus pneumoniae is the primary pathogen; E. coli may also occur).
Thromboembolic Events: Both arterial and venous thromboses occur secondary to hypercoagulability.
Iatrogenic: Complications from long-term medication use (steroid toxicity).
Prognosis: Excellent overall prognosis, although the majority of patients experience relapses extending into the second decade of life.

sections.title: Introduction
blocks: Intracranial Component: Formed of 2 cerebral hemispheres (frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes connected by the corpus callosum and cerebral peduncles), brain stem (midbrain, pons, and medulla), and cerebellum.
Spinal Component: Spinal cord and cauda equina.
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Anterior horn cells, peripheral nerves, motor end plates, and muscles or glands.

sections.title: Macrocephaly and Hydrocephalus
blocks: Definition: Head circumference measuring above the 97th percentile for age and sex.
Growth rate: 2 cm/month (1st 3 months), 1 cm/month (4–6 months), 0.5 cm/month (6–12 months).
Causes of Macrocephaly: Familial large head, Rickets, Chronic hemolytic anemia, Cretinism, Osteogenesis imperfecta, Achondroplasia, Hydrocephalus, Hydranencephaly, and Megalencephaly.
Causes of Increased Intracranial Pressure (ICT): Brain tumor, Mass (tuberculoma), Chronic brain abscess, and Intracranial hemorrhage.
Definition: Dilatation of the ventricular system due to either obstruction of CSF flow within the ventricular system or interference with its absorption in the subarachnoid space.
Secretion: Secreted by choroid plexus in lateral ventricles → Foramina of Monro → 3rd ventricle → Aqueduct of Sylvius → 4th ventricle → Foramina of Luschka and Magendie → Subarachnoid space.
Reabsorption: Reabsorbed into venous sinus circulation from the subarachnoid space via arachnoid villi.

Congenital: Congenital absence of foramina of Monro, Aqueductal stenosis, Vein of Galen malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation (membrane at 4th ventricle outlet with cystic expansion compressing the cerebellum).
Impaired Absorption: Arnold-Chiari malformation (downward displacement of medulla and cerebellum into cervical canal usually with meningomyelocele), Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Post-meningitic gliosis.

In Infants (before suture closure): Progressive increase in all skull diameters, thin shiny scalp skin with prominent dilated veins, widely open/tense/bulging anterior fontanel, widely separated sutures, Macewen's sign ("cracked-pot" sound) on percussion, craniotabes, "Sunset eye" sign (sclera visible above iris with downward globe displacement), associated meningocele or meningomyelocele, limb spasticity, hyperreflexia, 6th cranial nerve palsy, optic atrophy, and convulsions.
In Older Children (af ter suture closure): Head enlargement is less marked; presents with prominent signs of increased ICT (headache, vomiting, papilledema) and focal long-tract motor deficits.
Serial head circumference measurements and fundoscopy.
Skull X-Ray: Wide suture separation in infants; "silver-beaten" / "copper - beaten" appearance in older children.
CT or MRI Scan (Most Important): Assesses degree of ventricular dilatation, identifies site of obstruction, and excludes brain tumors.
Medical Management: Acetazolamide and Furosemide (to reduce CSF production).
Surgical Intervention: Placement of a Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) Shunt.

sections.title: Microcephaly
blocks: Definition: Head circumference measuring more than 3 standard deviations (SD) below the mean for age and sex.
1. Familial Autosomal Recessive (AR): Severe mental retardation, seizures, slanted forehead, prominent nose and ears.
2. Autosomal Dominant (AD): Mild mental retardation, seizures, mild slanted forehead, prominent ears.
3. Chromosomal Syndromes: Down syndrome, Edward syndrome.
4. Drugs / Toxins: Fetal alcohol syndrome, fetal hydantoin syndrome.
History: Family history of CNS diseases, history of repeated abortions.
Physical Exam: Serial head circumference measurements of the child and both parents.
Investigations: Maternal serum phenylalanine level (if cause is unknown), Karyotyping, Brain imaging (CT or MRI), Fasting serum and urine amino acid analysis, TORCH screen.
2. Appropriate educational and developmental support for mental retardation.

sections.title: Cerebral Palsy
blocks: Definition: A group of disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive (static), non-hereditary lesion in the developing brain. Although the underlying brain damage is static, the clinical symptoms can evolve or worsen with growth (e.g., increasing spasticity).
Associated Impairments: Epilepsy, visual and hearing impairments, speech/language difficulties, behavioral problems, and learning disabilities/intellectual delay.
Intrauterine / Prenatal: Intrauterine hypoxic-ischemic injury, intrauterine infections, and chromosomal disorders.
Perinatal (10%): Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE), intracranial hemorrhage, and bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus).
Postnatal (10%): Meningitis, encephalitis, trauma, and stroke.
Preterm Risk: Highly prevalent in preterm infants primarily due to intracerebral hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia (PVL).
1. Spastic CP (Most common): Initial hypotonia in infancy progresses to spasticity:
Spastic Diplegia: Bilateral spasticity predominantly affecting the lower limbs (legs > arms; commonly associated with PVL).
Spastic Quadriplegia: The most severe form, affecting all four extremities (commonly secondary to severe birth asphyxia).
Spastic Hemiplegia: Unilateral motor involvement (arm > leg; usually secondary to intrauterine or neonatal stroke).
2. Extrapyramidal (Choreo-Athetoid CP): Characterized by persistent hypotonia, involuntary movements, and poor head control (secondary to severe asphyxia or kernicterus).
3. Ataxic CP: Rare form marked by impaired balance, tremors, and incoordination.
4. Mixed CP: Combination of multiple types (most commonly spastic-dyskinesic CP).

Delay in reaching motor milestones, abnormal gait (e.g., toe walking, scissoring, or wide-based gait), feeding/swallowin g difficulties, persistent primitive neonatal reflexes, and abnormal muscle tone.
Differential Diagnosis: Degenerative brain diseases, metabolic disorders, spinal cord tumors, and muscular dystrophies.
Cranial ultrasound (in neonates) and brain MRI.
Comprehensive hearing, visual, genetic, and metabolic screening.
Multidisciplinary Team: Pediatricians, physical/occupational therapists, speech pathologists, educators, and psychologists.
Parental Guidance: Instruction on proper carrying, feeding, dressing, and bathing techniques to counteract abnormal muscle tone.
Pharmacotherapy for Spasticity: Oral Dantrolene sodium, Benzodiazepines, Baclofen, and local Botulinum toxin injections for focal muscle spasticity.

sections.title: Inborn Errors of Metabolism: Definition & Approach
blocks: Definition: A group of hereditary biochemical disorders caused by single-gene mutations encoding specific enzymes, transport proteins, or structural proteins.
1. Unexplained mental retardation, developmental delay, motor deficits, convulsions, or failure to thrive (FTT).
2. Unusual body or urine odor (especially during acute illness).
3. Intermittent unexplained vomiting, metabolic acidosis, or coma.
5. Renal calculi or abnormal ocular signs (e.g., cataracts).
Initial Screening: Blood glucose, serum ammonia, arterial blood gases/bicarbonate, and pH.
Urine Screen: Urinary glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) for Mucopolysaccharidoses.
Neuro/Electrophysiology & Imaging: Brain MRI, EEG, electromyography (EMG), and CSF analysis.
Definitive Tests: Tissue biopsy for direct enzyme assays and molecular genetic testing.
Newborn Screening: Tandem Mass Spectrometry (TMS) screening for congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, galactosemia, homocystinuria, and Maple Syrup Urine Disease.
Dietary restriction of offending precursors (e.g., phenylalanine-free diet in PKU).
Dietary supplementation (e.g., cornstarch to prevent hypoglycemia in Glycogen Storage Diseases).
Administration of binding/chelating agents (e.g., sodium benzoate for hyperammonemia in urea cycle defects, D-penicillamine in Wilson's disease).
Organ transplantation or Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT).
Supportive therapies: High-caloric non-protein nutrition, speech therapy, physiotherapy, and genetic counseling.

sections.title: Examples
blocks: Etiology: Autosomal recessive; classical form caused by deficiency of galactose- 1-phosphate uridyltransferase.

Clinical Picture: Ingestion of milk sugars leads to accumulation of toxic metabolites causing cataracts, liver damage (hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice), renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), lower extremity/scrotal edema, and brain damage.
Diagnosis: Presence of reducing substances in urine; confirmed by direct erythrocyte enzyme assay.
Treatment: Complete elimination of galactose a nd lactose from the diet (using soy-based or casein-hydrolysate formulas).
2. Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia (Von Gierke Disease) (Carbohydrate Metabolism):

Clinical Picture: Severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, ketosis, massive hepatomegaly, doll-like facies, short stature, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia. (Type Ib includes neutropenia and recurrent infections).
Treatment: Frequent enteral cornstarch administration to maintain normoglycemia.
Etiology: Autosomal recessive; deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase.

Clinical Picture (Untreated): Severe mental retardation, acquired microcephaly, seizures, hypopigmentation (blond hair, blue eyes, fair skin), eczema, hyperreflexia/spasticity, and a characteristic "mousy" body odor.
Diagnosis: Mass newborn screening via tandem mass spectrometry; confirmed by elevated plasma phenylalanine levels (> 20 mg/dL).
4. Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) (Amino Acid Metabolism):
Etiology: Deficiency of branched-chain α-keto acid decarboxylase complex, impairing metabolism of leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
Clinical Picture: Acute neonatal encephalopathy, opisthotonos, severe metabolic acidosis, mental retardation, and a characteristic sweet/maple syrup odor of urine and sweat.
Clinical Picture: Huge splenomegaly, hepatomegaly with abdominal distension, short stature, wasting, and bone pain/crises.
Treatment: Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT with recombinant glucocerebrosidase), splenectomy, and bone marrow transplantation.

Clinical Picture: Coarse facial features (frontal bossing, hypertelorism, depressed nasal bridge, thickened tongue, gingival hypertrophy), cloudy/steamy cornea, hepatosplenomegaly, short stature, claw hands, joint stiffness, and severe mental retardation.

sections.title: Cardio-Pulmonary Arrest
blocks: Definition: A child who is unresponsive, pale or cyanotic, non-breathing or exhibiting abnormal/gasping breathing, with no palpable carotid or femoral pulse, and inaudible heart sounds or severe bradycardia.
Resuscitation Sequence (CPR): Divided into 3 successive stages:

sections.title: Basic Life Support
blocks: BLS consists of the CAB sequence: Circulation → Airway → Breathing.
Single Rescuer: Compress the lower third of the sternum with two fingers (one finger's breadth below the inter-nipple line).
Two or More Healthcare Rescuers: Use the two-thumbed encircling hands technique (thumbs placed one finger's breadth below the inter-nipple line, fingers encircling the chest and supporting the back).
Compression rate: 100/min; Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 15:2 (or 30:2 if single rescuer).
Compress the lower sternum using the heel of one hand (while the other hand maintains head position).
Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 30:2 for 1 rescuer; 15:2 for 2 rescuers.
Use the standard adult two-handed interlocked technique on the lower sternum.
Compression depth: 4–5 cm; Rate: 90/min; Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 30:2.

sections.title: Airway
blocks: Positioning: Place the child supine on a hard, flat surface; immobilize the cervical spine if trauma is suspected.
Head Tilt–Chin Lift: Used when no cervical spine injury is suspected (one hand tilts the forehead, index finger of the other hand lifts the chin/mandible).
Jaw Thrust: Used when cervical spine injury is suspected.
1. Deliver 5 Back Blows: Position infant prone along the rescuer's forearm/thigh with head lower than chest; deliver up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades.
2. Follow with 5 Chest Thrusts: Position infant supine; deliver up to 5 sharp sternal thrusts (similar to compressions, but sharper and slower at 20/min).
3. Contraindication: Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated in infants due to high risk of visceral organ damage.
1. Deliver 5 Back Blows followed by 5 Abdominal Thrusts (Heimlich Maneuver).
2. Conscious Child: Upright position; deliver up to 5 sharp upward thrusts directed toward the diaphragm.
3. Unconscious Child: Lay child supine; place the heel of one hand in the middle of the upper abdomen between the xiphoid and umbilicus, and deliver up to 5 sharp upward thrusts.

sections.title: Breathing
blocks: Assessment: Look for chest rise, listen and feel for expired air.
Infant: Rescuer's mouth covers both the infant's mouth and nose to create an airtight seal.
Child: Rescuer's mouth covers the child's mouth, while pinching the nose closed with the thumb and forefinger.
Select an appropriately sized mask covering mouth and nose.
Maintain the head in a slight extension ("sniffing position").
Form a tight seal with the thumb and index finger forming a " C" on the mask rim, while the remaining fingers lift the jaw forward ("E" position).
If breathing resumes, place the child in the recovery position.
If the child remains apneic after 2 effective rescue breaths, immediately resume combined chest compressions and ventilations.

sections.title: Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
blocks: PALS aims to restore spontaneous circulation by supporting the cardiovascular system and managing life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

3. Central venous access (femoral) is best achieved using the catheter-over-a- guidewire technique.

Can be repeated up to 3 times within 1 hour if needed.
